lessons.title: Parotid Gland

slides.p: The parotid is the largest salivary gland. It lies in the parotid bed, anteroinferior to the external ear, between the ramus of mandible and mastoid region. Its capsule is derived from the investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
slides.remember: Think: gland, bed, capsule, contents, duct.
slides.q: Which salivary gland is the largest?
slides.why: The parotid is the largest of the major salivary glands.

slides.p: Within the gland, from superficial to deep, remember the facial nerve, retromandibular vein and external carotid artery. The facial nerve forms its parotid plexus and divides into terminal branches in the gland, but does not provide its secretomotor supply.
slides.remember: Superficial to deep: nerve → vein → artery.
slides.q: Which structure is most superficial among the three major structures within the gland?
slides.why: The facial nerve lies most superficially, followed by the retromandibular vein and external carotid artery.

slides.p: The parotid duct emerges from the anterior border, crosses the masseter, turns medially at its anterior edge, pierces buccinator and opens into the vestibule opposite the upper second molar tooth.
slides.remember: Masseter → buccinator → vestibule opposite upper second molar.
slides.q: The parotid duct opens opposite which tooth?
slides.why: The duct opens into the oral vestibule opposite the maxillary second molar.

slides.p: Parasympathetic secretomotor fibres originate from the glossopharyngeal nerve, pass through the tympanic branch and lesser petrosal nerve, relay in the otic ganglion, and reach the gland through the auriculotemporal nerve. Parotidectomy requires care to protect facial nerve branches.
slides.remember: IX → tympanic plexus → lesser petrosal → otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve.
slides.q: Which nerve carries postganglionic secretomotor fibres to the parotid?
slides.why: Postganglionic fibres from the otic ganglion reach the parotid through the auriculotemporal nerve.

lessons.exam: LAQ order: situation, capsule, relations, structures within gland, blood supply, lymphatic drainage, nerve supply, parotid duct and applied anatomy. Add a labelled diagram.

lessons.title: Thyroid Gland – Blood Supply & Applied Anatomy

slides.p: The thyroid lies in the lower anterior neck, deep to the infrahyoid muscles. It has right and left lobes connected by an isthmus, usually lying across the second to fourth tracheal rings. A pyramidal lobe may be present.
slides.remember: Two lobes + isthmus; remember the possible pyramidal lobe.
slides.q: The thyroid isthmus usually crosses which tracheal rings?
slides.why: The isthmus commonly overlies the second, third and fourth tracheal rings.

slides.p: The superior thyroid artery usually arises from the external carotid artery. The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk. A thyroid ima artery may be present as an additional vessel.
slides.remember: Superior = external carotid; inferior = thyrocervical trunk.
slides.q: The inferior thyroid artery usually arises from the:
slides.why: The inferior thyroid artery is typically a branch of the thyrocervical trunk.

slides.p: The superior and middle thyroid veins drain into the internal jugular vein. The inferior thyroid veins form a plexus and usually drain into the brachiocephalic veins.
slides.remember: Superior + middle → IJV; inferior → brachiocephalic veins.
slides.q: The inferior thyroid veins usually drain into the:
slides.why: The inferior thyroid venous plexus drains into the brachiocephalic veins.

slides.p: Thyroid enlargement may produce a goitre and compress nearby structures. During thyroid surgery, the recurrent laryngeal nerve and external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve are important structures to protect. The close relation of the inferior thyroid artery to the recurrent laryngeal nerve is variable.
slides.remember: Thyroidectomy: protect laryngeal nerves and identify vessels carefully.
slides.q: Which nerve is particularly at risk near the inferior thyroid artery during thyroid surgery?
opts: Vagus nerve in the carotid sheath only
slides.why: The recurrent laryngeal nerve has a close and variable relationship with the inferior thyroid artery.

lessons.title: Cavernous Sinus

slides.p: The cavernous sinus is a paired dural venous sinus situated on either side of the body of the sphenoid, in the middle cranial fossa. It extends from the superior orbital fissure anteriorly towards the apex of the petrous temporal bone posteriorly.
slides.remember: Paired sinus, either side of sphenoid body.
slides.q: The cavernous sinus is located in which cranial fossa?
opts: It is outside the cranial cavity
slides.why: The cavernous sinus is a dural venous sinus of the middle cranial fossa.

slides.p: The internal carotid artery and abducens nerve (CN VI) pass through the venous blood within the sinus.
slides.remember: Inside the sinus: ICA + VI.
slides.q: Which cranial nerve runs within the cavernous sinus alongside the internal carotid artery?
slides.why: The abducens nerve (CN VI) runs within the sinus beside the internal carotid artery.

slides.p: The lateral wall contains, from superior to inferior, the oculomotor nerve (III), trochlear nerve (IV), ophthalmic division (V1) and maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve.
slides.remember: Lateral wall: III, IV, V1, V2.
slides.q: Which nerve is the lowest of these in the lateral wall?
slides.why: V2 is the lowest of the listed nerves in the lateral wall.

slides.p: Infection from the face can spread through venous communications to the cavernous sinus. Cavernous sinus thrombosis can affect ocular movements and facial sensation in the territories of V1 and V2.
slides.remember: Dangerous facial venous connections; multiple cranial nerves at risk.
slides.q: Which nerve is especially vulnerable because it travels within the sinus rather than in its lateral wall?
slides.why: The abducens nerve runs within the sinus and is vulnerable in cavernous sinus pathology.

lessons.exam: Describe location, extent, relations, contents in the lateral wall and within the sinus, communications and applied anatomy. Draw a coronal section.

lessons.title: Cubital Fossa

slides.p: The cubital fossa is a triangular depression in front of the elbow. Its medial boundary is pronator teres; its lateral boundary is brachioradialis; its base is an imaginary line joining the humeral epicondyles.
slides.remember: Medial PT, lateral BR, base between epicondyles.
slides.q: The medial boundary of the cubital fossa is formed by:
slides.why: Pronator teres forms the medial boundary.

slides.p: The roof includes skin, superficial fascia with veins and cutaneous nerves, and deep fascia reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis. The floor is formed mainly by brachialis medially and supinator laterally.
slides.remember: Roof: superficial structures + bicipital aponeurosis; floor: brachialis and supinator.
slides.q: Which structure reinforces the roof of the cubital fossa?
slides.why: The bicipital aponeurosis reinforces the deep fascia forming the roof.

slides.p: From lateral to medial, the main contents are biceps tendon, brachial artery and median nerve. The radial nerve lies more laterally, near the lateral boundary, before dividing.
slides.remember: TAN from lateral to medial: tendon, artery, nerve.
slides.q: What is the order of the three classic contents from lateral to medial?
slides.why: The classic arrangement is biceps tendon, brachial artery and median nerve.

slides.p: The median cubital vein is commonly used for venepuncture. The bicipital aponeurosis provides a protective layer over the brachial artery and median nerve. The brachial pulse can be palpated in the fossa.
slides.remember: Venepuncture: median cubital vein; deep protection: bicipital aponeurosis.
slides.q: Which superficial vein is commonly used for venepuncture?
slides.why: The median cubital vein is a common accessible site for venepuncture.

lessons.title: Brachial Plexus

slides.p: The brachial plexus is formed by the anterior rami of spinal nerves C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1. It supplies most of the upper limb.
slides.remember: Roots: C5–T1.
slides.q: The usual roots of the brachial plexus are:
slides.why: The typical brachial plexus is formed by anterior rami C5 to T1.

slides.p: The roots form three trunks: upper (C5–C6), middle (C7) and lower (C8–T1). Each trunk divides into anterior and posterior divisions behind the clavicle.
slides.remember: Upper C5–6; middle C7; lower C8–T1.
slides.q: Which roots form the lower trunk?
slides.why: The lower trunk is formed by C8 and T1.

slides.p: The divisions reorganise into lateral, medial and posterior cords around the second part of the axillary artery. The five major terminal branches are musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median and ulnar nerves.
slides.remember: Roots → Trunks → Divisions → Cords → Branches.
slides.q: The cords are named according to their relation to the:
slides.why: The cords are named lateral, medial and posterior according to their relation to the second part of the axillary artery.

slides.p: Upper trunk injury (Erb palsy) classically affects C5–C6 contributions. Lower trunk injury (Klumpke palsy) affects C8–T1 contributions and may cause intrinsic hand muscle weakness.
slides.remember: Erb = upper trunk; Klumpke = lower trunk.
slides.q: Klumpke paralysis classically involves which part?
slides.why: Klumpke paralysis is associated with lower trunk C8–T1 injury.

lessons.title: Mammary Gland – Lymphatic Drainage

slides.p: Most lymph from the breast, especially the lateral quadrants, drains to the axillary lymph nodes, particularly the anterior (pectoral) group. A substantial portion from the medial quadrants drains to parasternal nodes.
slides.remember: Most → axillary; medial part → parasternal.
slides.q: Most lymph from the breast drains primarily to which group?
slides.why: Most breast lymph drains to axillary nodes.

slides.p: Some lymph may pass to posterior intercostal nodes. Lymph from the lower part may communicate with subdiaphragmatic and abdominal pathways. The two breasts can have cross-midline lymphatic connections.
slides.remember: Remember axillary, parasternal, posterior intercostal and inferior pathways.
slides.q: Medial breast lymph commonly drains to:
slides.why: Medial quadrants commonly drain to parasternal (internal thoracic) nodes.

slides.p: Breast carcinoma may spread through lymphatics to regional nodes. Axillary node involvement is clinically important in staging and surgical planning. Lymphatic drainage is variable, so assessment considers more than one nodal group.
slides.remember: Clinical link: lymphatic spread and nodal assessment.
slides.q: Why is axillary lymph node assessment important in breast carcinoma?
opts: It assesses a common route of lymphatic spread
It identifies the origin of the thoracic duct
slides.why: Axillary nodes receive much of the breast lymph and are important in regional spread assessment.

lessons.title: Shoulder Joint

slides.p: The shoulder (glenohumeral) joint is a synovial ball-and-socket joint. The head of the humerus articulates with the glenoid cavity of the scapula; the glenoid labrum deepens the cavity.
slides.remember: Ball-and-socket: humeral head + glenoid cavity.
slides.q: The shoulder joint is which type of synovial joint?
slides.why: The glenohumeral joint is a ball-and-socket synovial joint.

slides.p: The capsule is relatively loose to permit a wide range of movement. Stability is provided by the rotator cuff muscles, glenoid labrum, joint capsule and ligaments, and the long head of biceps tendon.
slides.remember: Mobility is high; dynamic stability depends strongly on rotator cuff.
slides.q: Which group provides major dynamic support to the shoulder joint?
slides.why: The rotator cuff muscles dynamically stabilize the humeral head.

slides.p: The joint permits flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, medial and lateral rotation, and circumduction. Deltoid is a major abductor after initiation; supraspinatus initiates abduction.
slides.remember: Supraspinatus initiates; deltoid continues abduction.
slides.q: Which muscle initiates the first part of shoulder abduction?
slides.why: Supraspinatus initiates abduction; deltoid is a major abductor thereafter.

slides.p: The joint is commonly dislocated anteriorly or anteroinferiorly. The axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels may be at risk in dislocation or fracture around the surgical neck.
slides.remember: Anterior dislocation: remember axillary nerve.
slides.q: Which nerve is particularly at risk in shoulder dislocation?
slides.why: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck and may be injured.

lessons.title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome

slides.p: The carpal tunnel is an osteofibrous passage at the wrist. Its floor and sides are formed by the carpal arch; the flexor retinaculum forms its roof.
slides.remember: Carpal arch + flexor retinaculum.
slides.q: What forms the roof of the carpal tunnel?
slides.why: The flexor retinaculum forms the roof of the carpal tunnel.

slides.p: The tunnel contains the median nerve and nine flexor tendons: four flexor digitorum superficialis, four flexor digitorum profundus and one flexor pollicis longus.
slides.remember: Median nerve + 9 tendons.
slides.q: How many flexor tendons pass through the carpal tunnel?
slides.why: There are nine flexor tendons: four FDS, four FDP and one FPL.

slides.p: Compression of the median nerve causes pain, tingling or numbness in its sensory distribution in the lateral three and a half digits, often worse at night. Thenar weakness and wasting can occur in advanced cases.
slides.remember: Median nerve compression; lateral 3½ digits; thenar weakness.
slides.q: Which nerve is compressed in carpal tunnel syndrome?
slides.why: Carpal tunnel syndrome is caused by compression of the median nerve.

lessons.title: Nasal Septum

slides.p: The nasal septum has bony and cartilaginous parts. The main components include septal cartilage, perpendicular plate of ethmoid, vomer and contributions from the maxillary and palatine crests.
slides.remember: Cartilage + ethmoid + vomer + crests.
slides.q: Which bone forms the posterosuperior part of the bony nasal septum?
slides.why: The perpendicular plate of the ethmoid forms the posterosuperior bony part.

slides.p: The septum is lined by nasal mucosa. Its anterior-inferior region contains an arterial anastomosis commonly called Kiesselbach’s area or Little’s area, a frequent site of epistaxis.
slides.remember: Little’s area = common anterior epistaxis site.
slides.q: Little’s area is clinically important because it is a common site of:
slides.why: The vascular area on the anterior-inferior septum is a common source of anterior nosebleeds.

slides.p: Deviation of the nasal septum may narrow a nasal passage and contribute to obstruction. Epistaxis from the anterior septum is often accessible to local examination and treatment.
slides.remember: Link structure to obstruction and epistaxis.
slides.q: A deviated nasal septum may directly cause:
opts: Loss of hearing in all cases
Loss of taste in posterior third
slides.why: Septal deviation can narrow the nasal airway.

lessons.title: Right Atrium

slides.p: The right atrium receives systemic venous blood. Its posterior smooth part (sinus venarum) is separated from the anterior rough part by the crista terminalis internally; pectinate muscles are prominent in the anterior part and auricle.
slides.remember: Smooth sinus venarum; rough pectinate part.
slides.q: Which ridge separates the smooth and rough parts internally?
slides.why: The crista terminalis separates the smooth sinus venarum from the rough pectinate part.

slides.p: The right atrium receives the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava and coronary sinus. It communicates with the right ventricle through the right atrioventricular (tricuspid) orifice.
slides.remember: SVC + IVC + coronary sinus.
slides.q: Which venous structure opens into the right atrium to return blood from the myocardium?
opts: Azygos vein directly in all cases
slides.why: The coronary sinus drains most venous blood from the myocardium into the right atrium.

slides.p: The interatrial septum shows the fossa ovalis, the remnant of the fetal foramen ovale. The limbus surrounds the fossa. Developmental persistence can result in an atrial septal communication.
slides.remember: Fossa ovalis = remnant of foramen ovale.
slides.q: The fossa ovalis is a remnant of the fetal:
slides.why: The fossa ovalis marks the site of the fetal foramen ovale.

lessons.title: Pancreas

slides.p: The pancreas is a soft, lobulated, mostly retroperitoneal gland lying across the posterior abdominal wall. It extends from the C-shaped curve of the duodenum towards the spleen. It is divided into head, uncinate process, neck, body and tail. The tail reaches the splenic hilum within the splenorenal ligament.
slides.remember: Head in the duodenal curve; tail towards the spleen.
slides.q: Which part of the pancreas reaches the splenic hilum?
slides.why: The tail extends towards the spleen and lies in the splenorenal ligament.

slides.p: The head is embraced by the duodenum. The uncinate process passes posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels. The portal vein is formed behind the neck by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. The body lies anterior to major posterior wall structures including the aorta and left kidney region.
slides.remember: Portal vein forms behind the neck of pancreas.
slides.q: The portal vein is formed posterior to which part?
slides.why: The splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein unite behind the neck of the pancreas.

slides.h: Ducts, blood supply and applied anatomy
slides.p: The main pancreatic duct usually joins the common bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, opening at the major duodenal papilla. The accessory duct, when present and patent, opens at the minor papilla. Blood supply comes mainly from superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries and branches of the splenic artery. Inflammation may cause severe epigastric pain radiating to the back; a tumour in the head may obstruct the bile duct and cause jaundice.
slides.remember: Main duct → major papilla; head mass → obstructive jaundice.
slides.q: A tumour in the head of pancreas may cause jaundice by compressing which structure?
slides.why: The common bile duct passes close to the head of the pancreas and may be compressed by a head-of-pancreas mass.

lessons.exam: LAQ framework: introduction and situation; parts; relations of head, neck, body and tail; pancreatic ducts; blood supply; development if prescribed; applied anatomy. Draw a labelled pancreas with duodenum, bile duct and major vessels.

lessons.title: Prostate

slides.p: The prostate is a fibromusculoglandular organ situated in the lesser pelvis, below the urinary bladder and around the proximal prostatic urethra. Its base is related to the bladder neck and its apex rests on the superior fascia of the urogenital diaphragm. It is anterior to the rectum, making it palpable on digital rectal examination.
slides.remember: Below bladder, around urethra, anterior to rectum.
slides.q: Which structure passes through the prostate?
slides.why: The prostatic urethra traverses the prostate.

slides.p: The prostate has a true fibrous capsule and a surrounding prostatic sheath derived from pelvic fascia. Anteriorly it is related to the pubic symphysis through the retropubic space; posteriorly it is related to the rectum; inferolaterally it is supported by levator ani. Traditional anatomy describes lobes; clinical imaging commonly uses zones, with the peripheral zone being a frequent site of carcinoma and the transition zone commonly involved in benign prostatic hyperplasia.
slides.remember: Posterior surface can be examined per rectum.
slides.q: Which enlargement commonly compresses the prostatic urethra in older men?
slides.why: Benign prostatic hyperplasia commonly arises in the transition zone and can obstruct urinary flow.

slides.h: Blood supply, venous drainage and clinical points
slides.p: Arterial supply is mainly from branches of the inferior vesical artery, with contributions that can vary. The prostatic venous plexus communicates with the vesical plexus and the internal vertebral venous plexus. This communication is clinically relevant in the spread of prostate carcinoma to vertebral bones. The prostate also receives autonomic fibres through the prostatic plexus.
slides.remember: Prostatic venous plexus communicates with vertebral venous plexus.
slides.q: The venous communication helps explain spread of prostate carcinoma to which site?
slides.why: Connections with the internal vertebral venous plexus provide a route for vertebral metastases.

lessons.exam: LAQ framework: situation, shape, capsule, relations, lobes/zones, blood supply, venous and lymphatic drainage, nerve supply and applied anatomy. Add a sagittal pelvic diagram.

lessons.title: Stomach

slides.p: The stomach is a J-shaped dilated part of the alimentary canal between the oesophagus and duodenum. It has cardia, fundus, body and pyloric part. It presents anterior and posterior surfaces, lesser and greater curvatures, and cardiac and pyloric openings. The pylorus is usually near the transpyloric plane in the supine adult, though its position varies.
slides.remember: Four parts: cardia, fundus, body, pyloric part.
slides.q: Which part of the stomach lies superior to the cardiac opening?
slides.why: The fundus is the dome-shaped part above and to the left of the cardiac opening.

slides.p: The lesser omentum attaches the lesser curvature to the liver, while the greater omentum hangs from the greater curvature. The stomach bed is the group of structures related to the posterior surface through the lesser sac; it includes the pancreas, spleen, left kidney and suprarenal gland, transverse mesocolon and related vessels. The exact list should be written as taught in the prescribed text.
slides.remember: Posterior stomach + lesser sac = stomach bed.
slides.q: The pancreas is related to the stomach through which space?
slides.why: The posterior surface of the stomach is separated from much of its bed by the lesser sac.

slides.p: The lesser curvature is supplied by right and left gastric arteries; the greater curvature by right and left gastro-omental arteries. Short gastric arteries supply the fundus. These vessels arise from the coeliac trunk system. Lymph follows the arteries towards gastric and coeliac nodes. Clinical topics include peptic ulceration, gastric carcinoma and vagotomy; relate symptoms and spread to the anatomy taught in class.
slides.remember: Lesser curve: gastric; greater curve: gastro-omental; fundus: short gastric.
slides.q: Which arteries chiefly supply the fundus?
slides.why: Short gastric arteries, usually from the splenic artery, supply the fundus.

lessons.exam: LAQ framework: situation, parts, external features, peritoneal attachments, relations and stomach bed, blood supply, venous drainage, lymphatics, nerve supply and applied anatomy. Practise a labelled stomach diagram.

lessons.title: Kidney

slides.p: The kidneys are paired, bean-shaped retroperitoneal organs on the posterior abdominal wall. The right kidney is usually slightly lower than the left because of the liver. Each kidney has anterior and posterior surfaces, medial and lateral borders, and upper and lower poles. The medial border bears the hilum, which opens into the renal sinus.
slides.remember: Right kidney usually lies lower than left.
slides.q: Why is the right kidney usually lower?
slides.why: The large right lobe of the liver occupies space superior to the right kidney.

slides.p: At the hilum, the usual anterior-to-posterior arrangement is renal vein, renal artery and renal pelvis/ureter (V-A-P). The kidney is covered by a fibrous capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia and pararenal fat. The renal pelvis continues as the ureter.
slides.remember: Hilum from anterior to posterior: V-A-P.
slides.q: What is the usual anterior-to-posterior order at the renal hilum?
slides.why: The commonly taught order is renal vein, renal artery and renal pelvis from anterior to posterior.

slides.p: Posterior relations include the diaphragm and posterior abdominal wall muscles, with the subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves nearby. Anterior relations differ on the two sides; the right kidney is related to the liver, second part of duodenum and right colic region, among other structures. Renal angle tenderness is a clinical examination point. Stones may cause colicky pain radiating along the ureter.
slides.remember: Learn right and left anterior relations separately; they are not identical.
slides.q: Which kidney is commonly related anteriorly to the second part of the duodenum?
slides.why: The descending (second) part of the duodenum is an anterior relation of the right kidney.

lessons.exam: LAQ framework: situation, size/shape, external features, hilum, coverings, relations (right and left separately), blood supply, lymphatics, nerve supply and applied anatomy. Draw a section showing cortex, medulla, pyramids and renal pelvis.

lessons.title: Urinary Bladder

slides.p: The urinary bladder is a hollow muscular reservoir for urine in the lesser pelvis when empty. It has an apex, base (fundus), neck and surfaces. As it fills, it rises into the abdomen. The neck is the most fixed part and continues into the urethra.
slides.remember: Empty bladder = pelvis; distended bladder = rises above pubis.
slides.q: Which part of the bladder continues into the urethra?
slides.why: The bladder neck is continuous with the urethra.

slides.p: The mucosa is generally folded when empty, except for the smooth trigone. The trigone is bounded by the two ureteric openings and the internal urethral opening. The detrusor is the muscular wall. Support is provided by pelvic floor and fascial structures; in females, the relation to the cervix and anterior vaginal wall is important.
slides.remember: Trigone = two ureteric openings + internal urethral opening.
slides.q: Which part of the bladder is characteristically smooth even when the bladder is empty?
slides.why: The trigone is firmly attached and remains smooth.

slides.p: Arterial supply is chiefly from superior vesical arteries, with inferior vesical contribution in males and corresponding vaginal contributions in females. Venous drainage forms vesical plexuses. Parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) promote detrusor contraction and facilitate micturition; sympathetic pathways contribute to storage. A distended bladder may be approached suprapubically when clinically indicated.
slides.remember: S2–S4 parasympathetic: emptying response.
slides.q: Which spinal segments provide the parasympathetic supply important for bladder emptying?
slides.why: Pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2–S4 carry parasympathetic fibres to the bladder.

lessons.exam: LAQ framework: situation, shape, parts, relations, interior (trigone), wall, supports, blood supply, nerve supply and applied anatomy. Draw the trigone and sagittal relations.

lessons.title: Inguinal Canal

slides.p: The inguinal canal is an oblique passage in the lower anterior abdominal wall, about 4 cm long, above the medial half of the inguinal ligament. It extends from the deep inguinal ring to the superficial inguinal ring. The deep ring is an opening in transversalis fascia; the superficial ring is a triangular gap in the external oblique aponeurosis.
slides.remember: Deep ring = transversalis fascia; superficial ring = external oblique aponeurosis.
slides.q: The deep inguinal ring is an opening in which layer?
slides.why: The deep ring is a defect in the transversalis fascia.

slides.p: The anterior wall is mainly external oblique aponeurosis, reinforced laterally by internal oblique. The posterior wall is mainly transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon. The roof is formed by arching fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis; the floor is the inguinal ligament, with lacunar ligament medially. The spermatic cord traverses it in males; the ilioinguinal nerve also passes through part of the canal. In females, the round ligament of uterus traverses it.
slides.remember: A-P-R-F: aponeurosis, transversalis fascia, arching muscles, inguinal ligament.
slides.q: Which structure forms the main floor of the inguinal canal?
slides.why: The inguinal ligament forms the floor, with medial reinforcement by the lacunar ligament.

slides.p: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the deep ring, passes through the canal lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, and may reach the scrotum. A direct inguinal hernia pushes through a weakness in the posterior wall in Hesselbach’s triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. This anatomical distinction is central to clinical examination and surgery.
slides.remember: Indirect = lateral to inferior epigastric vessels; direct = medial.
slides.q: A direct inguinal hernia lies on which side of the inferior epigastric vessels?
slides.why: Direct hernias protrude medial to the inferior epigastric vessels through the posterior wall.

lessons.exam: LAQ framework: definition, extent, rings, four walls, contents in male and female, blood supply/nerve supply if required, and direct versus indirect inguinal hernia. Draw the canal and Hesselbach’s triangle.

lessons.title: Anal Canal

slides.p: The anal canal is the terminal part of the large intestine, extending from the anorectal junction to the anus. The pectinate line is a major anatomical and clinical landmark. Above and below it, the canal differs in embryological origin, epithelium, arterial supply, venous drainage, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply. Learn these contrasts as a paired table.
slides.remember: Pectinate line divides two different anatomical territories.
slides.q: Which landmark is used to compare the upper and lower anal canal?
slides.why: The pectinate line is the key landmark separating upper and lower parts.

slides.p: The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of circular smooth muscle and is involuntary. The external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle and is voluntary, with subcutaneous, superficial and deep parts commonly described. Puborectalis forms a sling around the anorectal junction and helps maintain the anorectal angle.
slides.remember: Internal = smooth/involuntary; external = skeletal/voluntary.
slides.q: Which sphincter is composed of smooth muscle?
slides.why: The internal sphincter is formed by thickened circular smooth muscle.

slides.p: Internal haemorrhoids arise above the pectinate line and are classically less painful because the mucosa above the line has visceral innervation. External haemorrhoids occur below the line and can be painful due to somatic innervation. Anal fissures are commonly associated with severe pain during defecation. The exact arterial and venous territories should be revised using the standard above/below-line comparison.
slides.remember: Above line: visceral sensation; below line: somatic pain sensation.
slides.q: Why are external haemorrhoids often painful?
opts: They are above the pectinate line
They are below the line with somatic innervation
slides.why: The lower anal canal has somatic sensory innervation, making lesions there painful.

lessons.exam: LAQ framework: extent, direction, features, pectinate line, sphincters, relations, blood supply, venous and lymphatic drainage, nerve supply and applied anatomy. Prepare a comparison table above and below the pectinate line.

lessons.title: Hip Joint

slides.p: The hip is a synovial ball-and-socket joint between the head of femur and the acetabulum. The acetabular labrum deepens the socket. The capsule attaches around the acetabulum and to the femur; its fibres are reinforced by strong capsular ligaments. The joint is built for stability while allowing movement.
slides.remember: Ball = femoral head; socket = acetabulum.
slides.q: What type of synovial joint is the hip?
slides.why: The hip is a multiaxial ball-and-socket synovial joint.

slides.p: The iliofemoral, pubofemoral and ischiofemoral ligaments reinforce the capsule. The iliofemoral ligament is particularly strong and helps prevent hyperextension in standing. The ligament of the head of femur carries a small artery, which is more important in children than adults. Stability also depends on the depth of the acetabulum, labrum, muscles and surrounding capsule.
slides.remember: Three capsular ligaments: ilio-, pubo-, ischiofemoral.
slides.q: Which ligament is especially strong and resists hyperextension?
slides.why: The iliofemoral ligament is a strong anterior reinforcement of the hip capsule.

slides.h: Movements, blood supply and applied anatomy
slides.p: Movements include flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, medial and lateral rotation, and circumduction. Blood supply to the femoral head is mainly from retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery, with contributions from other vessels; the artery in the ligament of the head is variable. Fracture of the femoral neck can disrupt retinacular vessels and lead to avascular necrosis.
slides.remember: Femoral neck fracture → risk to retinacular vessels → avascular necrosis.
slides.q: Which artery is the major source for retinacular supply to the femoral head?
slides.why: Retinacular branches, particularly from the medial circumflex femoral artery, are crucial to femoral head blood supply.

lessons.exam: LAQ framework: type, articular surfaces, capsule, ligaments, relations, blood supply, nerve supply, movements with muscles and applied anatomy. Draw the joint and its ligaments.

lessons.title: Knee Joint

slides.p: The knee is a large synovial modified hinge joint. It includes femorotibial and patellofemoral articulations. The medial and lateral femoral condyles articulate with the tibial condyles; the patella articulates with the patellar surface of the femur. The menisci deepen the tibial surfaces and improve congruity.
slides.remember: Knee = femorotibial + patellofemoral components.
slides.q: The knee is best described as which type of joint?
slides.why: The knee is a modified hinge synovial joint.

slides.p: The medial and lateral menisci are fibrocartilaginous wedges. The medial meniscus is less mobile and is attached to the medial collateral ligament, making it more vulnerable to injury. The anterior cruciate ligament limits anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur and helps control rotation; the posterior cruciate ligament limits posterior translation. Collateral ligaments resist side-to-side stresses.
slides.remember: ACL checks anterior tibial displacement; PCL checks posterior displacement.
slides.q: Which ligament chiefly resists posterior displacement of the tibia?
slides.why: The posterior cruciate ligament limits posterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur.

slides.p: The main movements are flexion and extension, with a small amount of rotation when flexed. In terminal extension the knee undergoes a locking mechanism; popliteus helps unlock it at the start of flexion. The quadriceps mechanism stabilises the anterior aspect. Common clinical injuries include meniscal tears and cruciate ligament injuries; correlate examination tests with the structures they assess.
slides.remember: Popliteus unlocks the knee.
slides.q: Which muscle helps unlock the fully extended knee?
slides.why: Popliteus initiates unlocking by reversing the rotation associated with terminal extension.

lessons.exam: LAQ framework: type, articular surfaces, capsule, menisci, ligaments, relations, blood supply, nerve supply, movements, locking/unlocking and applied anatomy. Label the cruciate ligaments and menisci.

lessons.title: Popliteal Fossa

slides.p: The popliteal fossa is a diamond-shaped intermuscular space behind the knee. Superolaterally it is bounded by biceps femoris; superomedially by semimembranosus and semitendinosus; inferolaterally by lateral head of gastrocnemius and plantaris; inferomedially by medial head of gastrocnemius. The roof includes skin, superficial fascia and deep fascia.
slides.remember: Upper: hamstrings; lower: gastrocnemius heads.
slides.q: Which muscle forms the superolateral boundary?
slides.why: Biceps femoris forms the superolateral boundary of the popliteal fossa.

slides.p: The floor is formed from above downwards by the popliteal surface of femur, posterior capsule of the knee and popliteus fascia/muscle. Contents include the tibial nerve, common fibular nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery, lymph nodes and fat. From superficial to deep in the central neurovascular bundle, remember nerve, vein, artery.
slides.remember: Superficial to deep: N-V-A.
slides.q: What is the usual superficial-to-deep order of the central bundle?
slides.why: The tibial nerve is most superficial, then popliteal vein, then popliteal artery.

slides.p: The popliteal artery is relatively deep and may be difficult to palpate. A popliteal aneurysm can compress nearby structures. The fossa provides a route for vessels and nerves between thigh and leg. A Baker cyst is a distension of a bursa or joint-related synovial space in the popliteal region and may present as swelling behind the knee.
slides.remember: Deepest major structure = popliteal artery.
slides.q: Which major artery is deepest in the popliteal fossa?
slides.why: The popliteal artery lies deepest, close to the floor of the fossa.

lessons.exam: LAQ framework: boundaries, roof, floor, contents (arrangement), genicular anastomosis if included, and applied anatomy. Draw a diamond with boundaries and N-V-A arrangement.

lessons.title: Arch of Aorta

slides.p: The arch of aorta lies in the superior mediastinum behind the lower half of the manubrium sterni. It begins as the continuation of the ascending aorta behind the right 2nd sternocostal joint, arches upward, backward, and to the left over the root of the left lung, and ends on the left side of the lower border of the T4 vertebra (sternal angle level) by continuing as the descending thoracic aorta.
slides.remember: Starts and ends at the SAME horizontal level: Sternal angle (T4 lower border)! Lies in the superior mediastinum.
slides.q: At which vertebral level does the arch of the aorta begin and end?
slides.why: Both the beginning (right 2nd sternocostal joint) and termination (left side of T4 lower border) of the arch of aorta lie at the plane of the sternal angle (T4).

slides.p: Remembering the four sets of relations of the arch of aorta is the core of any Thorax LAQ:
bullets: Anterior & to the Left: Left lung & pleura, left phrenic nerve, left vagus nerve, and two cardiac nerves (superficial cardiac plexus). Left superior intercostal vein crosses obliquely upward between vagus and phrenic nerves.
Posterior & to the Right: Trachea, esophagus, left recurrent laryngeal nerve (in tracheoesophageal groove), thoracic duct, and T4 vertebral body.
Superiorly (3 Branches): From right to left (anterior to posterior): Brachiocephalic trunk, Left common carotid artery, and Left subclavian artery.
Inferiorly (Concavity): Bifurcation of pulmonary trunk, left principal bronchus, ligamentum arteriosum (with left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooking beneath it), and superficial cardiac plexus.
slides.remember: Superior branches (right to left): B-C-S (Brachiocephalic, Left Common Carotid, Left Subclavian). Under the arch: Left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks around ligamentum arteriosum!
slides.q: Which nerve hooks underneath the arch of the aorta just behind the ligamentum arteriosum?
slides.why: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve branches from the left vagus on the arch of the aorta and loops underneath the arch posterior to the ligamentum arteriosum to ascend in the tracheoesophageal groove.

slides.p: Because the arch of the aorta sits directly in front of the trachea and passes over the left bronchus, dilatation or aneurysm of the arch causes classic pressure symptoms:
bullets: Hoarseness of Voice: Compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve beneath the arch paralyzes the left vocal fold.
Dyspnea & Brassy Cough: Compression of the trachea and left principal bronchus.
Dysphagia: Compression of the esophagus posteriorly.
Tracheal Tug (Oliver's Sign): Downward pulling of the trachea/larynx with each heartbeat felt on palpating the cricoid cartilage, caused by an aortic arch aneurysm pressing on the left bronchus.
slides.remember: Aortic arch aneurysm = Hoarseness (left recurrent laryngeal nerve) + Dysphagia (esophagus) + Oliver's tracheal tug!
slides.q: Hoarseness of voice in an aneurysm of the arch of aorta is caused by compression of which nerve?
slides.why: Because the left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks beneath the arch of aorta, an aneurysm in this region stretches or compresses the nerve, causing left vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness.

lessons.exam: LAQ order: Introduction & situation (superior mediastinum) → Origin, course & termination (T4 plane) → Relations (anterior/left, posterior/right, superior, inferior) → Branches → Development (left 4th aortic arch) → Applied anatomy (aneurysm, tracheal tug, coarctation). Add two neat diagrams (anterior/left view + inferior view).

lessons.title: Bronchopulmonary Segments

slides.p: Bronchopulmonary segments are the largest, well-defined, anatomically and functionally independent subdivisions of a lung lobe. Each segment is pyramidal in shape, with its apex directed toward the hilum and its base facing the pleural surface.
bullets: Aeration: Each segment is aerated by its own tertiary (segmental) bronchus.
Arterial Supply: Each has its own segmental branch of the pulmonary artery (accompanying the segmental bronchus) and bronchial artery.
Venous Drainage (Crucial!): Intersegmental tributaries of the pulmonary veins run IN the connective tissue septa BETWEEN adjacent segments—NOT inside the segment with the bronchus!
Total Count: Typically 10 segments in the right lung and 8–10 segments in the left lung.
slides.remember: Bronchus + Pulmonary Artery = INSIDE the segment (center). Pulmonary Vein = BETWEEN segments (intersegmental plane — surgical guide!).
slides.q: Where do the tributaries of the pulmonary veins run in relation to bronchopulmonary segments?
opts: Inside the center of each segment alongside the segmental bronchus
In the connective tissue septa between adjacent segments (intersegmental)
Only on the mediastinal pleural surface
slides.why: Pulmonary veins run in the intersegmental connective tissue septa between adjacent bronchopulmonary segments, serving as crucial surgical landmarks during segmentectomy.

slides.h: 2. Complete List of Segments (Right vs Left Lung)
slides.p: Examiners frequently ask for the exact names of segments in both lungs (and specifically the left lung as a Short Note):
bullets: Right Lung (10 segments): Upper lobe (3): Apical, Posterior, Anterior. Middle lobe (2): Lateral, Medial. Lower lobe (5): Superior (apical), Medial basal, Anterior basal, Lateral basal, Posterior basal.

Left Lung (8–10 segments): Upper lobe (4–5): Apical & Posterior (often fused as Apicoposterior), Anterior, Superior lingular, Inferior lingular. Lower lobe (4–5): Superior (apical), Medial basal (often fused with Anterior basal as Anteromedial basal), Lateral basal, Posterior basal.
slides.remember: Right = 3 (Upper: A-P-A) + 2 (Middle: L-M) + 5 (Lower: S-M-A-L-P) = 10. Left replaces Middle lobe with Superior & Inferior Lingular segments!
slides.q: Which two segments in the left upper lobe correspond embryologically and functionally to the right middle lobe?
slides.why: The lingula of the left upper lobe divides into superior and inferior lingular segments, corresponding to the lateral and medial segments of the right middle lobe.

slides.p: Why are bronchopulmonary segments one of the most clinically important topics in Thorax?
bullets: Surgical Resection (Segmentectomy): Because each segment is an independent structural unit separated by connective tissue septa, a surgeon can resect a single diseased segment (e.g., localized tuberculosis or bronchiectasis) without removing the entire lobe, following the intersegmental pulmonary veins as a plane of cleavage.

Postural Drainage & Aspiration Pneumonia: Knowing the direction of each segmental bronchus guides chest physiotherapy. In a supine patient, aspirated material gravitates into the posterior segment of the right upper lobe or the superior (apical) segment of the right lower lobe.
slides.remember: Supine aspiration → Posterior segment of Right Upper Lobe or Superior (apical) segment of Right Lower Lobe!
slides.q: Which bronchopulmonary segment is most commonly involved in aspiration pneumonia when a patient is lying supine?
opts: Medial segment of right middle lobe
Superior (apical) segment of right lower lobe
Anterior basal segment of left lower lobe
slides.why: When lying flat on the back (supine), the bronchus to the superior (apical) segment of the right lower lobe (and posterior segment of right upper lobe) opens directly posteriorly, making it the dependent site for aspirated fluid.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Definition → Characteristic features (pyramidal, independent aeration/artery, intersegmental veins) → Tabular list of Right & Left lung segments → Applied anatomy (segmentectomy along intersegmental veins, postural drainage, aspiration sites) + Labelled diagram of both lungs.

lessons.title: Superior Mediastinum

slides.p: The superior mediastinum is the upper compartment of the mediastinum lying above the transverse thoracic plane (sternal angle). Think of it as the busy anatomical highway connecting the neck and upper limbs to the thorax:
bullets: Anteriorly: Manubrium sterni (with attachments of sternohyoid and sternothyroid muscles).
Posteriorly: Upper four thoracic vertebrae (T1 to T4) and anterior longitudinal ligament.
Superiorly: Plane of the thoracic inlet (superior thoracic aperture).
Inferiorly: An imaginary horizontal plane passing from the sternal angle (angle of Louis) in front to the lower border of T4 vertebra behind (separating it from the inferior mediastinum).
Laterally (on each side): Mediastinal pleura of the lungs.
slides.remember: Superior Mediastinum = Between Thoracic Inlet (top) and Sternal Angle–T4 Plane (bottom).
slides.q: Which anatomical plane forms the inferior boundary of the superior mediastinum?
opts: Plane from sternal angle to lower border of T4 vertebra
Plane from xiphoid process to T9 vertebra
slides.why: The horizontal plane passing through the sternal angle anteriorly and the lower border of T4 posteriorly separates the superior mediastinum from the inferior mediastinum.

slides.h: 2. Contents Arranged from Anterior to Posterior
slides.p: Examiners love when you list the contents of the superior mediastinum in neat layers from front to back:
bullets: 1. Retro-manubrial / Lymphoid Layer: Remains of the thymus, lower ends of sternohyoid & sternothyroid muscles.
2. Great Veins Layer: Right and left brachiocephalic veins uniting behind the right 1st costal cartilage to form the upper half of the Superior Vena Cava (SVC), plus left superior intercostal vein.
3. Great Arteries Layer: Arch of aorta and its three major branches (brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, left subclavian).
4. Nerves & Cardiac Plexus: Right & left vagus nerves, right & left phrenic nerves, left recurrent laryngeal nerve, and superficial & deep cardiac plexuses.
5. Visceral & Lymphatic Layer (Posterior): Trachea, esophagus, thoracic duct, and paratracheal/tracheobronchial lymph nodes.
slides.remember: Front to back in Superior Mediastinum: Thymus → Veins (Brachiocephalic/SVC) → Arteries (Aortic arch) → Nerves (Phrenic/Vagus) → Tubes (Trachea, Esophagus, Thoracic duct).
slides.q: Which of the following structures is located in the SUPERIOR mediastinum?
opts: Arch of aorta and brachiocephalic veins
slides.why: The arch of the aorta, its three branches, and the brachiocephalic veins lie within the superior mediastinum (whereas the heart and descending thoracic aorta lie in the inferior mediastinum).

slides.p: Because the superior mediastinum is tightly bounded by bone in front (manubrium) and behind (T1–T4 vertebrae), any space-occupying mass (retrosternal goitre, thymoma, lymphoma, or aortic aneurysm) quickly compresses its contents, producing Superior Mediastinal Syndrome:
bullets: SVC Obstruction: Engorged, non-pulsatile neck veins, facial/arm edema, and dilated chest-wall collateral veins.
Tracheal Compression: Dyspnea, stridor, and brassy cough.
Esophageal Compression: Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing).
Left Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve Compression: Hoarseness of voice.
slides.remember: Rigid bony box (Manubrium + T1–T4) → Any mass compresses SVC, trachea, esophagus & left recurrent laryngeal nerve!
slides.q: Compression of the superior vena cava in superior mediastinal syndrome classically produces:
opts: Engorged non-pulsatile jugular veins and edema of face and upper limbs
slides.why: Obstruction of the superior vena cava impedes venous return from the head, neck, and upper limbs, causing facial/arm swelling and distended neck veins.

lessons.exam: LAQ order: Definition → Boundaries (anterior, posterior, superior, inferior, lateral) → Contents arranged from anterior to posterior (Thymus, Veins, Arteries, Nerves, Viscera/Ducts) → Applied anatomy (Superior Mediastinal Syndrome, thymic enlargement) + Labelled sagittal & transverse diagrams.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Left Coronary Artery

slides.p: The left coronary artery (LCA) is larger in caliber than the right coronary artery and supplies the major bulk of the left ventricular myocardium. It arises from the left posterior aortic sinus of the ascending aorta.
bullets: Initial Course: Runs forward and to the left between the pulmonary trunk and the left auricle.

Termination (Bifurcation): After a short main stem (~1–2 cm), it reaches the coronary (atrioventricular) sulcus and divides into two main terminal branches: the Anterior Interventricular Artery (Left Anterior Descending / LAD) and the Circumflex Artery.
slides.remember: Left posterior aortic sinus → passes between Pulmonary Trunk & Left Auricle → splits into LAD + Circumflex!
slides.q: From which aortic sinus does the left coronary artery arise?
slides.why: The left coronary artery arises from the left posterior aortic sinus, whereas the right coronary artery arises from the anterior aortic sinus.

slides.p: Knowing the exact branches and myocardial territory of the LCA is essential for both Anatomy and Physiology:
bullets: 1. Anterior Interventricular Artery (LAD): Descends in the anterior interventricular groove toward the apex, winds around the inferior border to anastomose with the posterior interventricular artery. Gives off diagonal branches and anterior septal perforators.
2. Circumflex Artery: Curves to the left in the coronary sulcus around the left border onto the posterior surface, giving off the left marginal artery.

Territory Supplied: Left atrium, most of the left ventricle, a strip of right ventricle adjacent to the anterior interventricular groove, anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum, and part of the left bundle branch.
slides.remember: LAD supplies the Anterior 2/3 of the Interventricular Septum + Anterior/Apical Left Ventricle!
slides.q: Which part of the interventricular septum is supplied by the anterior interventricular branch (LAD) of the left coronary artery?
slides.why: Septal branches of the anterior interventricular artery (LAD) supply the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum, while the posterior one-third is supplied by the posterior interventricular artery.

slides.p: Coronary arteries are functional end-arteries—their anastomoses are too small to compensate for sudden occlusion:
bullets: LAD Occlusion ('Widow-Maker'): The anterior interventricular artery (LAD) is the most common site of coronary thrombosis (~40–50% of myocardial infarctions), causing infarction of the anterior wall of the left ventricle and anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum.

Angina Pectoris: Myocardial ischemia produces retrosternal squeezing chest pain radiating down the medial side of the left arm and forearm (shared T1–T4 spinal segments via intercostobrachial & medial cutaneous nerves).
slides.remember: LAD = #1 site of coronary thrombosis ('widow-maker')! Referred pain down left arm = T1–T4 dermatomes.
slides.q: Which coronary artery branch is the single most common site of occlusion in myocardial infarction?
slides.why: The anterior interventricular branch (LAD) of the left coronary artery is the most frequently thrombosed coronary vessel, leading to anterior wall and septal myocardial infarction.

lessons.exam: SN order: Origin (left posterior aortic sinus) → Course → Branches (LAD & Circumflex) → Area of distribution (LA, LV, anterior 2/3 IV septum) → Applied anatomy (LAD thrombosis, angina pectoris, dominance) + Labelled diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Thoracic Duct

slides.p: The thoracic duct is the largest lymphatic vessel in the body (~45 cm / 18 inches long), appearing beaded due to numerous valves. It drains lymph from the entire body EXCEPT the right upper quadrant (right head/neck, right upper limb, right thorax).
bullets: Origin: Begins in the abdomen at the lower border of T12 vertebra as an upward continuation of the cisterna chyli.
Entry to Thorax: Enters thorax through the aortic opening of the diaphragm (T12) between the aorta (left) and azygos vein (right).

Crossing at T5 (Crucial Landmark!): Ascends in the posterior mediastinum on the right of the midline up to T5 vertebra, where it crosses from right to left behind the esophagus to enter the superior mediastinum.
Termination: Arches laterally in the root of the neck (C7 level) to open into the junction of the left internal jugular and left subclavian veins.
slides.remember: Starts at T12 (cisterna chyli) → crosses right-to-left at T5 → ends at Left Jugulosubclavian angle (C7)!
slides.q: At which vertebral level does the thoracic duct cross from the right side to the left side of the midline?
slides.why: The thoracic duct ascends on the right side of the vertebral column in the lower posterior mediastinum and crosses obliquely to the left at the level of the T5 vertebra.

slides.p: Examiners love testing which regions drain into the thoracic duct versus the right lymphatic duct:
bullets: Area Drained (3/4 of body): Both lower limbs, abdomen, pelvis, left half of thorax, left upper limb, and left half of head & neck.
Abdominal Tributaries (into Cisterna Chyli): Right & left lumbar trunks + intestinal trunk (carrying milky fat-rich chyle from small intestine).
Thoracic Tributaries: Descending thoracic lymph trunks (lower intercostal nodes) and upper left intercostal trunks.
Cervical Tributaries (near termination): Left jugular trunk, left subclavian trunk, and left bronchomediastinal trunk.
slides.remember: Everything drains into the Thoracic Duct EXCEPT the Right Upper Quadrant (which drains into the Right Lymphatic Duct)!
slides.q: Which of the following body regions does NOT drain into the thoracic duct?
opts: Right side of head and neck
slides.why: The right upper quadrant of the body (right head/neck, right upper limb, and right half of thorax) drains into the right lymphatic duct, not the thoracic duct.

slides.p: Two classic clinical correlations complete your short note on the thoracic duct:
bullets: Chylothorax: Injury to the thin-walled thoracic duct during posterior mediastinal or neck surgery leaks milky, lipid-rich lymph (chyle) into the pleural cavity. Left-sided chylothorax occurs with injury above T5; right-sided chylothorax with injury below T5.

Virchow's Node (Troisier's Sign): Abdominal/gastric carcinoma cells can travel up the thoracic duct and metastasize to the left supraclavicular lymph nodes near its venous termination, producing a hard palpable node above the left clavicle.
slides.remember: Injury above T5 → Left chylothorax. Injury below T5 → Right chylothorax. Gastric cancer spreads up thoracic duct → Left supraclavicular (Virchow's) node!
slides.q: Damage to the thoracic duct below the T5 vertebral level classically results in:
slides.why: Below T5 the thoracic duct lies on the right side of the midline, so injury at this level causes chyle to leak into the right pleural cavity (right chylothorax).

lessons.exam: SN order: Introduction & length → Origin (cisterna chyli at T12) → Course & relations (aortic hiatus, T5 crossing, cervical arch) → Termination (left venous angle) → Tributaries & drainage area → Applied anatomy (chylothorax, Virchow's node) + Labelled diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Root of Right Lung

slides.p: The root of the lung is a short, broad pedicle of tubular structures connecting the medial surface of the lung to the mediastinum, enclosed by a cuff of pleura that hangs down below as the pulmonary ligament. It lies opposite the T5, T6, and T7 vertebrae.
bullets: Anterior Relation: Superior vena cava (SVC), right atrium, and right phrenic nerve (with pericardiophrenic vessels).
Posterior Relation: Right vagus nerve (forming posterior pulmonary plexus) and azygos vein.
Superior Relation: Arch of the azygos vein hooking forward over the root to enter the SVC.
Inferior Relation: Pulmonary ligament.
slides.remember: Phrenic nerve passes IN FRONT of lung root; Vagus nerve passes BEHIND lung root! Arch of Azygos hooks OVER the right lung root!
slides.q: Which venous structure arches superiorly directly over the root of the right lung to enter the superior vena cava?
slides.why: The azygos vein arches forward over the superior aspect of the right lung root at the T4 level to drain into the posterior aspect of the superior vena cava.

slides.h: 2. Arrangement of Structures at the Right Hilum
slides.p: Knowing the exact arrangement of structures from anterior to posterior and from superior to inferior in the right lung root is a classic viva and short-note staple:
bullets: Anterior to Posterior (SAME on both sides!): Vein → Artery → Bronchus (V-A-B). Specifically: Superior pulmonary vein (most anterior) → Pulmonary artery → Bronchus & bronchial vessels (most posterior).
Superior to Inferior (RIGHT Lung Root — unique!): Eparterial bronchus (highest!) → Pulmonary artery → Hyparterial bronchus → Inferior pulmonary vein (lowest!).

Why Right Differs from Left: The right principal bronchus gives off its superior lobar branch BEFORE entering the hilum, so two bronchi (eparterial above, hyparterial below the pulmonary artery) appear at the right hilum!
slides.remember: Front to back (both sides) = V-A-B (Vein, Artery, Bronchus). Top to bottom (Right side) = Eparterial bronchus → Artery → Hyparterial bronchus → Inferior vein!
slides.q: What is the uppermost structure in the root of the RIGHT lung from superior to inferior?
slides.why: Because the right superior lobar bronchus arises before the hilum and passes above the pulmonary artery, the eparterial bronchus is the highest structure in the right lung root.

slides.p: Alongside the main airways and great vessels, the root of the right lung contains smaller structures and is clinically important in thoracic surgery:
bullets: Additional Contents: Right bronchial artery (1 vessel, usually from 3rd right posterior intercostal artery), bronchial veins, anterior & posterior pulmonary nerve plexuses, bronchopulmonary lymph nodes, and areolar tissue.

Applied Anatomy: Enlargement of bronchopulmonary (hilar) lymph nodes in primary tuberculosis or bronchogenic carcinoma produces visible hilar lymphadenopathy on a chest X-ray and can compress adjacent bronchi or the right phrenic nerve.
slides.remember: Right bronchial artery = 1 artery. Left bronchial arteries = 2 arteries (from descending aorta). Inferior pulmonary vein is ALWAYS lowest!
slides.q: Which structure occupies the most inferior position in the root of BOTH the right and left lungs?
slides.why: In both the right and left lung roots, the inferior pulmonary vein is the lowest structure, lying just above the pulmonary ligament.

lessons.exam: SN order: Definition & vertebral level (T5–T7) → Constituents → Arrangement of structures (Anterior-to-Posterior V-A-B + Superior-to-Inferior Eparterial/Artery/Hyparterial/Inf. Vein) → Relations (anterior, posterior, superior, inferior) → Applied anatomy + Labelled right hilum diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Azygos Vein

slides.p: The azygos vein ('unpaired') is a crucial longitudinal venous channel on the right side of the thoracic vertebral column that drains the thoracic wall and upper lumbar region, and acts as a vital collateral bridge between the IVC and SVC.
bullets: Formation: Formed at the L1–L2 level by the union of the right ascending lumbar vein and the right subcostal vein (often also connected to the back of the IVC).
Entry to Thorax: Enters thorax through the aortic opening of the diaphragm (T12) on the right of the thoracic duct and aorta.

Course & Termination: Ascends in the posterior mediastinum to the right of the vertebral bodies up to T4 vertebra, where it arches forward over the root of the right lung to open into the posterior aspect of the Superior Vena Cava (SVC).
slides.remember: Formed by Right Ascending Lumbar + Right Subcostal veins → passes Aortic hiatus (T12) → arches over Right Lung Root at T4 → opens into SVC!
slides.q: The azygos vein enters the thorax by passing through which opening in the diaphragm?
slides.why: The azygos vein passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at the T12 level alongside the aorta and thoracic duct.

slides.p: Memorize the tributaries draining into the azygos system so you can draw a complete venous schematic in your exam:
bullets: 1. Right Superior Intercostal Vein: Formed by union of 2nd, 3rd, and 4th right posterior intercostal veins (opens into the arch of azygos).
2. Lower Eight Right Posterior Intercostal Veins (5th to 11th) + Right Subcostal Vein.
3. Hemiazygos Vein: Crosses from left to right at T8 vertebra behind aorta/esophagus/thoracic duct.
4. Accessory Hemiazygos Vein: Crosses from left to right at T7 vertebra.
5. Visceral Tributaries: Right bronchial veins, esophageal, mediastinal, and pericardial veins.
slides.remember: Hemiazygos crosses at T8; Accessory hemiazygos crosses at T7; Azygos arches over right lung root at T4!
slides.q: At which vertebral level does the hemiazygos vein cross the midline to join the azygos vein?
slides.why: The hemiazygos vein ascends on the left side of the lower thoracic vertebrae and crosses to the right at the T8 level to join the azygos vein.

slides.h: 3. Applied Anatomy — Collateral Bypass Between SVC & IVC
slides.p: Why is the azygos vein clinically indispensable?
bullets: Caval Obstruction Bypass: Because the azygos vein connects the inferior vena cava system (via lumbar/renal veins) directly to the superior vena cava, if the IVC is obstructed (or the SVC is obstructed below the azygos arch), blood detours through the azygos system to keep returning blood to the right atrium!

Azygos Lobe of Lung: A developmental variation where the azygos arch runs more laterally, invaginating a fold of pleura (mesoazygos) into the apex of the right lung to create an accessory 'azygos lobe' visible on chest X-ray.
slides.remember: Azygos = Backup highway connecting IVC and SVC when either vena cava is blocked!
slides.q: What is the major clinical significance of the azygos venous system?
opts: It supplies oxygenated blood to the right atrium
It provides an important collateral venous pathway between the SVC and IVC
It drains venous blood from the brain
It carries chyle from the small intestine
slides.why: The azygos vein links the inferior and superior vena caval territories, serving as an essential collateral bypass channel during obstruction of either vena cava.

lessons.exam: SN order: Introduction → Formation (L1–L2) → Course & relations (aortic hiatus, posterior mediastinum, arch at T4) → Termination (SVC) → Tributaries (including hemiazygos & accessory hemiazygos) → Applied anatomy (SVC/IVC collateral bypass, azygos lobe) + Labelled diagram.

lessons.title: Coronary Sinus

slides.p: The coronary sinus is the largest vein of the heart (~2–3 cm long), draining about 60–70% of the venous blood of the myocardium. It lies in the posterior part of the coronary (atrioventricular) sulcus between the left atrium and left ventricle.
bullets: Origin: Begins at the left end of the posterior coronary sulcus as the direct continuation of the great cardiac vein (marked internally by the valve of Vieussens).
Termination: Opens into the smooth posterior wall of the right atrium, between the inferior vena caval orifice and the right atrioventricular (tricuspid) orifice.
Guard Valve: Its atrial opening is guarded by a semicircular fold of endocardium called the valve of the coronary sinus (Thebesian valve).
slides.remember: Lies in posterior AV groove → opens into Right Atrium between IVC & Tricuspid orifice → guarded by Thebesian valve!
slides.q: The coronary sinus opens into the right atrium between which two openings?
opts: Superior vena cava and right auricle
Inferior vena cava orifice and right atrioventricular (tricuspid) orifice
Fossa ovalis and superior vena cava
slides.why: The orifice of the coronary sinus lies in the smooth sinus venarum of the right atrium between the IVC opening and the tricuspid orifice, guarded by the Thebesian valve.

slides.p: Memorize the five classic tributaries of the coronary sinus (and remember which cardiac veins do NOT enter it!):
bullets: 1. Great Cardiac Vein: Ascends in anterior interventricular groove alongside LAD → enters left end of coronary sinus.
2. Middle Cardiac Vein: Ascends in posterior interventricular groove alongside PDA → enters right end of coronary sinus.
3. Small Cardiac Vein: Runs along right margin with right marginal artery → enters right end of coronary sinus.
4. Posterior Vein of Left Ventricle: Drains diaphragmatic surface of left ventricle.
5. Oblique Vein of Left Atrium (of Marshall): Descends on back of left atrium (remnant of left common cardinal vein).
Veins that bypass Coronary Sinus: Anterior cardiac veins (3–4 small veins on anterior right ventricle) and Venae cordis minimae (Thebesian veins) open directly into the heart chambers!
slides.remember: 5 tributaries of Coronary Sinus: Great, Middle, Small, Posterior of LV, Oblique of LA. Anterior cardiac & Thebesian veins open directly into chambers!
slides.q: Which of the following cardiac veins opens directly into the anterior wall of the right atrium rather than into the coronary sinus?
slides.why: The anterior cardiac veins drain the anterior wall of the right ventricle, cross the coronary sulcus, and open directly into the right atrium.

slides.h: 3. Applied Anatomy — Retrograde Cardioplegia & Cardiac Resynchronization
slides.p: Modern cardiology uses the coronary sinus as an anatomical doorway to the left side of the heart:
bullets: Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy (CRT / Biventricular Pacing): A pacing lead is passed from the right atrium through the coronary sinus into a left ventricular tributary to pace the left ventricle.
Retrograde Cardioplegia: During open-heart surgery when coronary arteries are severely blocked, cardioplegic solution can be infused backward through the coronary sinus to protect the myocardium.
slides.remember: Coronary sinus = Venous backdoor to pace the Left Ventricle (CRT) or deliver retrograde cardioplegia!
slides.q: Which endocardial valve guards the opening of the coronary sinus into the right atrium?
slides.why: The valve of the coronary sinus is known as the Thebesian valve (whereas the Eustachian valve guards the inferior vena cava).

lessons.exam: SN order: Situation & extent → Opening into right atrium (Thebesian valve) → Five tributaries (plus note on anterior cardiac & Thebesian veins) → Development (left horn of sinus venosus) → Applied anatomy + Labelled posterior view of heart diagram.

lessons.title: Typical Intercostal Nerve

slides.h: 1. What is a Typical Intercostal Nerve & Its Course?
slides.p: The 3rd, 4th, 5th, and 6th thoracic spinal nerves (anterior primary rami) are called typical intercostal nerves because their entire course and distribution are confined strictly to the thoracic wall (unlike T1–T2 which contribute to the upper limb, and T7–T11 which continue into the anterior abdominal wall).
bullets: Course in Intercostal Space: Enters the posterior end of the intercostal space between the pleura and posterior intercostal membrane, then runs forward in the costal groove along the inferior border of the upper rib, lying below the posterior intercostal vein and artery (V-A-N from above downward).
Plane of Course: Travels between the internal intercostal and innermost intercostal (intercostalis intimi) muscles.

Termination: Near the sternum, crosses in front of the internal thoracic vessels, pierces internal intercostal, anterior intercostal membrane, and pectoralis major to end as the anterior cutaneous branch.
slides.remember: Typical intercostal nerves = T3, T4, T5, T6! Order in costal groove from top to bottom = V-A-N (Vein, Artery, Nerve)!
slides.q: Which thoracic spinal nerves are classified as 'typical' intercostal nerves?
slides.why: The 3rd through 6th intercostal nerves (T3–T6) are confined exclusively to the thoracic wall and are therefore termed typical intercostal nerves.

slides.h: 2. Branches of a Typical Intercostal Nerve
slides.p: Organize the branches clearly into Motor, Sensory, and Communicating branches:
bullets: 1. Muscular (Motor) Branches: Supply external intercostal, internal intercostal, innermost intercostal, subcostalis, and transversus thoracis muscles.
2. Collateral Branch: Arises near the angle of the rib and runs forward along the upper border of the lower rib (forming a lower neurovascular bundle).
3. Lateral Cutaneous Branch: Arises near the midaxillary line, pierces external intercostal, and divides into anterior and posterior branches supplying skin on the lateral chest wall.
4. Anterior Cutaneous Branch: Terminal sensory branch supplying skin near the midline (divides into medial & lateral branches).
5. Rami Communicantes: White (preganglionic) and grey (postganglionic) rami connecting the nerve to the corresponding thoracic sympathetic ganglion.
slides.remember: T4 dermatome = Nipple level! Lateral cutaneous branch pierces at the midaxillary line.
slides.q: In the costal groove along the inferior border of a rib, what is the arrangement of structures from superior to inferior?
slides.why: From superior to inferior inside the costal groove, the neurovascular bundle is arranged as Vein, Artery, Nerve (V-A-N), making the nerve the lowest and most exposed structure.

slides.h: 3. Applied Anatomy — Thoracocentesis, Herpes Zoster & Root Pain
slides.p: Three clinical pearls will make your Short Note stand out:
bullets: Thoracocentesis (Pleural Tap): Because the main intercostal V-A-N runs along the inferior border of the upper rib, a needle is always inserted along the superior border of the lower rib (in the midaxillary line) to avoid injuring the intercostal nerve and vessels.

Herpes Zoster (Shingles): Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus dormant in a thoracic dorsal root ganglion produces a painful vesicular rash strictly confined to a single unilateral intercostal dermatome belt.
Intercostal Neuralgia / Root Pain: Irritation of thoracic spinal roots (e.g., Pott's spine / TB of vertebra) causes sharp girdle-like pain radiating along the intercostal space.
slides.remember: Pleural tap needle goes ABOVE the lower rib (safe zone) to avoid V-A-N tucked under the upper rib!
slides.q: During thoracocentesis (pleural tapping), where should the needle be inserted to avoid damaging the main intercostal neurovascular bundle?
opts: Immediately below the inferior border of the upper rib
Just above the superior border of the lower rib
Directly through the center of the rib
Alongside the sternum in the 1st intercostal space
slides.why: Since the intercostal vein, artery, and nerve lie sheltered in the costal groove along the inferior border of the upper rib, inserting the needle just above the superior border of the lower rib avoids neurovascular injury.

lessons.exam: SN order: Definition (T3–T6) → Course & relations in costal groove (V-A-N, muscle plane) → Branches (muscular, collateral, lateral cutaneous, anterior cutaneous, rami communicantes) → Applied anatomy (thoracocentesis safe site, herpes zoster, intercostal nerve block) + Labelled diagram of intercostal space.

lessons.title: Ulnar Nerve

slides.h: 1. Root Value, Origin & Course in Arm & Elbow
slides.p: The ulnar nerve (C8, T1 — often with C7 fibres) is the direct continuation of the medial cord of the brachial plexus. It is called the 'musician's nerve' because it powers fine finger movements.
bullets: In Axilla & Upper Arm: Descends medial to the axillary and brachial arteries.
At Mid-Arm (Insertion of Coracobrachialis): Pierces the medial intermuscular septum to enter the posterior compartment of the arm alongside the superior ulnar collateral artery.
At Elbow (Superficial & Vulnerable!): Passes behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus ('funny bone') and enters the forearm between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris (cubital tunnel).
slides.remember: Medial cord (C8, T1) → pierces Medial Intermuscular Septum at mid-arm → runs BEHIND Medial Epicondyle → between 2 heads of FCU!
slides.q: The ulnar nerve is the direct continuation of which cord of the brachial plexus?
slides.why: The ulnar nerve arises as the largest terminal branch of the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C8, T1, with a C7 contribution to FCU).

slides.p: In the forearm, the ulnar nerve runs vertically on flexor digitorum profundus under cover of flexor carpi ulnaris. At the wrist, it enters the hand superficial to the flexor retinaculum through Guyon's canal (lateral to pisiform) and divides into superficial and deep terminal branches.
bullets: Forearm Muscular Branches (1½ muscles): Flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) and medial half of flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) (for ring & little fingers).
Cutaneous Branches: Palmar cutaneous branch (hypothenar skin) & dorsal cutaneous branch (dorsal medial 1½ digits).

Deep Terminal Branch in Hand (15 intrinsic muscles): Supplies 3 hypothenar muscles, medial 2 lumbricals (3rd & 4th), all 4 palmar & 4 dorsal interossei, adductor pollicis, and deep head of flexor pollicis brevis. (Superficial branch supplies palmaris brevis + palmar skin of medial 1½ digits).
slides.remember: Forearm = FCU + medial ½ FDP. Hand = ALL intrinsic muscles EXCEPT LOAF (Median nerve)!
slides.q: Which intrinsic muscle of the hand is innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve?
slides.why: Adductor pollicis, all interossei, hypothenar muscles, and the medial two lumbricals are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

slides.h: 3. Applied Anatomy — Ulnar Claw Hand, Ulnar Paradox & Froment's Sign
slides.p: Ulnar nerve injury (behind the medial epicondyle or at the wrist) produces hallmark clinical signs:
bullets: Ulnar Claw Hand: Hyperextension at MCP joints and flexion at IP joints of the ring and little fingers (paralysis of medial 2 lumbricals & interossei).
Ulnar Paradox: Clawing is MORE pronounced in a distal wrist lesion than in a proximal elbow lesion because an elbow lesion also paralyzes the medial half of FDP, removing unopposed DIP flexion.
Froment's Sign (Book Test): When gripping a paper between thumb and index finger, the patient flexes the thumb IP joint (recruiting median-supplied FPL) to compensate for paralyzed adductor pollicis.
slides.remember: Ulnar paradox = Wrist lesion claws MORE than elbow lesion! Froment's sign tests Adductor Pollicis!
slides.q: A positive Froment's sign (flexion of the thumb IP joint when holding paper) indicates paralysis of which muscle?
slides.why: Weakness of ulnar-innervated adductor pollicis forces the patient to flex the thumb IP joint using flexor pollicis longus.

lessons.exam: LAQ order: Root value & origin → Course & relations (axilla, arm, elbow/cubital tunnel, forearm, Guyon's canal) → Branches (muscular, cutaneous, articular) → Applied anatomy (ulnar claw hand, ulnar paradox, Froment's sign, medial 1½ digit sensory loss) + Labelled diagram.
