lessons.title: Radial Nerve

slides.h: 1. Root Value, Origin & Course in Spiral Groove
slides.p: The radial nerve (C5, C6, C7, C8, T1) is the largest branch of the brachial plexus and the direct continuation of the posterior cord—supplying the extensor compartments of both arm and forearm.
bullets: In Axilla & Upper Arm: Lies behind the 3rd part of axillary artery; passes through the lower triangular space into the radial (spiral) groove on the back of the humerus alongside the profunda brachii artery.
Lateral Side of Arm: Pierces the lateral intermuscular septum ~10 cm above the lateral epicondyle, descending between brachialis (medially) and brachioradialis + ECRL (laterally).
Termination: Anterior to the lateral epicondyle, divides into superficial radial nerve (sensory) and deep radial / posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) (pierces supinator).
slides.remember: Posterior cord (C5–T1) → Spiral groove with Profunda Brachii artery → Lateral epicondyle splits into Superficial (sensory) & Deep/PIN (motor)!
slides.q: Which artery accompanies the radial nerve inside the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus?
slides.why: The radial nerve runs obliquely across the posterior humerus in the spiral groove together with the profunda brachii vessels.

slides.p: Group radial nerve branches by anatomical segment for clear recall:
bullets: In Axilla (proximal to spiral groove): Long & medial heads of triceps brachii + posterior cutaneous nerve of arm.
In Spiral Groove: Lateral & medial heads of triceps, anconeus, lower lateral cutaneous nerve of arm, and posterior cutaneous nerve of forearm.
In Lateral Compartment (above lateral epicondyle): Brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus (ECRL), and proprioceptive twig to lateral brachialis.
Via Deep Branch / Posterior Interosseous Nerve (PIN): Supinator, ECRB, and all superficial & deep extensor muscles of posterior forearm (ED, EDM, ECU, APL, EPB, EPL, EI).
Via Superficial Branch: Dorsal skin of lateral 3½ digits up to distal phalanges.
slides.remember: BEST = Brachioradialis, Extensors, Supinator, Triceps! Only Brachioradialis & ECRL are supplied BEFORE the elbow bifurcation!
slides.q: Which two forearm muscles receive motor branches directly from the radial nerve trunk BEFORE it bifurcates at the elbow?
opts: Brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus (ECRL)
Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
slides.why: Brachioradialis and ECRL arise from the lateral supracondylar ridge and receive branches directly from the radial nerve trunk above the lateral epicondyle.

slides.h: 3. Applied Anatomy — Wrist Drop & Lesion Levels
slides.p: Clinical deficits vary sharply with the site of radial nerve injury:
bullets: 1. Injury in Axilla (Crutch Palsy): Loss of elbow extension (triceps) + Wrist drop + sensory loss over posterior arm, forearm & anatomical snuffbox.

2. Injury in Spiral Groove (Mid-shaft Humeral Fracture / 'Saturday Night Palsy'): Elbow extension is SPARED (nerves to long & medial heads of triceps arose higher in axilla!), but patient develops Wrist Drop + sensory loss over anatomical snuffbox.
3. Injury to Posterior Interosseous Nerve (PIN — Radial Neck Fracture): Finger drop (loss of MCP extension), but NO wrist drop (ECRL spared!) and NO sensory loss.
slides.remember: Spiral groove fracture → Triceps SPARED, Wrist Drop PRESENT! Anatomical snuffbox = autonomous sensory zone of radial nerve!
slides.q: Why is elbow extension usually spared when the radial nerve is injured in the spiral groove during a mid-shaft humeral fracture?
opts: Triceps is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve
Branches to the long and medial heads of triceps arise in the axilla proximal to the spiral groove
slides.why: Motor branches to the long head and upper part of the medial head of triceps arise in the axilla before the radial nerve enters the spiral groove.

lessons.exam: LAQ order: Root value & origin → Course & relations (axilla, spiral groove, cubital region, terminal branches) → Branches (by segment) → Applied anatomy (axillary vs spiral groove vs PIN lesions, wrist drop, anatomical snuffbox testing) + Labelled diagram.

lessons.title: Median Nerve

slides.h: 1. Root Value, Formation & Course in Arm & Forearm
slides.p: The median nerve (C5, C6, C7, C8, T1) is formed in the axilla by the union of the lateral root (lateral cord) and medial root (medial cord) embracing the 3rd part of the axillary artery—known as the 'labourer's nerve'.
bullets: In Arm (No muscular branches): Descends lateral to the brachial artery, crosses anteriorly from lateral to medial at mid-arm, and enters the cubital fossa medial to the brachial artery.
In Forearm: Exits cubital fossa between the two heads of pronator teres, passes deep to the tendinous arch of FDS, and descends adherent to the deep surface of FDS.
At Wrist: Lies between tendons of FCR and FDS (medial to palmaris longus), passes through the carpal tunnel deep to the flexor retinaculum, and divides into lateral & medial branches.
slides.remember: Lateral + Medial roots → crosses brachial artery frontally at mid-arm → between 2 heads of Pronator Teres → Carpal Tunnel!
slides.q: The median nerve enters the forearm by passing between the two heads of which muscle?
slides.why: The median nerve passes between the humeral and ulnar heads of pronator teres in the cubital region.

slides.p: The median nerve innervates most anterior forearm flexors/pronators and the thenar eminence:
bullets: Direct Forearm Branches: Pronator teres, Flexor carpi radialis (FCR), Palmaris longus, and Flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS).
Anterior Interosseous Nerve (AIN — pure motor): Supplies Flexor pollicis longus (FPL), lateral half of FDP (index & middle fingers), and Pronator quadratus.
Palmar Cutaneous Branch: Arises ABOVE the flexor retinaculum → supplies central palm/thenar skin (SPARED in carpal tunnel syndrome!).

Hand Branches (LOAF): Recurrent motor branch to the 3 thenar muscles (Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis) + Lateral 2 lumbricals (1st & 2nd) + palmar digital nerves to lateral 3½ digits (including dorsal nail beds).
slides.remember: Hand muscles = LOAF (Lumbricals 1 & 2, Opponens, Abductor, Flexor pollicis brevis). Palmar cutaneous branch passes OVER carpal tunnel!
slides.q: Which deep forearm flexor muscle is supplied by the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve?
opts: Medial half of flexor digitorum profundus
slides.why: The anterior interosseous nerve supplies flexor pollicis longus, the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus, and pronator quadratus.

slides.h: 3. Applied Anatomy — Ape Thumb, Pointing Index & Carpal Tunnel
slides.p: Clinical signs depend on whether the lesion is at the elbow or wrist:
bullets: Injury at Elbow (Supracondylar Fracture): Loss of pronation, weak wrist flexion with ulnar deviation, Pointing Index / Benediction Hand (on attempting a fist, index and middle fingers fail to flex because FDS & lateral FDP are paralyzed), and Ape Thumb Deformity (thenar wasting + thumb rotated into palm plane).
Injury at Wrist (Carpal Tunnel Syndrome): Nocturnal paresthesia in lateral 3½ digits and thenar wasting, while skin over the central palm/thenar eminence is SPARED.
Pen Test: Tests abductor pollicis brevis (thumb cannot abduct anteriorly to touch a pen held above the palm).
slides.remember: Elbow injury = Pointing Index + Ape Thumb. Wrist/Carpal tunnel = Lateral 3½ digits numb, palm skin SPARED!
slides.q: Why is skin sensation over the central palm spared in carpal tunnel syndrome?
opts: It is supplied by the radial nerve
The palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to and passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum
The ulnar nerve supplies the central palm
Sensory fibres lie deep to the carpal bones
slides.why: The palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve proximal to the wrist and travels superficial to the flexor retinaculum.

lessons.exam: LAQ order: Root value & formation → Course & relations (axilla, arm, cubital fossa, forearm, carpal tunnel, hand) → Branches (muscular, anterior interosseous, palmar cutaneous, digital) → Applied anatomy (pointing index, ape thumb, carpal tunnel syndrome, pen test) + Labelled diagram.

lessons.title: Axillary Artery

slides.h: 1. Extent, Course & Division into Three Parts
slides.p: The axillary artery continues the subclavian artery from the outer border of the 1st rib to the lower border of teres major (where it becomes the brachial artery). The pectoralis minor muscle crosses anteriorly and divides it into three parts:
bullets: 1st Part: Superior (proximal) to pectoralis minor (outer border of 1st rib to upper border of pectoralis minor).
2nd Part: Deep (posterior) to pectoralis minor.
3rd Part: Inferior (distal) to pectoralis minor (lower border of pectoralis minor to lower border of teres major).
slides.remember: 1st rib → divided into 3 parts by Pectoralis Minor → becomes Brachial artery at lower border of Teres Major!
slides.q: Which muscle crosses anterior to the axillary artery and divides it into three parts?
slides.why: Pectoralis minor crosses in front of the axillary artery, dividing it into 1st, 2nd, and 3rd parts.

slides.p: The cords of the brachial plexus are named according to their relation to the 2nd part of the axillary artery, and each part gives off branches equal to its own number:
bullets: 1st Part (1 branch): Superior thoracic artery.
2nd Part (2 branches): Thoracoacromial artery (4 branches: Pectoral, Acromial, Clavicular, Deltoid — 'ABCD') and Lateral thoracic artery (accompanies long thoracic nerve).

3rd Part (3 branches): Subscapular artery (largest branch! Splits into circumflex scapular & thoracodorsal arteries), Anterior circumflex humeral artery, and Posterior circumflex humeral artery (passes through quadrangular space with axillary nerve).
slides.remember: 1st part = 1 branch. 2nd part = 2 branches (Thoracoacromial, Lateral thoracic). 3rd part = 3 branches (Subscapular, Anterior & Posterior circumflex humeral)!
slides.q: Which is the largest branch of the axillary artery, arising from its third part?
slides.why: The subscapular artery is the largest branch of the axillary artery, arising from its 3rd part.

slides.p: Collateral circulation around the scapula protects the upper limb if the axillary artery is occluded:
bullets: Scapular Anastomosis: Connects branches of the 1st part of subclavian artery (suprascapular & dorsal scapular / deep branch of transverse cervical) with branches of the 3rd part of axillary artery (subscapular & circumflex scapular arteries).

Emergency Compression: The distal 3rd part of the axillary artery can be compressed against the medial aspect of the upper humeral shaft (near coracobrachialis insertion) to control upper-limb bleeding.
slides.remember: Scapular anastomosis links 1st part Subclavian with 3rd part Axillary!
slides.q: Where can the third part of the axillary artery be effectively compressed against bone to control distal arterial hemorrhage?
opts: Against the upper shaft of the humerus near coracobrachialis insertion
slides.why: The lower 3rd part lies superficially on the medial side of the upper humerus where it can be compressed directly against the shaft.

lessons.exam: LAQ order: Origin, course & termination → Divisions by pectoralis minor → Relations of 1st, 2nd, and 3rd parts (especially brachial plexus cords & terminal branches) → Six branches → Scapular anastomosis & applied anatomy + Labelled diagram.

lessons.title: Mid-Palmar Space

slides.p: The mid-palmar space (of Kanavel) is a deep triangular fascial space under the medial half of the hollow of the palm, behind the flexor tendons and in front of the medial three metacarpals.
bullets: Anterior (Roof): Flexor tendons of medial three fingers (FDS & FDP), 2nd, 3rd, and 4th lumbricals, palmar aponeurosis, and superficial palmar arch.
Posterior (Floor): Fascia covering the 3rd, 4th, and 5th metacarpals and medial interosseous muscles.
Medial Border: Medial palmar septum (from medial border of palmar aponeurosis to 5th metacarpal).
Lateral Border: Intermediate (oblique) palmar septum (from palmar aponeurosis to palmar border of 3rd metacarpal shaft, separating it from the thenar space).
slides.remember: Intermediate septum attaches to the 3rd Metacarpal — separating Thenar Space (lateral) from Mid-Palmar Space (medial)!
slides.q: To which metacarpal bone does the intermediate palmar septum attach to separate the mid-palmar space from the thenar space?
slides.why: The intermediate septum attaches to the anterior border of the 3rd metacarpal, separating the thenar and mid-palmar spaces.

slides.p: Understanding its communications explains both the spread and surgical drainage of palmar abscesses:
bullets: Proximally: Closed off by the ulnar bursa, though severe infection can rupture through the carpal tunnel into the forearm space of Parona.
Distally: Continuous with the medial three lumbrical canals (2nd, 3rd, 4th) leading to the medial web spaces.

Clinical Signs & Drainage: Pus causes loss (obliteration) of normal palmar concavity and marked dorsal hand edema (loose dorsal skin & dorsal lymphatic drainage). Drained surgically via longitudinal incisions in the 3rd or 4th web space along the lumbrical canal.
slides.remember: Mid-palmar space infection = Palm loses concavity + Dorsum swells + Drain via 3rd or 4th Web Space!
slides.q: What is the classic local physical sign of pus accumulating in the mid-palmar space?
opts: Loss (obliteration) of the normal concavity of the palm
slides.why: Pus beneath the taut palmar aponeurosis flattens or bulges out the normal hollow concavity of the palm.

lessons.exam: LAQ order: Definition & situation → Boundaries (anterior, posterior, medial, lateral/intermediate septum) → Communications (proximal with forearm space of Parona, distal with medial 3 lumbrical canals) → Applied anatomy (infection sources, clinical features, web-space surgical drainage) + Transverse section diagram of palm.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Erb's Paralysis

slides.p: Erb's paralysis (Erb-Duchenne palsy) results from traction injury to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5, C6) at Erb's point—where six nerves meet (C5 root, C6 root, anterior & posterior divisions of upper trunk, suprascapular nerve, and nerve to subclavius).
bullets: Mechanism: Undue separation of the head from the shoulder.
Causes: Birth traction injury, falling on the shoulder, or anesthesia malpositioning.
slides.remember: Erb's point = 6 nerves meeting at Upper Trunk (C5, C6)! Caused by excessive head-to-shoulder separation.
slides.q: Which part of the brachial plexus is injured in Erb's paralysis?
slides.why: Erb's paralysis involves the upper trunk (roots C5 and C6) at Erb's point.

slides.p: Loss of C5–C6 abductors/lateral rotators and flexors/supinators creates the classic 'Policeman's / Porter's Tip Hand':
bullets: Muscles Paralyzed: Supraspinatus & Infraspinatus (suprascapular nerve), Deltoid & Teres minor (axillary nerve), Biceps, Brachialis, Coracobrachialis (musculocutaneous nerve), and Brachioradialis & Supinator (radial nerve).
Deformity: Arm hangs adducted and medially rotated; forearm is extended and pronated; biceps & supinator jerks are lost; sensory loss over lower lateral arm.
slides.remember: Policeman's Tip = Arm Adducted & Medially Rotated + Forearm Extended & Pronated!
slides.q: What is the characteristic limb posture in Erb's paralysis ('Policeman's tip' deformity)?
opts: Arm abducted and laterally rotated; forearm flexed and supinated
Arm adducted and medially rotated; forearm extended and pronated
slides.why: Unopposed adductors/medial rotators and extensors/pronators hold the arm adducted & medially rotated and the forearm extended & pronated.

lessons.exam: SN order: Definition & site (Erb's point — 6 nerves) → Causes → Root value (C5, C6) → Muscles paralyzed → Deformity ('Policeman's tip' explained) → Sensory & reflex loss + Diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Klumpke's Paralysis

slides.h: 1. Site of Injury, Root Value & Causes
slides.p: Klumpke's paralysis is an injury to the lower trunk of the brachial plexus, affecting mainly T1 (and C8) due to undue upward traction (hyperabduction) of the arm.
bullets: Causes: Grabbing an overhead support while falling from a height, pulling the arm during breech birth, or compression by a cervical rib / apical lung (Pancoast) tumor.
slides.remember: Erb = Pulling arm DOWN (C5, C6). Klumpke = Pulling arm UP (C8, T1)!
slides.q: Klumpke's paralysis is caused by injury to which roots of the brachial plexus?
slides.why: Klumpke's paralysis damages the lower trunk (C8 and T1 roots, predominantly T1).

slides.h: 2. Clinical Features — Complete Claw Hand & Horner's Syndrome
slides.p: T1 supplies all intrinsic hand muscles and carries sympathetic outflow to the head and neck:
bullets: 1. Complete Claw Hand: Paralysis of all intrinsic muscles of the hand (lumbricals & interossei) → hyperextension at MCP joints and flexion at IP joints of all fingers.
2. Sensory Loss: Narrow strip along the medial border of forearm and hand (T1, C8).
3. Horner's Syndrome (if T1 root is injured proximal to white ramus communicans): Ptosis, Miosis, Anhidrosis, and enophthalmos.
slides.remember: Klumpke's triad = Complete Claw Hand + Medial forearm sensory loss + Horner's Syndrome!
slides.q: Why can Klumpke's paralysis be associated with Horner's syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis)?
opts: Injury to T1 root proximal to the white ramus communicans carrying sympathetic fibres to head and neck
slides.why: Preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the superior cervical ganglion leave the spinal cord in the T1 ventral root.

lessons.exam: SN order: Definition & root value (T1, C8) → Causes → Muscles paralyzed → Clinical features (Complete claw hand, medial forearm sensory loss, Horner's syndrome) + Comparison table with Erb's palsy.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Rotator Cuff (Musculotendinous Cuff)

slides.p: The rotator cuff is a musculotendinous collar formed by four scapular tendons blending with the shoulder joint capsule to dynamically stabilize the humeral head in the glenoid cavity:
bullets: Supraspinatus (Superior): Upper impression of greater tubercle (Suprascapular nerve, C5–C6).
Infraspinatus (Posterior): Middle impression of greater tubercle (Suprascapular nerve, C5–C6).
Teres Minor (Posteroinferior): Lower impression of greater tubercle (Axillary nerve, C5–C6).
Subscapularis (Anterior): Lesser tubercle (Upper & lower subscapular nerves, C5–C6).
Inferior Deficiency: The cuff is absent inferiorly, making anteroinferior shoulder dislocation most common.
slides.remember: SITS = Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor (Greater tubercle) + Subscapularis (Lesser tubercle). Inferiorly there is NO cuff!
slides.q: Which rotator cuff muscle inserts onto the LESSER tubercle of the humerus?
slides.why: Subscapularis inserts onto the lesser tubercle anteriorly, whereas the other three insert onto the greater tubercle.

slides.p: The rotator cuff holds the humeral head snugly against the glenoid during movement:
bullets: Supraspinatus Tendinitis & Painful Arc Syndrome: Supraspinatus is the most commonly torn cuff tendon (hypovascular critical zone beneath coracoacromial arch), causing pain during 60°–120° abduction.
slides.remember: Supraspinatus = Most commonly torn cuff tendon! Painful arc = 60°–120° abduction.
slides.q: Which rotator cuff tendon is most frequently degenerated or torn?
slides.why: Supraspinatus passes beneath the coracoacromial arch and has a hypovascular critical zone near its insertion.

lessons.exam: SN order: Definition → Four SITS muscles (attachments, nerve supply, action) → Subacromial bursa & inferior deficiency → Functions → Applied anatomy (supraspinatus tear, painful arc syndrome) + Diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Abduction at Shoulder Joint

slides.p: Overhead abduction (0°–180°) combines glenohumeral motion and scapular rotation in a 2:1 ratio (scapulohumeral rhythm) (10° glenohumeral : 5° scapular per 15°):
bullets: 0° to 15°: Initiated by Supraspinatus (suprascapular nerve, C5–C6).
15° to 90°: Performed by acromial fibres of Deltoid (axillary nerve, C5–C6).

90° to 180° (Overhead): Upward rotation of scapula by Serratus Anterior (long thoracic nerve) and Trapezius (spinal accessory nerve), with lateral rotation of humerus so greater tubercle clears the acromion.
slides.remember: 0–15° = Supraspinatus. 15–90° = Deltoid. 90–180° = Serratus Anterior + Trapezius!
slides.q: Which two muscles rotate the scapula upward during overhead abduction (90° to 180°)?
slides.why: Serratus anterior and trapezius form a force couple rotating the glenoid cavity upward beyond 90°.

slides.p: Each stage tests a specific nerve:
bullets: Cannot initiate 0°–15°: Suprascapular nerve / Supraspinatus tear.
Cannot lift 15°–90°: Axillary nerve injury (surgical neck fracture).
Cannot raise overhead 90°–180° + Winging of Scapula: Long thoracic nerve injury (serratus anterior paralysis).
slides.remember: Can't reach overhead (90–180°) + Winged scapula = Long Thoracic Nerve (Serratus Anterior)!
slides.q: Inability to abduct the arm from 90° to 180° accompanied by winging of the scapula indicates injury to which nerve?
slides.why: Long thoracic nerve injury paralyzes serratus anterior, preventing overhead scapular upward rotation and causing scapular winging.

lessons.exam: SN order: Range (0°–180°) → Scapulohumeral rhythm (2:1) → Three stages with muscles & nerve supply → Role of humeral lateral rotation → Applied anatomy + Diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Pronation and Supination

slides.p: Pronation and supination are rotatory forearm movements occurring at the superior and inferior radioulnar pivot joints around an oblique axis passing through the center of the radial head above and the base of the ulnar styloid below.
bullets: Mechanics: During pronation, the radial head spins in the annular ligament while the distal radius swings anteriorly and medially around the ulnar head.
Power: Supination is stronger than pronation.
slides.remember: Pivot joints (superior & inferior radioulnar). Axis = Radial head to Ulnar styloid base!
slides.q: What type of synovial joints are the superior and inferior radioulnar joints?
slides.why: Both superior and inferior radioulnar joints are uniaxial pivot joints.

slides.p: Memorize the prime movers for both directions:
bullets: Supinators: Supinator (deep radial / PIN — slow/unresisted) + Biceps brachii (musculocutaneous — powerful when elbow is flexed).
Pronators: Pronator quadratus (AIN — prime mover) + Pronator teres (median — rapid/resisted).
Pulled Elbow: Sudden traction on a pronated forearm in a child slips the radial head out of the annular ligament.
slides.remember: Supinators = Supinator + Biceps brachii. Pronators = Pronator quadratus + Pronator teres.
slides.q: Which muscle is the most powerful supinator when the elbow is flexed to 90°?
slides.why: Biceps brachii inserts onto the posterior radial tuberosity and acts as a powerful supinator when the elbow is flexed.

lessons.exam: SN order: Definition → Joints involved (superior & inferior radioulnar pivot joints) → Axis → Mechanics → Muscles with nerve supply → Applied anatomy (pulled elbow, radius shaft fractures) + Diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Clavipectoral Fascia

slides.p: The clavipectoral fascia is a strong fibrous sheet deep to pectoralis major bridging the gap between the clavicle and pectoralis minor:
bullets: Superiorly: Splits to enclose subclavius (attaching to lips of subclavian groove on clavicle).
Inferiorly: Splits to enclose pectoralis minor, then continues downward as the suspensory ligament of the axilla (attaching to axillary fascia to maintain the hollow armpit).
Costocoracoid Ligament: Thickened upper border between 1st rib and coracoid process.
slides.remember: Encloses Subclavius & Pectoralis Minor → continues as Suspensory Ligament of Axilla!
slides.q: The downward continuation of the clavipectoral fascia below pectoralis minor forms:
slides.why: Below pectoralis minor, the fascia continues as the suspensory ligament of the axilla.

slides.p: Between subclavius and pectoralis minor, four structures pierce the fascia:
bullets: 1. Cephalic vein, 2. Thoracoacromial artery, 3. Lateral pectoral nerve, and 4. Lymphatics from breast/pectoral region to apical axillary nodes.
Exam Trap: The medial pectoral nerve pierces pectoralis minor directly, NOT the clavipectoral fascia!
slides.remember: 4 piercing structures (C-T-L-L): Cephalic vein, Thoracoacromial artery, Lateral pectoral nerve, Lymphatics!
slides.q: Which of the following structures does NOT pierce the clavipectoral fascia?
slides.why: The medial pectoral nerve pierces pectoralis minor directly rather than the clavipectoral fascia.

lessons.exam: SN order: Situation → Extent & attachments (subclavius, costocoracoid ligament, pectoralis minor, suspensory ligament of axilla) → Four piercing structures → Applied anatomy + Sagittal diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Clawhand – Features and Causative Factors

slides.p: Clawhand is characterized by hyperextension at the MCP joints and flexion at the PIP and DIP joints due to paralysis of the lumbricals and interossei (leaving extensor digitorum and FDS/FDP unopposed).
bullets: Partial (Ulnar) Clawhand: Affects only ring & little fingers (medial 2 lumbricals & interossei paralyzed).
Complete Clawhand: Affects all four medial fingers (all lumbricals & interossei paralyzed).
slides.remember: Hyperextended MCP + Flexed IP = Clawhand (loss of lumbricals & interossei)!
slides.q: What is the characteristic finger joint posture in clawhand?
slides.why: Loss of intrinsic lumbricals/interossei causes unopposed MCP hyperextension and IP flexion.

slides.p: Distinguish partial vs complete clawhand causes in your exam:
bullets: Partial Clawhand: Ulnar nerve injury at wrist (more marked — ulnar paradox) or elbow, and leprosy.
Complete Clawhand: Klumpke's paralysis (C8, T1), combined ulnar + median nerve injury at wrist, Volkmann's ischemic contracture, and C8–T1 anterior horn cell lesions (syringomyelia/poliomyelitis).
slides.remember: Complete claw = Klumpke's palsy (T1), combined Median + Ulnar lesion, or Volkmann's ischemic contracture!
slides.q: Which lesion produces a COMPLETE clawhand involving all four medial fingers?
slides.why: Klumpke's paralysis paralyzes all T1-innervated intrinsic hand muscles, producing a complete clawhand.

lessons.exam: SN order: Definition & posture (MCP hyperextension + IP flexion) → Mechanism → Partial vs Complete clawhand causes (Ulnar lesion, Klumpke's, combined median+ulnar, Volkmann's, leprosy) + Ulnar paradox note.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Musculocutaneous Nerve

slides.p: The musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6, C7) arises from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus and supplies the anterior compartment of the arm.
bullets: Course: Pierces coracobrachialis, descends between biceps brachii and brachialis, and emerges lateral to the biceps tendon at the elbow to continue as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.
slides.remember: Lateral cord (C5–C7) → pierces Coracobrachialis → between Biceps & Brachialis → Lateral Cutaneous Nerve of Forearm!
slides.q: Which muscle is pierced by the musculocutaneous nerve in the arm?
slides.why: The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis after leaving the lateral cord.

slides.p: Supplies the BBC muscles and lateral forearm skin:
bullets: Muscular (BBC): Biceps brachii, Brachialis, Coracobrachialis.
Cutaneous & Articular: Lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm + elbow joint.
Clinical: Injury causes weak elbow flexion, weak supination, loss of biceps jerk (C5–C6), and lateral forearm sensory loss.
slides.remember: BBC = Biceps, Brachialis, Coracobrachialis!
slides.q: At the elbow, the musculocutaneous nerve continues into the forearm as the:
slides.why: It pierces deep fascia lateral to the biceps tendon to become the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

lessons.exam: SN order: Root value (C5–C7) & origin → Course & relations → Branches (BBC muscles, lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm) → Applied anatomy + Diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Tongue

slides.p: The tongue is a muscular organ in the oral cavity floor essential for taste, mastication, deglutition, and speech. The V-shaped sulcus terminalis (apex pointing backward at the foramen cecum) divides the dorsum into an oral part (anterior 2/3) and a pharyngeal part (posterior 1/3).
bullets: Vallate (Circumvallate) Papillae: 8–12 large circular papillae immediately in front of the sulcus terminalis (supplied by CN IX!).
Fungiform Papillae: Mushroom-shaped red spots mainly at tip & margins.
Filiform Papillae: Most numerous, pointed, keratinized, velvety texture, NO taste buds.
Posterior 1/3 (Pharyngeal Part): No papillae; studded with lymphoid nodules forming the lingual tonsil.
slides.remember: Sulcus terminalis splits tongue into Anterior 2/3 (oral) and Posterior 1/3 (pharyngeal). Circumvallate papillae sit IN FRONT of sulcus terminalis, yet get taste from CN IX!
slides.q: Which type of lingual papillae is the most numerous on the dorsum of the tongue and lacks taste buds?
slides.why: Filiform papillae are tiny conical projections covering the anterior two-thirds of the tongue; they provide friction and have no taste buds.

slides.h: 2. Muscles & Nerve Supply (Motor, General Sensory & Taste)
slides.p: Every single examiner asks for the muscles and triple nerve supply of the tongue:
bullets: Intrinsic Muscles (alter shape): Superior & inferior longitudinal, transverse, vertical.

Extrinsic Muscles (alter position): Genioglossus (protrudes tongue — 'safety muscle'!), Hyoglossus (depresses), Styloglossus (retracts/elevates), Palatoglossus (elevates root / narrows oropharyngeal isthmus).
Motor Nerve Supply: ALL intrinsic & extrinsic muscles are supplied by Hypoglossal Nerve (CN XII) EXCEPT Palatoglossus (supplied by Cranial Accessory via Pharyngeal Plexus / CN X!).

Sensory & Taste Supply: Anterior 2/3: General sensation = Lingual nerve (CN V3); Taste = Chorda tympani (CN VII) (except circumvallate papillae). Posterior 1/3 + Circumvallate papillae: Both general & taste = Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX). Posterior-most / Vallecula: Internal laryngeal nerve (CN X).
slides.remember: Motor = CN XII for all EXCEPT Palatoglossus (Pharyngeal plexus). Anterior 2/3 = V3 (touch) + VII chorda tympani (taste). Posterior 1/3 = IX (both)!
slides.q: Which extrinsic muscle of the tongue is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus/cranial accessory) rather than the hypoglossal nerve?
slides.why: Palatoglossus is developmentally a palatal muscle and is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X), whereas all other tongue muscles are supplied by CN XII.

slides.p: Understanding tongue lymphatics is critical because carcinoma of the tongue spreads early via lymph:
bullets: Tip of Tongue: Drains bilaterally into submental lymph nodes (then jugulo-omohyoid).
Anterior 2/3 Margins (unilateral): Drain into ipsilateral submandibular lymph nodes (central part drains bilaterally).
Posterior 1/3: Drains bilaterally into jugulodigastric and deep cervical nodes.
Principal Node of Tongue: Jugulo-omohyoid lymph node receives lymph from all parts of the tongue.

Applied Anatomy: Genioglossus is the 'safety muscle of the tongue' (prevents tongue from falling back and obstructing the airway during general anesthesia). In unilateral CN XII palsy, the protruded tongue deviates toward the paralyzed side.
slides.remember: Safety muscle = Genioglossus! Principal lymph node of tongue = Jugulo-omohyoid node! Central & posterior carcinoma spreads BILATERALLY!
slides.q: Which lymph node is known as the 'principal lymph node of the tongue' because it ultimately receives lymph from all parts of the organ?
slides.why: The jugulo-omohyoid node of the lower deep cervical chain receives lymph directly and indirectly from the entire tongue.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Parts & external features (sulcus terminalis, papillae) → Intrinsic & extrinsic muscles (table with origin, insertion, action) → Motor, general sensory & special sensory nerve supply → Blood supply → Lymphatic drainage (tip, margins, posterior 1/3, jugulo-omohyoid node) → Applied anatomy (genioglossus safety muscle, CN XII lesion, lingual carcinoma) + Diagrams.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Scalp

slides.h: 1. Five Layers of the Scalp (S-C-A-L-P Mnemonic)
slides.p: The scalp covers the cranial vault from the supraorbital margins anteriorly to the highest nuchal lines posteriorly, and between the superior temporal lines laterally. Its five layers spell S-C-A-L-P:
bullets: 1. S — Skin: Thick, hairy, contains numerous sebaceous glands (commonest site of sebaceous cysts!).

2. C — Connective Tissue (Superficial Fascia): Dense fibrofatty septa binding skin firmly to the aponeurosis; contains rich blood vessels and nerves. Because vessels are tethered to fibrous septa, they cannot retract when cut → profuse bleeding!

3. A — Aponeurosis (Epicranial Aponeurosis / Galea Aponeurotica) & Occipitofrontalis: Connects frontal belly (frontalis) to occipital belly (occipitalis). Note: First 3 layers (S-C-A) move together as one 'surgical layer of the scalp'.
4. L — Loose Areolar Tissue ('Dangerous Layer of Scalp'): Traversed by emissary veins connecting scalp veins to intracranial dural venous sinuses!
5. P — Pericranium: Outer periosteum of skull bones, loosely attached except at sutures where it dips in as sutural ligaments.
slides.remember: S-C-A-L-P! First 3 layers = Surgical layer. 4th layer (Loose areolar tissue) = Dangerous layer (emissary veins → intracranial sinuses)!
slides.q: Which layer of the scalp is known as the 'dangerous layer of the scalp' because it contains emissary veins communicating with intracranial dural venous sinuses?
slides.why: The 4th layer (loose areolar tissue) contains valveless emissary veins through which scalp infections can spread into intracranial dural venous sinuses.

slides.p: Ten nerves (5 in front of the ear, 5 behind the ear) and five arteries on each side supply the scalp:
bullets: In Front of Auricle (5 nerves): Supratrochlear (V1), Supraorbital (V1), Zygomaticotemporal (V2), Auriculotemporal (V3), and Temporal branch of Facial nerve (CN VII — motor to frontalis).

Behind Auricle (5 nerves): Posterior auricular branch of Facial nerve (CN VII — motor to occipitalis), Greater occipital (C2 dorsal ramus), Lesser occipital (C2 ventral ramus), Third occipital (C3 dorsal ramus), and Great auricular nerve (C2, C3).

Five Arteries on Each Side: Supratrochlear & Supraorbital (from ophthalmic/ICA) + Superficial temporal, Posterior auricular, and Occipital (from external carotid artery) — forming a free anastomosis across the midline between ICA and ECA!
slides.remember: 5 nerves in front + 5 behind auricle = 10 on each side! 5 arteries on each side unite ICA and ECA across the midline!
slides.q: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the frontal belly of the occipitofrontalis muscle?
opts: Temporal branch of facial nerve (CN VII)
slides.why: Frontalis is supplied by the temporal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII), while occipitalis is supplied by the posterior auricular branch of CN VII.

slides.h: 3. Applied Anatomy — Black Eye, Caput Succedaneum & Cephalhematoma
slides.p: Understanding the anatomical attachments of the 4th and 5th layers explains three classic clinical conditions:
bullets: Black Eye (Periorbital Hematoma): Frontalis has NO bony attachment in front (blends with orbicularis oculi), so blood or fluid in the 4th layer (loose areolar tissue) gravitates downward into the upper eyelids, causing a 'black eye' hours after a head injury.

Caput Succedaneum vs Cephalhematoma: Caput succedaneum is subcutaneous edema (2nd layer) from birth pressure that crosses suture lines and resolves quickly. Cephalhematoma is subperiosteal bleeding beneath the pericranium (5th layer), strictly limited by suture lines (usually over one parietal bone).
slides.remember: Black eye = blood tracking down from 4th layer (loose areolar tissue). Cephalhematoma = beneath pericranium, stops at sutures!
slides.q: Why is a cephalhematoma (subperiosteal hemorrhage) in a newborn strictly confined to the boundaries of a single cranial bone?
opts: Because skin is tightly bound to bone
Because the pericranium dips into the suture lines and fuses with the endosteum
Because emissary veins drain it at sutures
slides.why: The 5th layer (pericranium) is firmly attached at the suture lines where it continues as sutural ligaments, confining subperiosteal fluid to one bone.

lessons.exam: LAQ order: Definition & extent → Five layers (S-C-A-L-P) with features → Blood supply (5 arteries, ICA–ECA anastomosis) → Venous drainage & emissary veins → Nerve supply (5 anterior + 5 posterior) → Lymphatic drainage → Applied anatomy (profuse bleeding, dangerous layer, black eye, caput vs cephalhematoma) + Diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Middle Ear (Tympanic Cavity)

slides.p: The middle ear (tympanic cavity) is a narrow, air-filled, biconcave cleft inside the petrous temporal bone communicating anteriorly with the nasopharynx via the auditory (Eustachian) tube and posteriorly with the mastoid antrum via the aditus. It resembles a six-sided matchbox:
bullets: 1. Roof (Tegmental Wall): Thin plate of bone—tegmen tympani—separating middle ear from temporal lobe of brain & meninges (middle cranial fossa).
2. Floor (Jugular Wall): Thin bone separating it from the superior bulb of the internal jugular vein.
3. Anterior (Carotid) Wall: Thin bone separating it from the internal carotid artery, plus two openings: upper canal for tensor tympani and lower opening of auditory tube.
4. Posterior (Mastoid) Wall: Upper aditus to mastoid antrum, pyramid (conical projection housing stapedius tendon), and vertical facial nerve canal.
5. Lateral (Membranous) Wall: Mainly the tympanic membrane (plus outer attic wall / scutum above).

6. Medial (Labyrinthine) Wall: Promontory (rounded bulge produced by basal turn of cochlea, grooved by tympanic plexus), oval window (fenestra vestibuli) above/behind (closed by footplate of stapes), round window (fenestra cochleae) below/behind (closed by secondary tympanic membrane), and prominence of facial canal.
slides.remember: Roof = Brain (Tegmen tympani). Floor = IJV bulb. Front = ICA + Eustachian tube. Back = Mastoid antrum + Pyramid. Medial = Promontory + Oval & Round windows!
slides.q: Which structure forms the roof of the middle ear, separating it from the temporal lobe of the brain in the middle cranial fossa?
slides.why: The tegmen tympani is the thin bony plate forming the roof of the tympanic cavity, aditus, and mastoid antrum.

slides.p: Inside the middle ear sit the three auditory ossicles that amplify sound vibrations ~18–22 times onto the oval window, plus two protective dampening muscles:
bullets: Three Ossicles: Malleus (handle attached to tympanic membrane), Incus, and Stapes (smallest bone in body; footplate fits into oval window).
Two Muscles: Tensor tympani (attaches to handle of malleus; supplied by Mandibular nerve / CN V3) and Stapedius (attaches to neck of stapes; supplied by Facial nerve / CN VII).
Nerves Passing Through: Chorda tympani (branch of CN VII) runs across the medial surface of the upper tympanic membrane between malleus and incus; Tympanic plexus lies on the promontory.
slides.remember: Tensor tympani = CN V3 (5). Stapedius = CN VII (7). Chorda tympani crosses between Malleus & Incus!
slides.q: Which cranial nerve supplies the stapedius muscle in the middle ear?
slides.why: The nerve to stapedius arises from the facial nerve (CN VII) within the facial canal; paralysis causes hyperacusis (painful sensitivity to loud sounds).

slides.p: Because every wall of the middle ear borders a vital structure, untreated middle ear infection (otitis media) can spread in multiple directions:
bullets: Upward (through Tegmen Tympani): Meningitis or temporal lobe brain abscess.
Backward (through Aditus): Acute mastoiditis.
Medially (Facial Canal): Lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy.
Downward (Floor): Septic thrombosis of the internal jugular vein.
Myringotomy Incision: Performed in the posteroinferior quadrant of the tympanic membrane to drain pus safely—avoiding the ossicles and chorda tympani located in the upper quadrants!
slides.remember: Myringotomy goes in the POSTEROINFERIOR quadrant of the eardrum to avoid chorda tympani & ossicles above!
slides.q: In which quadrant of the tympanic membrane is a surgical incision (myringotomy) safely made to drain middle ear fluid?
slides.why: The posteroinferior quadrant is devoid of underlying ossicles and the chorda tympani nerve, making it the safest site for myringotomy.

lessons.exam: LAQ order: Definition & parts (tympanic cavity proper + epitympanic recess) → Six walls with exact relations → Contents (malleus, incus, stapes, tensor tympani, stapedius, chorda tympani, tympanic plexus) → Blood & nerve supply → Applied anatomy (otitis media routes of spread, myringotomy site, hyperacusis) + Diagram of medial wall.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Digastric Triangle (Submandibular Triangle)

slides.p: The digastric (submandibular) triangle is a paired subdivision of the anterior triangle of the neck located immediately beneath the body of the mandible:
bullets: Anteroinferiorly: Anterior belly of the digastric muscle.
Posteroinferiorly: Posterior belly of the digastric and stylohyoid muscle.
Superiorly (Base): Lower border of the body of the mandible and a line joining the angle of mandible to the mastoid process.
Roof: Skin, superficial fascia (with platysma & cervical branch of facial nerve), and investing layer of deep cervical fascia (splits to enclose submandibular gland).
Floor: Formed anteriorly by mylohyoid and posteriorly by hyoglossus (and a small part of middle constrictor).
slides.remember: Floor = Mylohyoid (in front) + Hyoglossus (behind)!
slides.q: Which two muscles form the floor of the digastric (submandibular) triangle?
slides.why: The floor of the digastric triangle is formed anteriorly by the mylohyoid muscle and posteriorly by the hyoglossus muscle.

slides.p: Organize the contents into Anterior Part and Posterior Part (separated by the stylomandibular ligament):
bullets: Anterior Part: Superficial part of submandibular salivary gland, facial vein (superficial to gland), facial artery (deep to gland, looping over it), submandibular lymph nodes, hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), and mylohyoid nerve & vessels.
Posterior Part: Lower part of parotid gland, external carotid artery (before entering parotid), internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve (deep).

Applied Anatomy: Submandibular lymphadenitis and submandibular sialolithiasis (salivary stones — commonest in submandibular duct!) present as tender swellings in this triangle. During excision of the submandibular gland, protect the marginal mandibular branch of CN VII, lingual nerve, and hypoglossal nerve.
slides.remember: Facial Vein runs SUPERFICIAL to submandibular gland; Facial Artery loops DEEP to it!
slides.q: Which nerve runs just below the lower border of the mandible in the roof of the digastric triangle and is at risk during submandibular gland surgery?
opts: Marginal mandibular branch of facial nerve (CN VII)
slides.why: The marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve loops slightly below the inferior border of the mandible and must be preserved to prevent drooping of the corner of the mouth.

lessons.exam: SN order: Situation → Boundaries (anteroinferior, posteroinferior, base, roof, floor) → Contents (anterior vs posterior parts, relation of facial vessels to submandibular gland) → Applied anatomy + Labelled triangle diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Carotid Triangle

slides.p: The carotid triangle is a major surgical landmark in the anterior triangle of the neck containing the bifurcation of the common carotid artery:
bullets: Anterosuperiorly: Posterior belly of digastric and stylohyoid.
Anteroinferiorly: Superior belly of omohyoid.
Posteriorly: Anterior border of sternocleidomastoid.
Floor: Formed by four muscles—thyrohyoid, hyoglossus, middle pharyngeal constrictor, and inferior pharyngeal constrictor.
slides.remember: Boundaries = Posterior belly of Digastric + Superior belly of Omohyoid + Anterior border of Sternocleidomastoid!
slides.q: Which muscle forms the posterior boundary of the carotid triangle?
slides.why: The anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle bounds the carotid triangle posteriorly.

slides.p: The carotid triangle houses the major neurovascular structures of the neck:
bullets: Arteries: Common carotid artery dividing at the upper border of thyroid cartilage (C3–C4 disc level) into Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) (no branches in neck, lies posterolateral initially) and External Carotid Artery (ECA) (gives 5 branches inside triangle: superior thyroid, lingual, facial, occipital, ascending pharyngeal), plus carotid sinus & carotid body.
Veins: Internal jugular vein (IJV) and common facial, lingual & superior thyroid tributaries.
Nerves: Vagus nerve (CN X), Internal & external laryngeal nerves, Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) crossing ICA & ECA, Ansa cervicalis, and Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI — upper corner).
Applied Anatomy: Carotid pulse palpation at the anterior border of SCM (cricoid/thyroid cartilage level) and carotid sinus hypersensitivity (pressure here triggers vagal bradycardia/syncope).
slides.remember: Common carotid bifurcates at UPPER BORDER OF THYROID CARTILAGE (C3–C4)! ECA has branches in neck; ICA has NO branches in neck!
slides.q: At which anatomical landmark does the common carotid artery bifurcate into internal and external carotid arteries inside the carotid triangle?
slides.why: The common carotid artery bifurcates at the level of the upper border of the lamina of the thyroid cartilage (intervertebral disc between C3 and C4).

lessons.exam: SN order: Situation → Boundaries (3 borders, roof, 4 floor muscles) → Contents (arteries, carotid sinus/body, veins, nerves) → Applied anatomy (carotid pulse, carotid sinus massage, surgical exposure of ECA/ICA) + Diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Carotid Sheath

slides.p: The carotid sheath is a tubular condensation of deep cervical fascia enclosing the great vessels and vagus nerve on each side of the neck:
bullets: Formation: Formed anteriorly by the pretracheal fascia and posteriorly by the prevertebral fascia; thick over the arteries (allows pulsation) and thin over the vein (allows expansion).
Extent: From the base of the skull (around carotid canal & jugular foramen) down to the arch of the aorta in the superior mediastinum.
Key Relations: Ansa cervicalis is embedded in its anterior wall; Cervical sympathetic trunk lies directly behind its posterior wall (embedded in prevertebral fascia).
slides.remember: Ansa cervicalis = IN anterior wall. Sympathetic chain = BEHIND posterior wall!
slides.q: Which neural structure is embedded directly in the anterior wall of the carotid sheath?
slides.why: The ansa cervicalis lies embedded in the anterior wall of the carotid sheath (or just anterior to it), whereas the sympathetic trunk lies posterior to the sheath.

slides.p: Inside the carotid sheath sit three main structures in a precise spatial relationship:
bullets: Contents: 1. Common carotid artery (below) / Internal carotid artery (above) — medially; 2. Internal jugular vein (IJV) — laterally; 3. Vagus nerve (CN X) — posteriorly in the groove between artery and vein.

Applied Anatomy: Provides a low-resistance fascial pathway along which deep neck infections can track downward into the superior mediastinum. Deep cervical lymph nodes lie closely adherent to the IJV.
slides.remember: Inside Carotid Sheath: Artery Medial, Vein Lateral, Vagus Posteriorly between them!
slides.q: What is the normal arrangement of contents inside the carotid sheath?
opts: IJV medially, carotid artery laterally, vagus anteriorly
Carotid artery medially, internal jugular vein laterally, vagus nerve posteriorly between them
Vagus medially, carotid artery laterally, IJV posteriorly
External carotid artery medially, IJV laterally, phrenic nerve posteriorly
slides.why: Within the carotid sheath, the common/internal carotid artery lies medially, the internal jugular vein lies laterally, and the vagus nerve lies posteriorly between the two vessels.

lessons.exam: SN order: Definition & fascial formation → Extent (skull base to aortic arch) → Contents & their spatial arrangement → Relations (ansa cervicalis, sympathetic chain, deep cervical nodes) → Applied anatomy + Transverse section diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Muscles of Mastication

slides.h: 1. The Four Primary Muscles & Common Features
slides.p: The four primary muscles of mastication act on the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) to chew food. All four share three embryological and anatomical hallmarks:
bullets: 1. Development: All develop from mesoderm of the 1st pharyngeal (mandibular) arch.
2. Nerve Supply: All are supplied by the Mandibular nerve (CN V3) (anterior division, except medial pterygoid from main trunk).
3. Insertion: All insert onto the ramus of the mandible.

The Four Muscles: 1. Masseter (zygomatic arch → lateral ramus; elevates mandible), 2. Temporalis (temporal fossa → coronoid process; anterior fibres elevate, posterior fibres retract mandible), 3. Medial Pterygoid (pterygoid plate/maxilla → medial angle of mandible; elevates & protrudes), 4. Lateral Pterygoid (sphenoid → pterygoid fovea of neck of mandible + TMJ articular disc & capsule; depresses mandible to open mouth & protrudes!).
slides.remember: All 4 insert on Mandible + supplied by CN V3 + 1st arch! ONLY Lateral Pterygoid OPENS the mouth (depresses mandible); the other 3 CLOSE it!
slides.q: Which muscle of mastication is the ONLY primary muscle that depresses the mandible to open the mouth?
slides.why: Lateral pterygoid pulls the condyle of the mandible and articular disc forward onto the articular tubercle, opening the mouth; masseter, temporalis, and medial pterygoid all elevate (close) the mandible.

slides.p: Summarize how these muscles coordinate during chewing and what happens when CN V3 is injured:
bullets: Elevation (Closing): Temporalis, Masseter, Medial pterygoid.
Depression (Opening): Lateral pterygoid (assisted by digastric, mylohyoid, geniohyoid).
Protrusion: Lateral & medial pterygoids acting bilaterally.
Retraction: Posterior fibres of temporalis.
Side-to-Side Grinding: Alternating medial & lateral pterygoids of opposite sides.
Applied Anatomy: In unilateral mandibular nerve (CN V3) palsy, when the patient opens the mouth, the jaw deviates toward the paralyzed side (pushed over by the intact opposite lateral pterygoid!).
slides.remember: Unilateral CN V3 palsy → Chin/jaw deviates TOWARD the paralyzed side on opening the mouth!
slides.q: In a patient with right-sided mandibular nerve (CN V3) paralysis, which way does the jaw deviate when the mouth is opened?
slides.why: The unopposed left lateral pterygoid pulls the left mandibular condyle forward, swinging the chin toward the paralyzed right side.

lessons.exam: SN order: Common embryology (1st arch) & nerve supply (CN V3) → Tabular breakdown of Masseter, Temporalis, Medial Pterygoid & Lateral Pterygoid (origin, insertion, action) → Summary of TMJ movements → Applied anatomy (jaw deviation in CN V3 palsy, TMJ dislocation).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Little's Area of Nose – Clinical Significance

slides.h: 1. Location & Four Arteries Forming Kiesselbach's Plexus
slides.p: Little's area is a highly vascular region in the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum just above the vestibule, where four arteries anastomose to form Kiesselbach's plexus:
bullets: 1. Anterior ethmoidal artery (branch of ophthalmic artery — ICA system).
2. Sphenopalatine artery (septal branch — maxillary artery / ECA system).
3. Greater palatine artery (ascending through incisive canal — maxillary artery / ECA system).
4. Superior labial artery (septal branch — facial artery / ECA system).
Note: The Posterior ethmoidal artery does NOT participate in Little's area!
slides.remember: 4 arteries in Little's area = Anterior ethmoidal, Sphenopalatine, Greater palatine, Superior labial (uniting ICA & ECA)!
slides.q: Which of the following arteries does NOT contribute to Kiesselbach's plexus in Little's area of the nasal septum?
slides.why: Little's area is formed by the anterior ethmoidal, sphenopalatine, greater palatine, and septal branch of the superior labial artery; the posterior ethmoidal artery supplies the posterosuperior septum.

slides.p: Why is Little's area clinically famous?
bullets: Commonest Site of Epistaxis (~90% of nosebleeds): Especially in children and young adults due to nose-picking (digital trauma), dry air/crusting, or rhinitis.

First-Aid Control (Trotter's / Pinch Method): Because Little's area lies in the cartilaginous anterior septum, bleeding is easily controlled by pinching the soft cartilaginous part of the nose firmly for 5–10 minutes while leaning slightly forward (to prevent blood trickling down the pharynx).
slides.remember: Little's area = #1 site of nosebleed (epistaxis) → controlled by pinching the soft part of the nose for 5–10 minutes!
slides.q: Where is Little's area located on the nasal septum?
opts: Anteroinferior part just above the vestibule
slides.why: Little's area sits on the anteroinferior part of the nasal septum just above the nasal vestibule.

lessons.exam: SN order: Definition & exact location (anteroinferior nasal septum) → Four arteries forming Kiesselbach's plexus (ICA + ECA anastomosis) → Clinical significance (commonest site of epistaxis, causes, first-aid pinching & cauterization) + Diagram of nasal septum.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Lateral Rectus Muscle of Eyeball

slides.p: The lateral rectus is one of the six extraocular muscles moving the eyeball:
bullets: Origin: Lateral part of the common tendinous ring (annulus of Zinn) bridging the superior orbital fissure, with a small slip from the orbital surface of the greater wing of sphenoid.
Insertion: Into the lateral aspect of the sclera ~6.9 mm behind the corneoscleral junction (limbus).
Nerve Supply: Abducens nerve (CN VI) (enters its ocular/medial surface; LR6!).
Action: Pure abduction of the eyeball (turns cornea laterally away from midline).
slides.remember: LR6 = Lateral Rectus supplied by CN VI! Pure abductor of the eyeball.
slides.q: Which cranial nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle of the eyeball?
slides.why: The lateral rectus is supplied exclusively by the abducens nerve (CN VI).

slides.h: 2. Relations in Superior Orbital Fissure & Clinical Paralysis
slides.p: The structures passing through the common tendinous ring between the two heads of lateral rectus are vital for orbit questions:
bullets: Structures Inside Tendinous Ring: Upper & lower divisions of CN III, Nasociliary nerve, and Abducens nerve (CN VI).

Applied Anatomy (CN VI Palsy): Because CN VI has a long intracranial course and passes through the cavernous sinus, it is frequently injured (e.g., raised intracranial pressure). Paralysis of lateral rectus causes inability to abduct the eye, medial (convergent) squint / esotropia (unopposed medial rectus), and horizontal diplopia worst when looking toward the paralyzed side.
slides.remember: LR6 palsy = Cannot look laterally + Convergent (medial) squint + Horizontal diplopia!
slides.q: Paralysis of the right lateral rectus muscle causes which type of strabismus (squint)?
slides.why: Loss of lateral rectus abduction leaves the medial rectus unopposed, pulling the eye medially into a convergent squint (esotropia).

lessons.exam: SN order: Origin (common tendinous ring) → Course & relations (structures inside tendinous ring) → Insertion → Nerve supply (CN VI) → Action (pure abduction) → Applied anatomy (CN VI palsy, convergent squint, diplopia).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Hyoid Bone

slides.p: The hyoid bone is a U-shaped bone suspended in the anterior neck at the level of C3 vertebra between the mandible and thyroid cartilage. Unique among human bones, it does NOT articulate with any other bone—it is slung entirely by muscles and ligaments.
bullets: Parts: Central Body + two pairs of horns: Greater cornua (project backward & upward) and Lesser cornua (conical projections at junction of body & greater cornua).
Development: Lesser cornu & upper half of body = 2nd pharyngeal arch; Greater cornu & lower half of body = 3rd pharyngeal arch.
slides.remember: C3 vertebral level! No bony articulations! 2nd arch = upper body & lesser horn; 3rd arch = lower body & greater horn!
slides.q: At which vertebral level does the hyoid bone lie in the anterior neck?
slides.why: The hyoid bone lies in the anterior midline of the neck opposite the C3 vertebra.

slides.p: A clean list of suprahyoid/infrahyoid attachments plus medicolegal significance makes this Short Note shine:
bullets: Body: Mylohyoid, geniohyoid, hyoglossus (above); sternohyoid, omohyoid, thyrohyoid (below); thyrohyoid membrane.
Greater Cornu: Middle pharyngeal constrictor, hyoglossus, thyrohyoid, fibrous pulley for digastric tendon.
Lesser Cornu: Stylohyoid ligament (connects to styloid process).
Clinical / Forensic Significance: Fracture of the hyoid bone (especially the greater cornua) is a classic medicolegal sign of manual strangulation (throttling).
slides.remember: Forensic pearl: Fracture of greater cornua of hyoid bone = sign of manual strangulation!
slides.q: Fracture of the greater cornua of the hyoid bone is a classic forensic finding in:
slides.why: Direct lateral compression of the neck during manual strangulation frequently fractures the greater cornua of the hyoid bone.

lessons.exam: SN order: Situation (C3 level, no bony articulation) → Parts (body, greater & lesser cornua) → Muscle & ligament attachments → Development (2nd & 3rd arches) → Clinical & medicolegal importance (manual strangulation fracture).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Palatine Tonsil – Applied Anatomy

slides.p: The palatine tonsil is an almond-shaped mass of lymphoid tissue (part of Waldeyer's lymphatic ring) lodged in the tonsillar fossa between the palatoglossal arch (anterior) and palatopharyngeal arch (posterior).
bullets: Medial Surface: Covered by stratified squamous epithelium pitted by 12–15 tonsillar crypts (largest = intratonsillar cleft).

Lateral Surface (Tonsillar Bed): Covered by a fibrous hemicapsule separated from the superior constrictor by loose areolar tissue containing the paratonsillar vein (commonest source of post-tonsillectomy bleeding!). Beyond superior constrictor lie styloglossus, CN IX, and facial artery.
Main Arterial Supply: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery (main artery!) + ascending palatine, dorsal lingual, ascending pharyngeal, and descending palatine arteries.
slides.remember: Main artery = Tonsillar branch of Facial Artery. Main culprit in post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage = Paratonsillar vein!
slides.q: Which vessel is the most frequent source of troublesome venous hemorrhage following tonsillectomy?
slides.why: The paratonsillar vein descends on the lateral surface of the tonsillar capsule in the tonsillar bed and is frequently torn during tonsillectomy.

slides.h: 2. Applied Anatomy — Quinsy, Jugulodigastric Node & Referred Earache
slides.p: Every clinical pearl here is a high-yield viva and short-note point:
bullets: Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy): Suppuration in the loose areolar tissue outside the tonsillar capsule pushes the tonsil medially and the uvula toward the opposite side; drained by incising the most prominent bulge.
Enlarged Jugulodigastric Node: Lymph from the palatine tonsil drains directly into the jugulodigastric (tonsillar) lymph node below the angle of the mandible—enlarged and tender in acute tonsillitis.

Referred Ear Pain: Because CN IX (glossopharyngeal nerve) supplies both the tonsil and the middle ear (via tympanic branch), tonsillitis or tonsillar carcinoma often causes referred otalgia (earache).
slides.remember: Tonsil lymph → Jugulodigastric node! Tonsillitis → Referred earache via CN IX! Pus outside capsule = Quinsy!
slides.q: To which lymph node does lymph from the palatine tonsil primarily drain?
slides.why: The jugulodigastric node of the upper deep cervical group is the principal draining node of the palatine tonsil.

lessons.exam: SN order: Situation & Waldeyer's ring → Surfaces, crypts & tonsillar bed → Blood supply (tonsillar branch of facial artery, paratonsillar vein) → Lymphatic drainage (jugulodigastric node) & nerve supply (CN IX) → Applied anatomy (tonsillitis, quinsy, tonsillectomy bleeding, referred earache).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Dangerous Area of Face

slides.h: 1. Boundaries & Venous Pathways to Cavernous Sinus
slides.p: The dangerous area of the face comprises the upper lip, lower part of the nose, and adjacent medial cheek (roughly a triangle from the bridge of the nose to the corners of the mouth).
bullets: Why is it Dangerous? Veins draining this region are valveless and communicate directly with the cavernous sinus via two routes:
Route 1 (Anterior): Facial vein → angular vein → superior ophthalmic vein → passes through superior orbital fissure → cavernous sinus.
Route 2 (Deep): Facial vein → deep facial vein → pterygoid venous plexus → emissary veins (through foramen ovale / lacerum) → cavernous sinus.
Muscular Squeezing: Facial muscles attach directly to skin and lack deep fascia, so facial movements/squeezing pimples pump infected thrombi backward into the cavernous sinus.
slides.remember: 2 routes from Facial Vein to Cavernous Sinus: (1) Superior Ophthalmic Vein, (2) Deep Facial Vein → Pterygoid Plexus → Emissary Veins!
slides.q: Through which two venous pathways can infection from the dangerous area of the face spread to the cavernous sinus?
opts: Internal jugular vein and subclavian vein
Superior ophthalmic vein and deep facial vein via pterygoid venous plexus
Lingual vein and superior thyroid vein
slides.why: The valveless facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus anteriorly via the superior ophthalmic vein and deeply via the deep facial vein and pterygoid plexus.

slides.p: Squeezing a boil or furuncle on the upper lip or nasal vestibule can trigger retrograde septic thrombophlebitis:
bullets: Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis: Presents with high spiking fever, severe headache, periorbital edema, proptosis (bulging eye), chemosis (conjunctival edema), and ophthalmoplegia (especially lateral rectus / CN VI palsy first, followed by CN III, IV, V1, V2).
slides.remember: Never squeeze a boil in the nose/upper lip triangle → risk of Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis!
slides.q: Which cranial nerve is typically the FIRST to be affected in cavernous sinus thrombosis resulting from facial infection?
slides.why: CN VI runs directly through the interior of the cavernous sinus alongside the internal carotid artery, making it the earliest nerve affected.

lessons.exam: SN order: Boundaries (upper lip, lower nose, medial cheek) → Anatomical reasons (valveless veins, absence of deep fascia, facial muscle action) → Two venous routes to cavernous sinus → Clinical features of cavernous sinus thrombosis + Schematic venous diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Nasal Meatuses (Lateral Wall of Nose)

slides.h: 1. The Three Conchae & Meatuses + Sphenoethmoidal Recess
slides.p: The lateral wall of each nasal cavity features three curved bony projections—the superior, middle, and inferior nasal conchae (turbinates)—each overhanging a corresponding passage called a meatus, plus the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha:
bullets: 1. Sphenoethmoidal Recess (above superior concha): Receives opening of the sphenoidal air sinus.
2. Superior Meatus (below superior concha): Receives openings of the posterior ethmoidal air sinuses.

3. Middle Meatus (below middle concha): Features a rounded bulge—the bulla ethmoidalis (bearing middle ethmoidal sinus openings)—and a curved groove below it, the hiatus semilunaris, into which open (from front to back): Frontal sinus (via frontonasal duct/infundibulum), Anterior ethmoidal sinuses, and Maxillary sinus!
4. Inferior Meatus (below inferior concha): Receives the lower opening of the nasolacrimal duct (guarded by Hasner's valve).
slides.remember: Sphenoethmoidal = Sphenoid. Superior = Posterior ethmoid. Middle = Frontal + Anterior & Middle ethmoid + Maxillary. Inferior = Nasolacrimal duct!
slides.q: Which duct opens into the inferior meatus of the nasal cavity?
slides.why: The nasolacrimal duct drains tears from the lacrimal sac into the anterior part of the inferior nasal meatus.

slides.h: 2. Clinical Significance — Maxillary Sinusitis & Osteomeatal Complex
slides.p: Why does the maxillary sinus get infected so frequently?
bullets: Unfavorable Drainage of Maxillary Sinus: Its ostium opens high up on its medial wall into the hiatus semilunaris of the middle meatus—so gravity cannot drain it when upright!
Osteomeatal Complex: Narrow drainage channel in the middle meatus where frontal, anterior ethmoidal, and maxillary sinuses converge; mucosal swelling here blocks all three sinuses simultaneously.
slides.remember: Maxillary sinus ostium sits near its ROOF (hiatus semilunaris) → poor gravity drainage → #1 sinusitis!
slides.q: The maxillary sinus opens into which meatus of the nasal cavity?
slides.why: The maxillary sinus drains into the posterior part of the hiatus semilunaris in the middle nasal meatus.

lessons.exam: SN order: Lateral wall overview (3 conchae) → Openings into Sphenoethmoidal recess, Superior meatus, Middle meatus (bulla ethmoidalis & hiatus semilunaris), and Inferior meatus → Clinical significance (maxillary sinus drainage, osteomeatal complex, epiphora) + Diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Ansa Cervicalis

slides.p: The ansa cervicalis ('handle of the neck') is a thin U-shaped nerve loop embedded in the anterior wall of the carotid sheath that supplies the infrahyoid ('strap') muscles:
bullets: Superior Root (Descendens Hypoglossi — C1 fibres): Derived from the 1st cervical spinal nerve (C1); hitchhikes briefly along the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) before descending in front of the internal and common carotid arteries.

Inferior Root (Descendens Cervicalis — C2, C3 fibres): Derived from the 2nd and 3rd cervical spinal nerves (C2, C3); winds around the lateral side of the internal jugular vein to join the superior root in front of the common carotid artery.
slides.remember: Superior root = C1 (via CN XII). Inferior root = C2, C3 (around IJV). Loop sits on front of Carotid Sheath!
slides.q: Which cervical spinal nerve roots form the loop of the ansa cervicalis?
slides.why: Ansa cervicalis is formed by the union of the superior root (C1) and the inferior root (C2, C3).

slides.p: Remember which strap muscles it supplies—and which ONE is the exception:
bullets: Muscles Supplied (3 of 4 infrahyoids): Sternohyoid, Sternothyroid, and Omohyoid (both superior & inferior bellies).
Exception (Trap!): Thyrohyoid (and geniohyoid) are supplied directly by C1 fibres travelling via CN XII, NOT by the loop of ansa cervicalis!
Clinical Use: Used in nerve-muscle pedicle grafting to reinnervate a paralyzed larynx (recurrent laryngeal nerve injury).
slides.remember: Ansa cervicalis supplies Sternohyoid, Sternothyroid & Omohyoid — NOT Thyrohyoid (supplied directly by C1 via CN XII)!
slides.q: Which infrahyoid ('strap') muscle is NOT supplied by the loop of the ansa cervicalis?
slides.why: Thyrohyoid receives C1 fibres directly from the hypoglossal nerve (nerve to thyrohyoid), whereas sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid are supplied by the ansa cervicalis.

lessons.exam: SN order: Definition & situation (anterior wall of carotid sheath) → Formation (Superior root C1 + Inferior root C2, C3) → Distribution (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, omohyoid; note thyrohyoid exception) → Applied anatomy + Diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Falx Cerebri

slides.p: The falx cerebri is a large, sickle-shaped fold of the inner (meningeal) layer of dura mater descending vertically into the median longitudinal fissure between the right and left cerebral hemispheres:
bullets: Anterior Apex: Attached to the crista galli of the ethmoid bone (in front of foramen cecum).
Posterior Base: Slopes downward and backward to fuse with the upper surface of the tentorium cerebelli along the midline.
Upper Convex Border: Attached to the lips of the sagittal sulcus on the cranial vault; encloses the Superior Sagittal Sinus.
Lower Concave Free Border: Overhangs the corpus callosum; encloses the Inferior Sagittal Sinus.
Line of Attachment to Tentorium Cerebelli: Encloses the Straight Sinus.
slides.remember: Sickle-shaped fold between hemispheres! 3 sinuses: Superior sagittal (top), Inferior sagittal (bottom free edge), Straight sinus (back attachment to tentorium)!
slides.q: Which dural venous sinus is enclosed along the posterior line of attachment where the falx cerebri meets the tentorium cerebelli?
slides.why: The straight sinus runs along the junction where the base of the falx cerebri attaches to the upper surface of the tentorium cerebelli.

slides.p: Why does the falx cerebri matter clinically?
bullets: Function: Acts as a rigid midline partition limiting excessive side-to-side displacement of the cerebral hemispheres during head rotation.
Nerve Supply: Anterior cranial fossa nerves (anterior & posterior ethmoidal nerves — CN V1) and tentorial nerves (CN V1).

Clinical — Subfalcine (Cingulate) Herniation: A unilateral cerebral mass (hematoma or tumor) can push the cingulate gyrus underneath the free inferior edge of the falx cerebri, compressing the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and causing contralateral leg weakness.
slides.remember: Subfalcine herniation = Cingulate gyrus pushed under free edge of falx cerebri → compresses ACA!
slides.q: In subfalcine herniation, which cerebral gyrus is displaced beneath the free inferior margin of the falx cerebri?
slides.why: Increased unilateral supratentorial pressure forces the cingulate gyrus under the free concave edge of the falx cerebri (subfalcine herniation).

lessons.exam: SN order: Definition & situation (longitudinal fissure) → Shape & attachments (crista galli, sagittal sulcus, tentorium cerebelli) → Three enclosed venous sinuses → Nerve & blood supply → Applied anatomy (subfalcine herniation, falx calcification) + Sagittal diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Sciatic Nerve

slides.h: 1. Root Value, Formation & Course in Gluteal Region and Thigh
slides.p: The sciatic nerve (L4, L5, S1, S2, S3) is the thickest nerve in the human body (~2 cm wide at its origin), arising from the sacral plexus. It consists of two distinct components bound together by a common epineurial sheath: the tibial component (ventral divisions of L4–S3) and the common peroneal / fibular component (dorsal divisions of L4–S2).
bullets: Exit from Pelvis: Leaves pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen BELOW the piriformis muscle.

Course in Gluteal Region: Curves downward and laterally midway between the ischial tuberosity (medially) and greater trochanter (laterally), resting successively on: posterior surface of ischium → obturator internus with gemelli → quadratus femoris, covered posteriorly by gluteus maximus.

Course in Back of Thigh: Descends on adductor magnus, crossed obliquely by the long head of biceps femoris, and divides at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa (junction of upper 2/3 and lower 1/3 of thigh) into tibial nerve and common fibular (peroneal) nerve.
slides.remember: Thickest nerve (L4–S3)! Exits below Piriformis → midway between Ischial Tuberosity & Greater Trochanter → splits at apex of Popliteal Fossa!
slides.q: The sciatic nerve leaves the pelvis to enter the gluteal region by passing through the greater sciatic foramen:
slides.why: In ~85–90% of individuals, the sciatic nerve exits the greater sciatic foramen inferior to the piriformis muscle.

slides.p: Remember the muscular branches in the thigh plus its major clinical correlations:
bullets: Muscular Branches (in Thigh): Tibial component supplies semitendinosus, semimembranosus, long head of biceps femoris, and ischial head of adductor magnus (all hamstrings!). Common fibular component supplies ONLY the short head of biceps femoris!

Safe Site for Gluteal Intramuscular Injection: Always give IM injections in the upper outer quadrant of the buttock (gluteus medius) to avoid damaging the sciatic nerve lying in the lower medial quadrant.

Sciatica & Sleeping Foot: Compression of L4–S3 nerve roots (e.g., lumbar disc prolapse) causes shooting pain radiating down the back of the thigh and leg ('sciatica'). Sitting on a hard edge compresses the nerve against the femur, causing temporary numbness ('sleeping foot').
slides.remember: Short head of biceps femoris = Common fibular nerve; all other hamstrings = Tibial nerve! Safe gluteal injection = Upper Outer Quadrant!
slides.q: Which hamstring muscle in the posterior thigh is innervated by the common fibular (peroneal) division of the sciatic nerve?
slides.why: The short head of biceps femoris is supplied by the common fibular division, whereas all other true hamstrings are supplied by the tibial division.

lessons.exam: LAQ order: Root value (L4–S3) & two components → Course & relations (gluteal region & back of thigh) → Termination (apex of popliteal fossa) → Branches (muscular & articular) → Applied anatomy (safe IM injection quadrant, sciatica, posterior hip dislocation) + Labelled diagram.
