lessons.title: Femoral Triangle

slides.p: The femoral triangle (Scarpa's triangle) is a triangular depression on the upper front of the thigh just below the inguinal ligament:
bullets: Superior (Base): Inguinal ligament.
Lateral Boundary: Medial border of sartorius.
Medial Boundary: Medial border of adductor longus.
Apex: Meeting of sartorius and adductor longus (continues into the adductor / Hunter's canal).

Roof: Skin, superficial fascia (superficial inguinal lymph nodes, great saphenous vein termination, superficial branches of femoral artery), and fascia lata (with saphenous opening covered by cribriform fascia).
Floor (lateral to medial): Iliacus, Psoas major, Pectineus, and Adductor longus.
slides.remember: SAIL = Sartorius (lateral), Adductor longus (medial), Inguinal Ligament (base)! Floor (lateral to medial) = I-P-P-A (Iliacus, Psoas, Pectineus, Adductor longus)!
slides.q: Which muscle forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle?
slides.why: The medial border of adductor longus forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle, while sartorius forms the lateral boundary.

slides.p: From lateral to medial, the contents of the femoral triangle spell N-A-V-E-L:
bullets: N — Femoral Nerve: Lies OUTSIDE the femoral sheath, lateral to the femoral artery.
A — Femoral Artery (and its branches, including profunda femoris): Occupies the lateral compartment of the femoral sheath; enters at mid-inguinal point.
V — Femoral Vein (receiving great saphenous vein): Occupies the intermediate compartment of the femoral sheath, medial to the artery.
E — Empty Space (Femoral Canal): Medial compartment of the femoral sheath containing fat and Cloquet's lymph node.
L — Lymphatics (Deep inguinal lymph nodes): Medial to femoral vein.

Clinical Importance: Femoral artery pulse is palpated at the mid-inguinal point (used for arterial blood gas sampling & cardiac catheterization); femoral vein lies just medial to the palpable femoral pulse; site of femoral hernia.
slides.remember: Lateral to medial = N-A-V-E-L! Femoral Nerve is OUTSIDE the femoral sheath! Femoral pulse = Mid-inguinal point!
slides.q: What is the correct order of the major structures in the femoral triangle from lateral to medial?
slides.why: From lateral to medial, the structures are Femoral Nerve (outside sheath), Femoral Artery, Femoral Vein, and Femoral Canal (NAVEL).

lessons.exam: LAQ order: Definition & situation → Boundaries (base, lateral, medial, apex, roof, 4 floor muscles) → Contents (N-A-V-E-L) → Applied anatomy (femoral pulse at mid-inguinal point, arterial catheterization, femoral venepuncture, femoral hernia) + Labelled diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Venous Drainage of Lower Limb ( & Great Saphenous Vein)

slides.p: Venous blood from the lower limb returns against gravity via three interconnected systems:
bullets: 1. Superficial Veins (in superficial fascia): Great saphenous vein and Small saphenous vein (draining dorsal venous arch).
2. Deep Veins (beneath deep fascia, accompanying arteries): Anterior & posterior tibial veins → popliteal vein → femoral vein → external iliac vein.

3. Perforating Veins (Perforators): Piercing deep fascia to connect superficial veins to deep veins, equipped with one-way valves allowing blood to flow ONLY from superficial → deep (e.g., Dodd's in thigh, Boyd's below knee, Cockett's medial ankle perforators).
Calf Muscle Pump ('Peripheral Heart'): Contraction of soleus & gastrocnemius squeezes deep veins upward while valves prevent backflow.
slides.remember: Perforator valves allow blood ONLY from Superficial → Deep! Soleus & Gastrocnemius = 'Peripheral Heart'!
slides.q: In healthy lower limb perforating veins, which direction do one-way valves permit venous blood to flow?
opts: From deep veins to superficial veins
From superficial veins to deep veins
slides.why: Valves in perforating veins direct blood exclusively from the superficial venous system into the high-pressure deep venous system.

slides.h: 2. Great Saphenous Vein — Course, Tributaries & Termination
slides.p: The great (long) saphenous vein is the longest vein in the body (and also appears separately as a starred Short Note topic):
bullets: Origin & Ankle Landmark: Formed on the dorsum of the foot by the union of the medial end of the dorsal venous arch and the medial marginal vein; ascends in front of the medial malleolus (accompanied by the saphenous nerve).

Course in Leg & Thigh: Ascends along the medial border of the tibia, passes a hand's breadth behind the medial femoral condyle at the knee, runs up the anteromedial thigh, pierces the cribriform fascia at the saphenous opening (~3–4 cm inferolateral to pubic tubercle), and drains into the femoral vein.
Tributaries before Saphenous Opening (3 superficial): Superficial circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, and superficial external pudendal veins (plus posteromedial & anterolateral thigh veins).
slides.remember: Great saphenous vein passes IN FRONT OF medial malleolus (with saphenous nerve) → pierces cribriform fascia at Saphenous Opening → Femoral Vein!
slides.q: Where does the great saphenous vein lie in relation to the medial malleolus at the ankle?
opts: In front of (anterior to) the medial malleolus
slides.why: The great saphenous vein ascends directly anterior to the medial malleolus, making this a reliable site for emergency venous cut-down.

slides.h: 3. Applied Anatomy — Varicose Veins, CABG & Venous Cut-Down
slides.p: Every clinical application here is a high-yield exam favorite:
bullets: Varicose Veins & Trendelenburg Test: Incompetence of saphenofemoral or perforator valves allows high-pressure deep venous blood to reflux into superficial veins, causing dilated, tortuous varicose veins and venous ulcers above the medial malleolus.
Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG): Segments of the great saphenous vein are harvested and reversed (so its valves don't obstruct arterial flow!) to bypass blocked coronary arteries.
Venous Cut-Down: Performed anterior to the medial malleolus (take care not to injure the adjacent saphenous nerve!).
slides.remember: CABG graft = Great saphenous vein REVERSED so valves point toward blood flow! Cut-down = Anterior to medial malleolus!
slides.q: When a segment of the great saphenous vein is used as a graft in coronary artery bypass surgery (CABG), why must it be inverted (reversed)?
opts: Because its wall is thicker proximally
So that its venous valves do not obstruct arterial blood flow
To prevent thrombosis of the vasa vasorum
Because it lacks smooth muscle distally
slides.why: Venous valves in the great saphenous vein permit flow only toward the heart; reversing the vein segment allows unobstructed arterial flow.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Classification (Superficial, Deep, Perforators) → Great Saphenous Vein (origin, ankle relation, course, saphenous opening, tributaries, valves) → Small Saphenous Vein (briefly) → Perforators & Calf muscle pump → Applied anatomy (varicose veins, Trendelenburg test, DVT, CABG graft, venous cut-down) + Labelled diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Longitudinal Arches of Foot – Medial Longitudinal Arch & Lateral Longitudinal Arch

slides.h: 1. Medial vs Lateral Longitudinal Arch — Bones & Structure
slides.p: The human foot is arched longitudinally and transversely to distribute body weight, absorb shock during walking/jumping, and protect plantar vessels and nerves. Compare the Medial and Lateral Longitudinal Arches:
bullets: Medial Longitudinal Arch (Higher, more resilient/elastic): Posterior pillar: Medial half of calcaneus. Summit (Keystone): Head of Talus. Anterior pillar: Navicular, three cuneiforms (medial, intermediate, lateral), and medial three metatarsals (1st, 2nd, 3rd).
Lateral Longitudinal Arch (Lower, flatter, weight-bearing/rigid): Posterior pillar: Lateral half of calcaneus. Summit (Keystone): Cuboid. Anterior pillar: Lateral two metatarsals (4th and 5th).
slides.remember: Medial arch = High & springy; Keystone = Talus; Anterior = Medial 3 metatarsals. Lateral arch = Low & rigid; Keystone = Cuboid; Anterior = Lateral 2 metatarsals!
slides.q: Which bone forms the summit (keystone) of the medial longitudinal arch of the foot?
slides.why: The talus (specifically its head) forms the summit/keystone of the high, resilient medial longitudinal arch.

slides.h: 2. Four Factors Maintaining the Arches & Applied Anatomy
slides.p: Every examiner expects the four classic factors maintaining the arches (especially for the starred Short Note on Medial Longitudinal Arch):
bullets: 1. Shape of Bones: Wedge-shaped tarsals & metatarsals interlocking like stones in a masonry bridge.

2. Intersegmental Ties (Ligaments): Spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular ligament) — supports head of talus in medial arch! Long & short plantar ligaments — support lateral arch! Plantar aponeurosis acts as a strong tie-beam for both arches.
3. Bowstrings (Long Tendons): Flexor hallucis longus (medial arch), Flexor digitorum longus, and intrinsic plantar muscles.
4. Slings (Suspension from Above): Tibialis anterior & Tibialis posterior (suspend medial arch from above) and Fibularis (peroneus) longus (supports both lateral and transverse arches).
Applied Anatomy: Loss of the medial longitudinal arch produces Pes Planus (Flat Foot) (fatigue, loss of springiness); exaggeration produces Pes Cavus (High-arched foot).
slides.remember: 4 Factors = Bones + Ligaments (Spring ligament!) + Bowstrings (FHL/FDL) + Slings (Tibialis anterior & posterior)! Flat foot = Pes Planus.
slides.q: Which ligament directly supports the head of the talus and is critical in maintaining the medial longitudinal arch of the foot?
slides.why: The plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament bridges the sustentaculum tali to the navicular, directly supporting the head of the talus.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Introduction & functions of arches → Comparison table of Medial vs Lateral Longitudinal Arch (ends, summit/keystone, pillars) → Four factors maintaining the arches (shape of bones, intersegmental ligaments/spring ligament, tie-beams/bowstrings, muscular slings) → Applied anatomy (pes planus, pes cavus) + Labelled diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Femoral Sheath, Femoral Canal & Femoral Hernia

slides.p: The femoral sheath is a 3–4 cm funnel-shaped fascial sleeve surrounding the proximal femoral vessels below the inguinal ligament:
bullets: Formation: Anterior wall = downward prolongation of fascia transversalis; Posterior wall = downward prolongation of fascia iliaca.

Three Compartments (from lateral to medial): 1. Lateral compartment: Femoral artery + femoral branch of genitofemoral nerve. 2. Intermediate compartment: Femoral vein. 3. Medial compartment: Femoral canal (conical space ~1.25 cm long containing fat & Cloquet's / Rosenmüller's lymph node).
Note: The femoral nerve lies OUTSIDE the femoral sheath laterally!
slides.remember: Front wall = Fascia transversalis; Back wall = Fascia iliaca. 3 compartments: Artery (lateral) | Vein (middle) | Femoral Canal (medial). Nerve is OUTSIDE!
slides.q: Which fascial layer forms the anterior wall of the femoral sheath?
slides.why: The anterior wall of the femoral sheath is formed by fascia transversalis, while the posterior wall is formed by fascia iliaca.

slides.p: The upper abdominal mouth of the femoral canal is the femoral ring (closed by the femoral septum). Memorize its four boundaries and surgical importance:
bullets: Femoral Ring Boundaries: Anteriorly: Inguinal ligament; Posteriorly: Pectineus & pectineal ligament (Cooper's ligament); Medially: Sharp crescentic edge of lacunar ligament (Gimbernat's ligament); Laterally: Septum separating it from the femoral vein.

Femoral Hernia: Protrusion of abdominal viscera through the femoral ring into the femoral canal and out through the saphenous opening (more common in females due to wider pelvis and smaller femoral vessels).

Surgical Pearl — Strangulation & Abnormal Obturator Artery: Because the femoral ring is narrow and bounded medially by the rigid lacunar ligament, femoral hernias have a high risk of strangulation. When incising the lacunar ligament medially to relieve strangulation, watch out for an abnormal obturator artery running along its edge!
slides.remember: Femoral Hernia = More common in FEMALES; lies BELOW & LATERAL to pubic tubercle (Inguinal hernia lies ABOVE & MEDIAL to pubic tubercle)!
slides.q: Which structure forms the sharp medial boundary of the femoral ring that frequently causes strangulation of a femoral hernia?
slides.why: The sharp medial margin of the lacunar ligament bounds the femoral ring medially and is the primary constricting agent in strangulated femoral hernias.

lessons.exam: SN order: Femoral sheath formation & 3 compartments → Femoral canal (extent, contents, Cloquet's node) → Four boundaries of femoral ring → Femoral hernia (anatomical course, relation to pubic tubercle vs inguinal hernia, high strangulation risk, abnormal obturator artery) + Diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Foot Drop – Anatomical Basis

slides.h: 1. Definition, Nerve Injured & Site of Vulnerability
slides.p: Foot drop is the inability to dorsiflex the ankle (and extend the toes), causing the forefoot to hang downward in plantarflexion and drag on the ground during walking.
bullets: Nerve Injured: Common Fibular (Peroneal) Nerve (L4, L5, S1, S2) (or selectively its deep fibular branch).

Commonest Site of Injury: Where the common fibular nerve winds subcutaneously around the lateral aspect of the neck of the fibula (vulnerable in fibular neck fractures, tight plaster casts, or crossing legs).

Muscles Paralyzed: Anterior compartment (Deep fibular nerve): Tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, fibularis tertius (loss of dorsiflexion!). Lateral compartment (Superficial fibular nerve): Fibularis longus & brevis (loss of eversion!).
slides.remember: Neck of Fibula fracture → Common Fibular Nerve injured → Loss of Dorsiflexion + Loss of Eversion = Foot Drop!
slides.q: Fracture at which bony site most commonly injures the common fibular (peroneal) nerve to produce foot drop?
slides.why: The common fibular nerve lies directly against the periosteum as it winds around the lateral side of the neck of the fibula, making it highly vulnerable to trauma or tight casts.

slides.p: Describe the gait and sensory findings clearly to earn full marks:
bullets: Foot Posture: Equinovarus attitude (plantarflexed by unopposed gastrocnemius-soleus + inverted by unopposed tibialis posterior).

High-Stepping (Steppage) Gait: To prevent the drooping toes from scraping the floor during the swing phase of walking, the patient lifts the knee unusually high by exaggerating hip and knee flexion, and the foot slaps down on the ground.
Sensory Loss: Over the anterolateral lower leg and dorsum of the foot (except medial border = saphenous nerve, and lateral border = sural nerve).
slides.remember: Common fibular nerve injury → Foot Drop + High-stepping gait + Sensory loss on dorsum of foot!
slides.q: Why does a patient with foot drop exhibit a characteristic 'high-stepping gait'?
opts: Because the hip flexors are paralyzed
To lift the plantarflexed toes clear of the ground during the swing phase of walking
Due to spasticity of the quadriceps
Due to loss of knee extension
slides.why: Because the ankle cannot dorsiflex, the patient excessively flexes the hip and knee to raise the drooping forefoot off the ground when advancing the leg.

lessons.exam: SN order: Definition → Anatomical basis (Common fibular nerve at neck of fibula → anterior & lateral compartment muscles paralyzed) → Posture of foot (equinovarus) → High-stepping gait mechanism → Sensory loss over dorsum of foot.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Inversion and Eversion – Inverters and Everters with Nerve Supply

slides.p: Inversion (turning the sole of the foot medially so the medial border is raised) and eversion (turning the sole laterally so the lateral border is raised) occur primarily at the subtalar (talocalcaneal) and transverse tarsal (talocalcaneonavicular & calcaneocuboid) joints—NOT at the ankle joint!
bullets: Axis of Movement: Oblique axis passing forward, upward, and medially from the back of the calcaneus through the sinus tarsi to the superomedial aspect of the neck of the talus.
Range: Inversion has a wider range than eversion and is coupled with plantarflexion/adduction; eversion is coupled with dorsiflexion/abduction.
slides.remember: Inversion & Eversion happen at Subtalar & Transverse Tarsal joints (NOT the ankle joint)!
slides.q: At which joints of the foot do inversion and eversion primarily take place?
slides.why: The ankle joint is a uniaxial hinge permitting only dorsiflexion and plantarflexion; inversion and eversion occur at the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints.

slides.h: 2. Inverters & Everters with Nerve Supply + Clinical Link
slides.p: Memorize the exact muscles and nerve supplies for both movements:
bullets: Inverters (2 Main + 2 Assisting): 1. Tibialis Anterior (Deep fibular nerve, L4–L5) and 2. Tibialis Posterior (Tibial nerve, L4–L5) — assisted by Flexor hallucis longus & Flexor digitorum longus.

Everters (3 Fibular/Peroneal Muscles): 1. Fibularis (Peroneus) Longus (Superficial fibular nerve), 2. Fibularis (Peroneus) Brevis (Superficial fibular nerve), and 3. Fibularis (Peroneus) Tertius (Deep fibular nerve).
Clinical — Inversion Sprain: Forced over-inversion tears the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) (commonest ankle sprain!) or avulses the base of the 5th metatarsal (fibularis brevis pull).
slides.remember: Inverters = BOTH Tibialis muscles (Tibialis anterior [Deep fibular] + Tibialis posterior [Tibial]). Everters = ALL THREE Fibularis muscles!
slides.q: Which two muscles are the primary inverters of the foot?
opts: Extensor digitorum longus and fibularis tertius
slides.why: Tibialis anterior (deep fibular nerve) and tibialis posterior (tibial nerve) both insert on the medial border of the foot and act together as the main inverters.

lessons.exam: SN order: Definitions → Joints involved (subtalar & transverse tarsal) → Oblique axis → Inverters with nerve supply (Tibialis anterior & posterior) → Everters with nerve supply (Fibularis longus, brevis, tertius) → Applied anatomy (inversion ankle sprain, ATFL tear).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Gluteus Maximus & Structures Under Gluteus Maximus

slides.h: 1. Gluteus Maximus — Attachments, Nerve Supply & Actions
slides.p: Gluteus maximus is the largest, coarsest, and most superficial muscle of the gluteal region:
bullets: Origin: Outer slope of dorsal segment of iliac crest, posterior gluteal line & area behind it, posterior surface of sacrum & coccyx, and sacrotuberous ligament.
Insertion: Deep 1/4 of lower fibres → gluteal tuberosity of femur; Superficial 3/4 → iliotibial tract.
Nerve Supply: Inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2) (the ONLY muscle supplied by this nerve!).
Actions: Chief extensor of the flexed thigh (rising from sitting, climbing stairs, running) and lateral rotator of thigh; stabilizes knee via iliotibial tract.
slides.remember: Gluteus maximus = Inferior Gluteal Nerve (L5, S1, S2)! Main extensor of flexed thigh (climbing stairs / standing up from chair)!
slides.q: Which nerve innervates the gluteus maximus muscle?
slides.why: Gluteus maximus is supplied exclusively by the inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2).

slides.h: 2. Complete List of Structures Under Gluteus Maximus (LAQ Diagram)
slides.p: Organize all structures lying deep to gluteus maximus into Bones/Ligaments, Muscles, Vessels, and Nerves so your diagram and list are effortless:
bullets: 1. Bones & Ligaments: Ilium, sacrum, coccyx, ischial tuberosity, greater trochanter, sacrotuberous & sacrospinous ligaments.

2. Muscles (from above downward): Gluteus medius & minimus, Piriformis (key landmark!), Superior gemellus, Obturator internus tendon, Inferior gemellus (triceps coxae), Quadratus femoris, upper border of adductor magnus, and origin of hamstrings from ischial tuberosity.
3. Vessels: Superior gluteal vessels (emerging ABOVE piriformis) and Inferior gluteal & Internal pudendal vessels (emerging BELOW piriformis) + trochanteric & cruciate anastomoses.

4. Nerves: Superior gluteal nerve (above piriformis); 7 nerves BELOW piriformis: Sciatic nerve, Posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh, Inferior gluteal nerve, Nerve to quadratus femoris, Nerve to obturator internus, Pudendal nerve (plus perforating cutaneous nerve).
slides.remember: Piriformis is the key landmark under Gluteus Maximus: Superior gluteal vessels & nerve emerge ABOVE it; Sciatic & 6 other nerves emerge BELOW it!
slides.q: Which neurovascular structures emerge through the greater sciatic foramen SUPERIOR to the piriformis muscle under cover of gluteus maximus?
opts: Sciatic nerve and inferior gluteal vessels
Superior gluteal nerve and superior gluteal vessels
Pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels
slides.why: Only the superior gluteal nerve and superior gluteal vessels emerge above the piriformis muscle; all other structures exit below piriformis.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Gluteus maximus (origin, insertion into gluteal tuberosity & iliotibial tract, inferior gluteal nerve, actions, trochanteric bursae) → Structures under gluteus maximus grouped as Bones/Ligaments, Muscles, Vessels, and Nerves (above vs below piriformis) + Labelled diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Sartorius*, Popliteus**, Gastrocnemius & Intra-Articular Structures of Knee Joint*

slides.p: Sartorius is the longest muscle in the human body, running obliquely across the front of the thigh:
bullets: Origin & Insertion: From anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) → upper medial surface of shaft of tibia in front of gracilis & semitendinosus (forming pes anserinus — 'guy ropes').
Nerve Supply & Action: Femoral nerve (L2, L3). Flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates the thigh + flexes and medially rotates the leg (cross-legged sitting position!).
Relations: Forms lateral boundary of femoral triangle and roof of adductor (Hunter's) canal.
slides.remember: Sartorius = Longest muscle (ASIS → Pes anserinus), Femoral nerve, Tailor's cross-legged position!
slides.q: Which three muscles insert together onto the upper medial surface of the tibia to form the pes anserinus?
opts: Rectus femoris, vastus medialis, and gracilis
slides.why: Sartorius (femoral nerve), gracilis (obturator nerve), and semitendinosus (tibial nerve) insert together at the pes anserinus on the proximal medial tibia.

slides.p: Popliteus** is a flat triangular muscle forming the lower part of the floor of the popliteal fossa:
bullets: Origin & Insertion (Intracapsular tendon!): Arises inside the knee joint capsule from the anterior end of the popliteal groove on the lateral femoral condyle (plus lateral meniscus & arcuate popliteal ligament) → inserts onto the posterior surface of the tibia above the soleal line.

Nerve Supply & Action: Tibial nerve (L4, L5, S1). When the foot is fixed on the ground, popliteus laterally rotates the femur on the tibia to unlock the fully extended knee at the start of flexion, and pulls the lateral meniscus backward to prevent crushing.
slides.remember: Popliteus** = Intracapsular origin on lateral femoral condyle, Tibial nerve, laterally rotates femur to UNLOCK the knee!
slides.q: How does the popliteus muscle unlock the fully extended knee joint when the foot is planted on the ground?
opts: By medially rotating the femur on the tibia
By laterally rotating the femur on the tibia
By pulling the medial meniscus forward
slides.why: With the tibia fixed on the ground, popliteus laterally rotates the femur on the tibial condyles, reversing the medial rotation of terminal locking.

slides.p: Complete your Lower Limb muscle & knee review with Gastrocnemius and Intra-articular structures of the knee joint*:
bullets: Gastrocnemius: Superficial two-headed calf muscle (medial & lateral heads from femoral condyles) joining soleus to form the tendo calcaneus (Achilles tendon) → inserts into middle 1/3 of posterior calcaneus; supplied by Tibial nerve (S1, S2); plantarflexes ankle & flexes knee; forms lower boundaries of popliteal fossa.

Intra-Articular Structures of Knee Joint*: 1. Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) (resists anterior tibial translation), 2. Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) (resists posterior tibial translation), 3. Medial meniscus (C-shaped, attached to tibial collateral ligament → injured 20x more often!), 4. Lateral meniscus (circular, mobile), 5. Transverse ligament, and 6. Tendon of popliteus.
slides.remember: Gastrocnemius + Soleus = Triceps surae → Achilles tendon (Tibial nerve). Knee intra-articular = ACL, PCL, Medial & Lateral Menisci, Transverse ligament, Popliteus tendon!
slides.q: Which intra-articular structure of the knee joint is C-shaped, firmly attached to the tibial collateral ligament, and much more frequently torn than its lateral counterpart?
slides.why: The medial meniscus is less mobile because of its firm attachment to the tibial (medial) collateral ligament, making it far more susceptible to tearing.

lessons.exam: Write each under: Origin, Insertion, Nerve supply, Action & Applied anatomy (Pes anserinus for Sartorius; Knee unlocking & intracapsular tendon for Popliteus**; Achilles tendon & calf pump for Gastrocnemius; List & diagram of ACL/PCL/menisci for Intra-articular structures of knee*).

lessons.title: Superficial Inguinal Lymph Nodes

slides.p: The superficial inguinal lymph nodes lie in the superficial fascia of the groin arranged in the shape of a letter 'T' (a horizontal upper group below the inguinal ligament and a vertical lower group along the termination of the great saphenous vein):
bullets: 1. Upper Horizontal Group (Lateral & Medial): Drains skin of anterior abdominal wall below umbilicus, gluteal region & lower back, perineum & anal canal below pectinate line, external genitalia (penis/scrotum or vulva/lower vagina), and uterine cornu (via round ligament).
2. Lower Vertical Group: Drains almost the entire superficial lymph of the lower limb (EXCEPT the posterolateral calf & lateral foot, which drain first into popliteal nodes!).
Efferents: Pierce cribriform fascia to drain into deep inguinal nodes and external iliac nodes.
slides.remember: T-shaped arrangement! Drains everything below umbilicus + perineum/external genitalia + lower limb (EXCEPT testes → para-aortic nodes, and glans penis/clitoris → Cloquet's deep node)!
slides.q: Which of the following structures does NOT drain into the superficial inguinal lymph nodes?
opts: Anal canal below the pectinate line
Skin of the anterior abdominal wall below the umbilicus
slides.why: The testes develop on the posterior abdominal wall and drain directly into the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes, whereas the scrotum drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

slides.p: Clinical examination of the groin nodes helps localize occult infections or tumors:
bullets: Inguinal Lymphadenopathy: Enlargement of the horizontal group points toward perineal, genital, lower anal canal, or infraumbilical lesions; enlargement of the vertical group points toward lower-limb infection or melanoma.
slides.remember: Horizontal group enlarged = Perineum / Genitalia / Lower anal canal. Vertical group enlarged = Lower limb!
slides.q: Which part of the anal canal drains into the medial group of superficial inguinal lymph nodes?
opts: Upper anal canal above the pectinate line
Lower anal canal below the pectinate line
slides.why: Lymph from the anal canal below the pectinate line drains into the superficial inguinal lymph nodes (whereas above the pectinate line drains to internal iliac nodes).

lessons.exam: SN order: Situation & T-shaped arrangement (upper horizontal vs lower vertical groups) → Areas drained by each group (with key exceptions: testes, glans, lateral foot) → Efferent drainage → Applied anatomy + Diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Extra-Hepatic Biliary Apparatus

slides.p: The extra-hepatic biliary apparatus collects bile from the liver, stores and concentrates it (~10-fold) in the gallbladder, and delivers it into the 2nd part of the duodenum:
bullets: Components: Right & left hepatic ducts → Common hepatic duct (~3 cm) + Cystic duct (~3–4 cm, containing spiral valve of Heister) → Common bile duct (CBD) (~8 cm) + Gallbladder.

Gallbladder (Fundus, Body, Neck): Lies in the gallbladder fossa on the visceral surface of the right lobe of the liver; fundus projects at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage (where lateral border of right rectus abdominis meets costal margin). A posteromedial dilatation of the neck is called Hartmann's pouch (common site where gallstones lodge!).
slides.remember: Fundus of gallbladder = Tip of Right 9th Costal Cartilage (Murphy's sign spot)! Hartmann's pouch = Gallstone trap!
slides.q: At which surface anatomical landmark does the fundus of the gallbladder reach the anterior abdominal wall?
slides.why: The fundus of the gallbladder lies behind the anterior abdominal wall at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage (junction of right semilunar line and costal margin).

slides.h: 2. Common Bile Duct (4 Parts), Calot's Triangle & Applied Anatomy
slides.p: Every surgeon and anatomy examiner tests the four parts of the CBD and Calot's (cystohepatic) triangle:
bullets: Four Parts of CBD: 1. Supraduodenal (in right free margin of lesser omentum, anterior to epiploic foramen, to the right of hepatic artery & anterior to portal vein), 2. Retroduodenal (behind 1st part of duodenum), 3. Infraduodenal (grooving posterior aspect of head of pancreas), and 4. Intraduodenal (joins main pancreatic duct to form hepatopancreatic ampulla of Vater, guarded by sphincter of Oddi, opening at major duodenal papilla ~8–10 cm distal to pylorus).

Calot's Triangle Boundaries: Medially = Common hepatic duct; Inferiorly = Cystic duct; Superiorly = Inferior surface of liver. Content = Cystic artery (branch of right hepatic artery — must be ligated during cholecystectomy!).
Applied Anatomy: Gallstones blocking CBD cause obstructive jaundice; inflammation of gallbladder causes Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest on palpating right 9th costal cartilage tip).
slides.remember: Lesser omentum free edge: CBD on right, Hepatic Artery on left, Portal Vein behind! Calot's triangle contains Cystic Artery!
slides.q: Which key artery lies within Calot's (cystohepatic) triangle and must be identified during cholecystectomy?
slides.why: The cystic artery (usually arising from the right hepatic artery) traverses Calot's triangle to supply the gallbladder.

lessons.exam: LAQ order: Components → Gallbladder (parts, relations, Hartmann's pouch, blood supply) → Hepatic, cystic & common bile ducts (4 parts & relations of CBD, sphincter of Oddi) → Calot's triangle → Applied anatomy (gallstones, obstructive jaundice, Murphy's sign) + Labelled diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Duodenum – 2nd Part

slides.h: 1. Extent, Course & Key Relations of the 2nd (Descending) Part
slides.p: The second (descending) part of the duodenum (~7.5–10 cm long) is entirely retroperitoneal, descending vertically along the right side of the L1, L2, and L3 vertebrae from the superior duodenal flexure to the inferior duodenal flexure:
bullets: Anterior Relations (top to bottom): Right lobe of liver, gallbladder, transverse colon & transverse mesocolon (crosses middle of 2nd part — bare of peritoneum here!), and coils of small intestine.
Posterior Relations: Hilum & anterior surface of right kidney, right renal vessels, right ureter, right psoas major, and edge of IVC.
Medial Relation: Head of the pancreas and common bile duct.
Lateral Relation: Right colic (hepatic) flexure.
slides.remember: 2nd part of duodenum sits at L1–L3 in front of Right Kidney hilum, crossed anteriorly by Transverse Colon, embracing Head of Pancreas medially!
slides.q: Which large bowel structure crosses anteriorly across the middle of the second part of the duodenum?
slides.why: The transverse colon (and root of transverse mesocolon) crosses directly in front of the descending (2nd) part of the duodenum.

slides.h: 2. Interior Features (Major & Minor Papillae), Blood Supply & Applied Anatomy
slides.p: Inside the posteromedial wall of the 2nd part lies the embryological junction between the foregut and midgut:
bullets: Major Duodenal Papilla: Conical elevation on posteromedial wall (~8–10 cm distal to pylorus), hooded by plica semicircularis, receiving the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater) (CBD + main pancreatic duct).
Minor Duodenal Papilla: Lies ~2 cm anterosuperior to major papilla; receives the accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini).

Dual Blood Supply (Foregut–Midgut Junction!): Above major papilla = Superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (coeliac trunk / foregut); Below major papilla = Inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (SMA / midgut).
Applied Anatomy: Posterior duodenal ulcer perforation can erode the gastroduodenal artery (behind 1st part) or irritate the right kidney; ERCP cannulates the major duodenal papilla.
slides.remember: Major duodenal papilla = Foregut–Midgut junction (Superior vs Inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries)! Minor papilla sits 2 cm ABOVE major papilla!
slides.q: Where is the minor duodenal papilla located relative to the major duodenal papilla inside the 2nd part of the duodenum?
opts: On the lateral wall opposite the major papilla
slides.why: The minor duodenal papilla (opening of the accessory pancreatic duct) sits about 2 cm anterosuperior to the major duodenal papilla.

lessons.exam: LAQ order: Extent & vertebral level (L1–L3) → Peritoneal covering → Relations (anterior, posterior, medial, lateral) → Interior (plicae circulares, major & minor duodenal papillae) → Blood supply (foregut/midgut dual supply) → Applied anatomy + Labelled diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Rectus Sheath

slides.h: 1. Formation at Three Levels (Above Costal Margin, Mid-Abdomen, Below Arcuate Line)
slides.p: The rectus sheath is an aponeurotic envelope enclosing the rectus abdominis and pyramidalis muscles, formed by the aponeuroses of the three flat abdominal muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis). Its wall composition changes at three levels:
bullets: 1. Above Costal Margin: Anterior wall: External oblique aponeurosis only. Posterior wall: Deficient (rectus rests directly on 5th, 6th, 7th costal cartilages).

2. Between Costal Margin & Arcuate Line (Midway between Umbilicus & Pubis): Anterior wall: External oblique aponeurosis + anterior lamina of split internal oblique aponeurosis. Posterior wall: Posterior lamina of internal oblique aponeurosis + transversus abdominis aponeurosis.

3. Below Arcuate Line (of Douglas): Anterior wall: ALL THREE aponeuroses pass in front of rectus abdominis! Posterior wall: Deficient of aponeurosis (rectus rests directly on fascia transversalis, extraperitoneal fat, and peritoneum).
slides.remember: Above costal margin = No posterior sheath. Mid-abdomen = Internal oblique splits around rectus! Below Arcuate Line = ALL 3 aponeuroses go IN FRONT!
slides.q: Below the arcuate line (of Douglas), which structures form the anterior wall of the rectus sheath?
opts: Aponeuroses of all three flat muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis)
Internal oblique and transversus abdominis only
slides.why: Below the arcuate line, the aponeuroses of external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis all pass anterior to rectus abdominis, leaving only fascia transversalis behind it.

slides.h: 2. Contents & Applied Anatomy (Rectus Sheath Hematoma & Incisions)
slides.p: List the exact contents and surgical significance of the rectus sheath:
bullets: Contents: 1. Muscles: Rectus abdominis & Pyramidalis; 2. Arteries: Superior epigastric artery (branch of internal thoracic) and Inferior epigastric artery (branch of external iliac — enters posterior to rectus at arcuate line!); 3. Veins: Superior & inferior epigastric veins; 4. Nerves: Terminal parts of lower 5 intercostal nerves (T7–T11) and subcostal nerve (T12).

Applied Anatomy: Rupture of the inferior epigastric artery (e.g., severe coughing or trauma) produces a painful rectus sheath hematoma confined to one side by the linea alba. Paramedian surgical incisions retract rectus abdominis laterally to preserve its segmental nerve supply entering from the lateral side.
slides.remember: Inferior epigastric artery enters rectus sheath at the Arcuate Line! Nerves (T7–T12) enter LATERALLY → retract rectus laterally in paramedian incisions!
slides.q: At which anatomical landmark does the inferior epigastric artery enter the rectus sheath?
slides.why: The inferior epigastric artery ascends extraperitoneally and enters the rectus sheath by passing anterior to the arcuate line.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Definition → Formation at three levels (above costal margin, between costal margin & arcuate line, below arcuate line) → Linea alba & linea semilunaris → Contents (2 muscles, 2 arteries, 2 veins, 6 nerves) → Applied anatomy (rectus sheath hematoma, paramedian incision, divarication of recti) + Three transverse section diagrams.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Diaphragm (Thoracoabdominal Diaphragm)

slides.p: The diaphragm is the dome-shaped musculofibrous partition separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities and serves as the principal muscle of inspiration:
bullets: Peripheral Origin (3 parts): 1. Sternal part: Back of xiphoid process (2 fleshy slips). 2. Costal part: Inner surfaces of lower 6 costal cartilages & ribs (7–12). 3. Lumbar part: Right crus (bodies of L1–L3), Left crus (bodies of L1–L2), plus medial arcuate ligament (over psoas major) and lateral arcuate ligament (over quadratus lumborum).
Insertion: Trifoliate central tendon (fused superiorly with fibrous pericardium).
Nerve Supply: Motor + central sensory = Phrenic nerves (C3, C4, C5) ('C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive!'); peripheral sensory = lower 6 intercostal nerves (T7–T12).
slides.remember: Right crus = L1–L3; Left crus = L1–L2! Motor nerve = Phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5)!
slides.q: Which spinal nerve roots provide the motor innervation to the thoracoabdominal diaphragm via the phrenic nerve?
slides.why: The phrenic nerve arises from the ventral rami of C3, C4, and C5 and is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm.

slides.h: 2. Three Major Openings (T8, T10, T12) & Applied Anatomy
slides.p: Memorize the vertebral levels, shapes, and structures passing through the three major openings ('I Ate 10 Eggs At 12'):
bullets: 1. Vena Caval Opening (T8 — in Central Tendon, right of midline): Quadrilateral; transmits Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) and right phrenic nerve. Stretches open during inspiration to assist venous return!

2. Esophageal Opening (T10 — in Muscular part, split of Right Crus): Elliptical; transmits Esophagus, right & left vagal trunks, and esophageal branches of left gastric vessels. Contracts during inspiration to prevent acid reflux!
3. Aortic Opening (T12 — behind Median Arcuate Ligament, osseoaponeurotic): Round; transmits Abdominal Aorta, Thoracic Duct, and Azygos Vein ('A-T-A'). Unaffected by diaphragmatic contraction!
Applied Anatomy: Congenital diaphragmatic hernias occur at the foramen of Bochdalek (posterolateral pleuroperitoneal canal — commonest, usually left-sided!) or foramen of Morgagni (retrosternal gap).
slides.remember: T8 = IVC + Right phrenic (in central tendon). T10 = Esophagus + Vagi (right crus sling). T12 = Aorta + Thoracic duct + Azygos!
slides.q: Which structure passes through the vena caval opening of the diaphragm at the T8 level alongside the inferior vena cava?
slides.why: The right phrenic nerve traverses the vena caval opening in the central tendon at T8 along with the inferior vena cava.

lessons.exam: LAQ order: Definition & domes → Origin (sternal, costal, lumbar crura & arcuate ligaments) → Central tendon → Three major openings (T8, T10, T12 table with shape, location & structures) & minor openings → Nerve & blood supply → Actions & applied anatomy (hiatus hernia, Bochdalek & Morgagni hernias, phrenic nerve palsy) + Inferior view diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Portacaval Anastomosis*, Caput Medusae & Umbilicus

slides.h: 1. Five Major Sites of Portacaval (Portosystemic) Anastomosis
slides.p: When liver cirrhosis or portal vein thrombosis obstructs portal venous blood flow (portal hypertension), blood detours into the systemic venous system through five natural portacaval anastomoses (since portal veins have NO valves!):
bullets: 1. Lower End of Esophagus: Esophageal tributaries of left gastric vein (portal) ↔ Esophageal tributaries of azygos/hemiazygos veins (systemic) → Dilatation causes Esophageal Varices (life-threatening hematemesis!).
2. Lower Anal Canal: Superior rectal vein (portal) ↔ Middle & inferior rectal veins (systemic) → Dilatation causes Anorectal Varices / Hemorrhoids.

3. Umbilicus (Paraumbilical Region): Paraumbilical veins of Sappey (portal, along ligamentum teres) ↔ Superficial & inferior epigastric veins (systemic) → Dilated tortuous veins radiating from umbilicus = Caput Medusae!
4. Bare Area of Liver: Portal radicles in liver ↔ Diaphragmatic/phrenic systemic veins.
5. Retroperitoneal (Ascending/Descending Colon, Duodenum, Pancreas): Colic/splenic portal veins ↔ Renal/lumbar systemic veins (veins of Retzius).
slides.remember: Esophagus (varices) + Anal canal (piles) + Umbilicus (Caput medusae) + Bare area of liver + Retroperitoneum!
slides.q: In portal hypertension, dilatation of portosystemic anastomoses at the lower end of the esophagus involves which portal tributary?
slides.why: At the gastroesophageal junction, esophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein (portal) anastomose with esophageal veins draining into the azygos system (systemic).

slides.h: 2. Caput Medusae & Umbilicus — Anatomical & Clinical Importance
slides.p: Caput Medusae and Umbilicus both appear as Short Notes in your PDF—here is how they connect:
bullets: Caput Medusae: Tortuous, engorged superficial veins radiating outward from the umbilicus (resembling the snake-haired head of Medusa), caused by recanalization of paraumbilical veins in portal hypertension; blood flows away from the umbilicus (unlike IVC obstruction where collateral flow goes upward from groin to chest).

Umbilicus — Anatomical & Clinical Importance: 1. Dermatome landmark: Supplied by T10 spinal segment (referred pain of early appendicitis!). 2. Watershed line: Venous & lymphatic drainage above umbilicus goes upward (axillary nodes / SVC), below goes downward (superficial inguinal nodes / IVC). 3. Embryological remnants: Patent urachus (urine leak), Meckel's diverticulum / vitellointestinal fistula (fecal discharge), and congenital umbilical hernia (omphalocele).
slides.remember: Umbilicus = T10 dermatome + Venous/Lymphatic watershed + Site of Caput Medusae in portal hypertension!
slides.q: Which spinal cord segment supplies the skin at the level of the umbilicus?
slides.why: The T10 dermatome encircles the trunk at the level of the umbilicus, explaining why visceral pain from the midgut (appendix) is initially referred to the periumbilical region.

lessons.exam: SN order: Definition of portacaval anastomosis → Table of 5 sites (Portal vein vs Systemic vein + Clinical manifestation) → Caput medusae (mechanism & flow direction vs IVC obstruction) → Umbilicus (T10 dermatome, watershed line, embryological remnants) + Diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Lesser Omentum* & Stomach Bed*

slides.h: 1. Lesser Omentum* — Attachments, Parts & Free Margin Contents
slides.p: The lesser omentum is a double-layered peritoneal fold extending from the lesser curvature of the stomach and proximal 2 cm of duodenum to the visceral surface of the liver:
bullets: Attachments: Inferiorly = Lesser curvature of stomach + first 2 cm of duodenum; Superiorly = L-shaped attachment to fissure for ligamentum venosum & margins of porta hepatis.
Two Parts: Hepatogastric ligament (stomach to liver) and Hepatoduodenal ligament (thickened right free margin forming the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen of Winslow).

Contents: Along lesser curvature = Right & left gastric vessels, gastric lymph nodes & vagal branches. Inside right free margin (hepatoduodenal ligament) = Portal Triad: Common bile duct (anterior right), Hepatic artery proper (anterior left), and Portal vein (posterior)!

Applied Anatomy (Pringle's Maneuver): Compressing the right free margin of the lesser omentum between index finger (in epiploic foramen) and thumb controls brisk hepatic bleeding during liver surgery!
slides.remember: Right free margin of Lesser Omentum = Portal Triad (CBD right, Hepatic artery left, Portal vein behind) → pinched in Pringle's maneuver!
slides.q: Which three major structures lie inside the right free margin (hepatoduodenal ligament) of the lesser omentum?
opts: Splenic artery, splenic vein, and tail of pancreas
Portal vein, hepatic artery proper, and common bile duct
Inferior vena cava, abdominal aorta, and right ureter
Superior mesenteric artery, superior mesenteric vein, and uncinate process
slides.why: The hepatoduodenal ligament encloses the portal triad: common bile duct (anterior right), hepatic artery proper (anterior left), and portal vein (posterior).

slides.h: 2. Stomach Bed* — Structures Behind the Stomach
slides.p: The stomach bed* consists of the structures on which the posterior surface of the stomach rests when supine, separated from the stomach by the lesser sac (omental bursa) (except the spleen, separated by the greater sac):
bullets: Seven Classic Structures of Stomach Bed: 1. Diaphragm (left crus), 2. Left suprarenal gland, 3. Upper part of anterior surface of left kidney, 4. Pancreas (anterior surface of body), 5. Splenic artery (tortuous along upper border of pancreas), 6. Transverse mesocolon (and transverse colon), and 7. Gastric surface of spleen.

Clinical Correlation: A posterior gastric ulcer can perforate into the lesser sac and erode the underlying splenic artery (causing torrential hemorrhage) or penetrate into the pancreas (causing severe back pain).
slides.remember: Stomach Bed = Diaphragm, Left kidney & suprarenal, Pancreas, Splenic artery, Transverse mesocolon, Spleen!
slides.q: Which of the following structures does NOT form part of the stomach bed?
slides.why: The stomach bed lies on the left side of the posterior abdominal wall and includes the left kidney and left suprarenal gland, not the right suprarenal gland.

lessons.exam: SN order: Lesser omentum (definition, attachments, hepatogastric vs hepatoduodenal ligaments, contents of lesser curvature & free edge, Pringle's maneuver); Stomach bed (definition, lesser sac separation, list of 7 structures, posterior gastric ulcer perforation) + Diagrams.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Meckel's Diverticulum* & McBurney's Point

slides.p: Meckel's diverticulum is the commonest congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract, representing the persistent proximal (intestinal) remnant of the embryonic vitellointestinal (omphalomesenteric) duct:
bullets: Classic Rule of 2s: Present in ~2% of population; located ~2 feet (60 cm) proximal to the ileocecal valve on the antimesenteric border of the ileum; measures ~2 inches (5 cm) long; has its own mesentery & blood supply (vitelline artery); and may contain 2 types of ectopic mucosa (gastric & pancreatic).
Clinical Significance: Ectopic acid-secreting gastric mucosa causes painless lower GI bleeding/peptic ulceration in children; inflammation (Meckel's diverticulitis) closely mimics acute appendicitis!
slides.remember: Meckel's Rule of 2s: 2% population, 2 feet from ileocecal valve, 2 inches long, antimesenteric border, 2 ectopic tissues (gastric & pancreatic)!
slides.q: On which border of the ileum is Meckel's diverticulum located?
slides.why: Meckel's diverticulum is a true diverticulum (containing all three gut layers) arising from the antimesenteric border of the ileum about 2 feet proximal to the ileocecal junction.

slides.p: McBurney's point is the classic surface landmark corresponding to the base of the vermiform appendix:
bullets: Exact Location: Lies at the junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of the right spinoumbilical line (an imaginary line drawn from the right anterior superior iliac spine [ASIS] to the umbilicus).

Clinical Significance: 1. Site of maximum tenderness (McBurney's sign) in acute appendicitis once parietal peritoneum is irritated; 2. Center of McBurney's gridiron muscle-splitting incision for open appendicectomy; 3. Pain Shift: Visceral pain starts at the umbilicus (T10) and shifts to McBurney's point when inflamed appendix touches parietal peritoneum (somatic nerves).
slides.remember: McBurney's point = Junction of lateral 1/3 & medial 2/3 of line from Right ASIS to Umbilicus!
slides.q: Where is McBurney's point located on the anterior abdominal wall?
opts: Midpoint between xiphoid process and umbilicus
Junction of lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of the line joining right ASIS to the umbilicus
Junction of medial one-third and lateral two-thirds of the line joining left ASIS to umbilicus
slides.why: McBurney's point lies at the junction of the lateral 1/3 and medial 2/3 of the right spinoumbilical line, marking the base of the appendix.

lessons.exam: SN order: Meckel's diverticulum (embryological basis — vitellointestinal duct, location on antimesenteric ileum, Rule of 2s, clinical complications); McBurney's point (exact anatomical definition, T10 to RIF pain shift, gridiron incision) + Surface diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Inferior Vena Cava (IVC)

slides.p: The inferior vena cava (IVC) is the largest vein in the body, returning deoxygenated blood from the lower limbs, pelvis, and abdomen to the right atrium:
bullets: Formation: Formed at the L5 vertebral level (just below & to the right of the aortic bifurcation) by the union of the right and left common iliac veins behind the right common iliac artery.

Course & Relations: Ascends vertically on the posterior abdominal wall to the right of the abdominal aorta, grooves the posterior surface of the liver (bare area), pierces the central tendon of the diaphragm at T8, and opens into the lower posterior part of the right atrium (guarded by the rudimentary Eustachian valve).
slides.remember: Formed at L5 (behind right common iliac artery) → ascends right of aorta → pierces diaphragm at T8 → Right Atrium!
slides.q: At which vertebral level is the inferior vena cava formed by the union of the right and left common iliac veins?
slides.why: The IVC is formed anterior to the L5 vertebral body (slightly to the right of the midline) by the confluence of the two common iliac veins.

slides.h: 2. Tributaries & Applied Anatomy (IVC Compression in Pregnancy)
slides.p: Notice the asymmetry between right and left gonadal/suprarenal venous drainage:
bullets: Tributaries: Right & left common iliac veins, 3rd & 4th lumbar veins, Right testicular/ovarian vein, Right & left renal veins, Right suprarenal vein, Inferior phrenic veins, and Right, middle & left hepatic veins (just below diaphragm).
Key Asymmetry: Left testicular/ovarian vein and Left suprarenal vein drain into the LEFT RENAL VEIN—NOT directly into the IVC!
Applied Anatomy: In late pregnancy, the gravid uterus compresses the IVC when lying supine (supine hypotensive syndrome) — relieved by turning onto the left lateral side!
slides.remember: Right gonadal & Right suprarenal → IVC directly. Left gonadal & Left suprarenal → Left Renal Vein! Supine pregnancy → turn onto LEFT side!
slides.q: Which vein drains directly into the left renal vein rather than directly into the inferior vena cava?
slides.why: The left gonadal (testicular/ovarian) vein and left suprarenal vein terminate in the left renal vein, whereas their right-sided counterparts open directly into the IVC.

lessons.exam: SN order: Formation (L5) → Course & relations (posterior abdominal wall, liver groove, T8 diaphragmatic opening) → Termination (right atrium) → Tributaries (highlighting left gonadal/suprarenal drainage into left renal vein) → Applied anatomy (supine hypotensive syndrome, IVC obstruction collaterals) + Diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Uterus, Supports of Uterus*, Uterine Tube, Ovary* & Hysterosalpingography

slides.h: 1. Uterus — Parts, Normal Position (Anteversion & Anteflexion) & Blood Supply
slides.p: The uterus is a thick-walled, pear-shaped muscular organ in the lesser pelvis between the urinary bladder (in front) and rectum (behind):
bullets: Parts: Fundus (above tubal openings), Body (main cavity), Isthmus (narrow lower 0.5 cm forming lower uterine segment in pregnancy), and Cervix (supravaginal & vaginal parts; external os opens into vagina).
Normal Position: Anteverted (~90° forward angle between cervix and vagina) and Anteflexed (~125° forward bend between body and cervix at internal os).
Blood Supply: Uterine artery (branch of anterior division of internal iliac artery — crosses ABOVE the ureter ['water under the bridge'] ~2 cm lateral to cervix!) + anastomosing ovarian artery.
slides.remember: Normal position = Anteverted & Anteflexed! 'Water under the bridge' = Uterine artery crosses ABOVE the ureter!
slides.q: What is the anatomical relationship between the uterine artery and the ureter near the lateral fornix of the vagina?
opts: Ureter crosses above the uterine artery
Uterine artery crosses superior (above) to the ureter ('water under the bridge')
Uterine artery passes inside the ureteric wall
slides.why: The uterine artery crosses superiorly over the ureter ('water under the bridge') about 1.5–2 cm lateral to the supravaginal cervix—a crucial surgical landmark during hysterectomy.

slides.h: 2. Supports of Uterus* (Primary vs Secondary Supports)
slides.p: Preventing uterine prolapse depends on Primary Supports (muscular + fibromuscular ligaments) and Secondary peritoneal folds:
bullets: A. Muscular Supports: Pelvic diaphragm (levator ani), Perineal body (central anchor of pelvic floor!), and urogenital diaphragm.

B. Fibromuscular (Condensation of Endopelvic Fascia) Ligaments: 1. Transverse cervical (Mackenrodt's / Cardinal) ligaments (most important lateral support from cervix/lateral fornix to lateral pelvic wall), 2. Pubocervical ligaments (anteriorly to pubis), 3. Uterosacral ligaments (posteriorly to sacrum — keep cervix pulled back so body stays anteverted!), and 4. Round ligament of uterus (keeps fundus pulled forward).
Clinical: Weakness of pelvic floor & cardinal/uterosacral ligaments after childbirth causes uterine prolapse.
slides.remember: 3 true fascial ligaments = Cardinal (Mackenrodt's), Pubocervical, Uterosacral + Pelvic diaphragm & Perineal body! Broad ligament is only a secondary peritoneal fold!
slides.q: Which ligamentous condensation of endopelvic fascia attaches the cervix and lateral vaginal fornix to the lateral pelvic wall and serves as a major support of the uterus?
slides.why: The transverse cervical (cardinal / Mackenrodt's) ligaments are strong fibromuscular condensations anchoring the cervix laterally to the pelvic wall.

slides.p: Master these three companion female reproductive topics together:
bullets: Uterine (Fallopian) Tube (~10 cm): Lies in upper free edge of broad ligament (mesosalpinx). Four parts from lateral to medial: 1. Infundibulum (funnel-shaped with fimbriae, ovarian fimbria attached to ovary; abdominal ostium opens into peritoneal cavity!), 2. Ampulla (widest, longest part — commonest site of fertilization!), 3. Isthmus (narrowest), and 4. Intramural (uterine) part.

Ovary*: Almond-shaped gonad in ovarian fossa on lateral pelvic wall (bounded by external iliac vessels in front, ureter & internal iliac vessels behind; obturator nerve lies in its floor!). Attached to broad ligament by mesovarium, uterus by ligament of ovary, and pelvic wall by suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament (carrying ovarian vessels). Lymph drains to para-aortic nodes!

Hysterosalpingography (HSG): Radiographic contrast study injecting radiopaque dye through the cervical canal to visualize the triangular uterine cavity and patency of both uterine tubes (spillage of dye into peritoneal cavity confirms tubal patency in infertility workup!).
slides.remember: Fertilization site = Ampulla of uterine tube! Obturator nerve runs in floor of ovarian fossa (referred pain to medial thigh)! HSG tests tubal patency!
slides.q: In which part of the uterine (Fallopian) tube does fertilization normally take place?
slides.why: The ampulla is the widest and longest segment of the uterine tube and is the usual site of fertilization.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Uterus (parts, anteversion/anteflexion, relations, uterine artery 'water under bridge', primary muscular & ligamentous supports*, prolapse); Uterine tube (4 parts, ampulla fertilization, ectopic pregnancy); Ovary* (ovarian fossa boundaries, ligaments, para-aortic lymphatics); HSG (procedure & tubal patency).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Ischiorectal Fossa*, Superficial Perineal Pouch & Perineal Body

slides.h: 1. Ischiorectal (Ischioanal) Fossa* — Wedge Shape, Boundaries & Pudendal Canal
slides.p: The ischiorectal fossa* is a wedge-shaped, fat-filled space on each side of the anal canal below the pelvic diaphragm:
bullets: Base (Inferior): Skin of anal region.
Apex (Superior): Line where obturator fascia meets inferior fascia of pelvic diaphragm (anal fascia).
Medial Wall: External anal sphincter (below) and levator ani covered by anal fascia (above).
Lateral Wall: Obturator internus covered by obturator fascia containing Alcock's (pudendal) canal, and ischial tuberosity.
Anterior & Posterior Recesses: Extends forward above urogenital diaphragm and backward deep to sacrotuberous ligament.

Contents & Applied Anatomy: Ischiorectal fat pad (allows anal canal expansion during defecation), inferior rectal nerve & vessels crossing transversely, and pudendal nerve + internal pudendal vessels inside Alcock's canal. Poorly vascularized fat is prone to ischiorectal abscess (can spread across midline behind anal canal to form a 'horseshoe abscess').
slides.remember: Lateral wall of Ischiorectal Fossa = Obturator internus + Alcock's (Pudendal) Canal! Fat pad lets anal canal expand during defecation!
slides.q: Which neurovascular structures run inside Alcock's (pudendal) canal in the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa?
opts: Sciatic nerve and superior gluteal vessels
Pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels
Ilioinguinal nerve and inferior epigastric vessels
slides.why: Alcock's canal is a fascial tunnel in the obturator fascia along the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa enclosing the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels.

slides.p: Master these two high-yield perineal Short Notes:
bullets: Superficial Perineal Pouch: Potential space between Colles' fascia (membranous layer of superficial perineal fascia) below and perineal membrane (inferior fascia of urogenital diaphragm) above. Closed posteriorly & laterally, OPEN anteriorly onto anterior abdominal wall (beneath Scarpa's fascia)! Contains root of penis/clitoris (crura + bulb), 3 superficial perineal muscles (bulbospongiosus, ischiocavernosus, superficial transverse perinei), and greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands in females. Rupture of bulbous urethra extravasates urine into superficial pouch → scrotum → penis → anterior abdominal wall!

Perineal Body (Central Tendon of Perineum): Fibromuscular node in the midline between the anal canal and vagina/bulb of penis (~1.25 cm in front of anal margin). Up to 8–10 perineal & pelvic floor muscles converge here (levator ani, external anal sphincter, bulbospongiosus, superficial & deep transverse perinei). Essential for supporting the posterior vaginal wall and uterus; protected during childbirth by episiotomy.
slides.remember: Superficial perineal pouch is OPEN anteriorly → urethral rupture extravasates urine up onto abdominal wall! Perineal body = Central anchor of pelvic floor (protected by episiotomy)!
slides.q: Why does urine extravasate upward onto the anterior abdominal wall following rupture of the spongy (bulbous) urethra into the superficial perineal pouch?
opts: Because the superficial perineal pouch is closed posteriorly and laterally, but open anteriorly beneath Scarpa's fascia
Because the perineal membrane is absent in males
Because Colles' fascia attaches to the umbilicus
Because the pelvic diaphragm is perforated
slides.why: Colles' fascia fuses posteriorly with the perineal membrane and laterally with the ischiopubic rami, leaving an open anterior communication with the space deep to Scarpa's fascia on the anterior abdominal wall.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Ischiorectal fossa* (shape, boundaries, Alcock's canal, contents, ischiorectal abscess & fistula-in-ano + Coronal diagram); Superficial perineal pouch (boundaries, contents in male/female, urethral rupture extravasation); Perineal body (location, converging muscles, obstetrical importance/episiotomy).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Testes & Male Urethra

slides.h: 1. Testes — Coverings, Structure, Blood Supply & Lymphatics
slides.p: The testis is the paired oval male gonad suspended in the scrotum by the spermatic cord (left testis hangs slightly lower than right):
bullets: Three Coverings (outer to inner): 1. Tunica vaginalis (double-layered serous sac — parietal & visceral layers — derived from processus vaginalis; covers all except posterior border), 2. Tunica albuginea (dense white fibrous capsule; thickens posteriorly as mediastinum testis sending septa to form 200–300 lobules), and 3. Tunica vasculosa.
Seminiferous Tubules → Pathway: 2–3 coiled seminiferous tubules per lobule → straight tubules → rete testis → 12–20 efferent ductules → head of epididymis → vas deferens.

Blood Supply & Lymphatics: Testicular artery (branch of abdominal aorta at L2); Pampiniform venous plexus (countercurrent heat exchange cooling blood by ~2–3°C; drains into right testicular vein → IVC, left testicular vein → left renal vein). Lymphatics drain to Para-aortic (lumbar) nodes at L2!
slides.remember: Testis coverings: Tunica Vaginalis, Albuginea, Vasculosa! Lymphatics drain to PARA-AORTIC nodes (NOT inguinal nodes)! Left varicocele is commoner because left testicular vein enters left renal vein at 90°!
slides.q: To which group of lymph nodes does lymph from the testes primarily drain?
slides.why: Because the testes develop on the posterior abdominal wall near L2 before descending, their blood vessels and lymphatics retain their connection to the para-aortic (lumbar) region.

slides.h: 2. Male Urethra — Three Parts & Applied Anatomy
slides.p: The male urethra (~18–20 cm long) extends from the internal urethral orifice of the urinary bladder to the external urethral meatus at the tip of the glans penis, divided into three parts:
bullets: 1. Prostatic Urethra (~3 cm — widest & most dilatable part!): Traverses prostate; posterior wall shows urethral crest, verumontanum (colliculus seminalis) with central prostatic utricle and two ejaculatory duct openings, and flanking prostatic sinuses (receiving prostatic ducts).

2. Membranous Urethra (~1.5–2 cm — shortest, narrowest & least dilatable part except external meatus!): Pierces urogenital diaphragm surrounded by voluntary external urethral sphincter (sphincter urethrae) and flanked by bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands.

3. Spongy / Penile Urethra (~15 cm — longest part): Traverses corpus spongiosum; shows two dilatations—intrabulbar fossa (proximal) and navicular fossa (in glans penis); receives bulbourethral & urethral (Littré's) glands.
Applied Anatomy: Narrowest points where urinary calculi impact or catheters injure the urethra = External urethral meatus and Membranous urethra (pelvic fracture tears membranous urethra!).
slides.remember: Widest part = Prostatic urethra. Shortest & most vulnerable in pelvic fracture = Membranous urethra. Longest = Spongy urethra!
slides.q: Which part of the male urethra is the widest and most dilatable?
slides.why: The prostatic urethra is the widest and most distensible portion of the male urethra, whereas the membranous urethra and external urethral orifice are the narrowest.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Testes (coverings, mediastinum testis & lobules, blood supply & pampiniform plexus, para-aortic lymphatics, hydrocele & varicocele); Male urethra (length, 3 parts with dimensions, features of prostatic urethra, narrowest/widest points, catheterization & rupture).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Internal Iliac Artery & Anatomical Basis of Contraception

slides.p: The internal iliac artery is the principal artery of the pelvis and perineum, arising at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery in front of the sacroiliac joint (lumbosacral disc level). At the upper margin of the greater sciatic foramen, it divides into Anterior and Posterior divisions:
bullets: Posterior Division (3 Parietal Branches — 'I-L-S'): 1. Iliolumbar artery, 2. Lateral sacral arteries, and 3. Superior gluteal artery (largest branch; exits above piriformis).

Anterior Division (Visceral + Parietal Branches): 1. Superior vesical artery (from patent proximal umbilical artery; distal part = medial umbilical ligament), 2. Inferior vesical artery (in males; replaced by vaginal artery in females), 3. Middle rectal artery, 4. Uterine artery (in females), 5. Obturator artery, 6. Internal pudendal artery (main artery of perineum!), and 7. Inferior gluteal artery (exits below piriformis).
slides.remember: Posterior division = I-L-S (Iliolumbar, Lateral sacral, Superior gluteal). Anterior division supplies pelvic viscera + Obturator, Internal pudendal & Inferior gluteal!
slides.q: Which three branches arise from the POSTERIOR division of the internal iliac artery?
opts: Uterine, vaginal, and middle rectal arteries
Iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and superior gluteal arteries
Obturator, internal pudendal, and inferior gluteal arteries
Superior vesical, inferior vesical, and umbilical arteries
slides.why: The posterior division of the internal iliac artery gives off three parietal branches: iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and superior gluteal arteries.

slides.p: Surgical sterilization procedures rely directly on pelvic and scrotal anatomy:
bullets: 1. Vasectomy (Male Sterilization): Bilateral ligation and resection of a small segment of the vas deferens (ductus deferens) through a small incision in the upper scrotum. The vas deferens is easily palpated in the posteromedial part of the spermatic cord as a firm, cord-like ('whipcord') structure; care is taken to preserve the testicular artery and pampiniform plexus.

2. Tubectomy / Tubal Ligation (Female Sterilization): Bilateral occlusion/resection of the isthmus (or ampullary-isthmic junction) of the uterine tubes via laparoscopy or minilaparotomy (Pomeroy's technique), preventing sperm from reaching the ovum in the ampulla.
3. Intrauterine Contraceptive Device (IUCD): Inserted through the cervical canal into the endometrial cavity of the body of the uterus (conforming to the anteverted/anteflexed axis).
slides.remember: Vasectomy = Ligate thick 'whipcord' Vas Deferens in upper scrotum! Tubectomy = Ligate Isthmus of uterine tube!
slides.q: Which part of the uterine tube is most commonly ligated and resected during female surgical sterilization (tubectomy)?
slides.why: The narrow, straight isthmus of the uterine tube is the standard anatomical site for tubal ligation/resection.

lessons.exam: LAQ / SN order: Internal iliac artery (origin at SI joint, anterior vs posterior division branches, clinical ligation in postpartum hemorrhage); Contraception anatomical basis (vasectomy — palpation & coverings of vas deferens; tubectomy — uterine tube anatomy; IUCD — uterine cavity & axis).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Suprarenal Gland*, Interior of Urinary Bladder & Anterior Relations of Right Kidney

slides.h: 1. Suprarenal (Adrenal) Gland* — Shape, Relations & Triple Arterial Supply
slides.p: The suprarenal glands* are paired yellowish retroperitoneal endocrine glands sitting on the upper poles of the kidneys within the renal fascia (separated from the kidney by a fascial septum so they do NOT descend in nephroptosis!):
bullets: Shape & Relations: Right suprarenal gland = Triangular / Pyramidal (behind IVC & right lobe of liver). Left suprarenal gland = Semilunar / Crescentic (behind stomach/lesser sac & pancreas).

Three Arteries Supplying Each Gland: 1. Superior suprarenal artery (from inferior phrenic artery), 2. Middle suprarenal artery (directly from abdominal aorta), and 3. Inferior suprarenal artery (from renal artery).
Single Venous Drainage (Asymmetric!): Right suprarenal vein → directly into IVC (very short!); Left suprarenal vein → into Left renal vein.
slides.remember: Right = Triangular, vein → IVC. Left = Semilunar, vein → Left renal vein! 3 arteries (Inferior phrenic, Aorta, Renal) → 1 vein!
slides.q: What is the characteristic shape of the RIGHT suprarenal gland compared to the left?
slides.why: The right suprarenal gland is pyramidal/triangular in shape, whereas the left suprarenal gland is semilunar (crescentic).

slides.h: 2. Interior of Urinary Bladder & Anterior Relations of Right Kidney
slides.p: Complete the final two Abdomen & Pelvis checklist items:
bullets: Interior of Urinary Bladder: Transitional epithelium (urothelium) thrown into irregular folds (rugae) when empty, EXCEPT over the smooth triangular trigone on the base. Three angles of Trigone: Superolateral angles = Right & left ureteric orifices (connected by interureteric ridge / Mercier's bar); Inferior angle = Internal urethral orifice (just behind it lies a slight elevation produced by median lobe of prostate = uvula vesicae).

Anterior Relations of Right Kidney (6 structures — diagram!): 1. Right suprarenal gland (upper pole), 2. Visceral surface of right lobe of liver (largest area, peritoneal), 3. Second part of duodenum (medially, non-peritoneal), 4. Right colic (hepatic) flexure (inferolaterally, non-peritoneal), and 5. Coils of small intestine (inferomedially, peritoneal).
slides.remember: Trigone = 2 Ureteric orifices + Internal urethral orifice + Interureteric ridge + Uvula vesicae! Right kidney front = Suprarenal, Liver, 2nd Duodenum, Right colic flexure, Small intestine!
slides.q: Which ridge connects the two ureteric orifices at the upper border of the trigone inside the urinary bladder?
slides.why: The interureteric ridge is a transverse mucosal fold formed by underlying muscle fibres connecting the right and left ureteric openings across the base of the trigone.

lessons.exam: Write under: Suprarenal gland* (shape, relations, 3 arteries, asymmetric venous drainage, cortex vs medulla development); Interior of urinary bladder (rugae vs trigone, 3 orifices, interureteric ridge, uvula vesicae); Anterior relations of right kidney (labelled diagram showing peritoneal vs non-peritoneal areas).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Synovial Joint – Classification, Structure & Examples

slides.h: 1. Characteristic Features of a Synovial Joint
slides.p: Synovial joints (diarthroses) are the most mobile joints in the body and are characterized by four essential features:
bullets: Articular Cartilage: Hyaline cartilage covers articular surfaces (except fibrocartilage in TMJ, sternoclavicular, and acromioclavicular joints); avascular, aneural, nourished by synovial fluid.
Joint Cavity & Synovial Fluid: Potential space containing viscous, hyaluronic-acid-rich synovial fluid for lubrication and nutrition.
Fibrous Capsule & Synovial Membrane: Outer tough fibrous capsule reinforced by ligaments; inner vascular synovial membrane lines all non-articular surfaces.
slides.remember: 4 Hallmarks of Synovial Joint: Hyaline cartilage + Joint cavity + Fibrous capsule + Synovial membrane!
slides.q: Which of the following synovial joints has articular surfaces covered by fibrocartilage instead of hyaline cartilage?
slides.why: Membrane-ossifying bones like the clavicle and mandible (TMJ, sternoclavicular, acromioclavicular joints) have fibrocartilage covering their articular surfaces.

slides.h: 2. Classification of Synovial Joints with Examples
slides.p: Synovial joints are classified by axis of movement and shape of articular surfaces:
bullets: Plane (Gliding): Intercarpal, intertarsal, acromioclavicular, facet joints.
Uniaxial: Hinge (Ginglymus) — elbow, ankle, interphalangeal; Pivot (Trochoid) — median atlantoaxial, superior & inferior radioulnar.
Biaxial: Condylar — knee, TMJ; Ellipsoid — wrist (radiocarpal), MCP joints.
Multiaxial: Saddle (Sellar) — 1st carpometacarpal (thumb), sternoclavicular; Ball & Socket (Spheroidal) — shoulder, hip, incudostapedial.
slides.remember: Saddle = 1st CMC (thumb)! Pivot = Median atlantoaxial & Radioulnar! Ball & Socket = Shoulder, Hip, Incudostapedial!
slides.q: The first carpometacarpal joint (at the base of the thumb) is a classic example of which type of synovial joint?
slides.why: The 1st carpometacarpal joint between the trapezium and 1st metacarpal is a biaxial saddle joint enabling opposition of the thumb.

lessons.exam: General Anatomy IMP order: Definition → 4 characteristic features → Classification table (Plane, Hinge, Pivot, Condylar, Ellipsoid, Saddle, Ball & Socket) with 2 examples each → Labelled diagram of a typical synovial joint + Hilton's law.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Classification of Fibrous Joint

slides.p: In fibrous joints, bones are united by dense fibrous connective tissue, permitting little or no movement:
bullets: 1. Sutures (Skull only): Bound by sutural ligament; types include Plane (internasal), Serrate (sagittal), Denticulate (lambdoid), Squamous (temporoparietal), and Schindylesis (rostrum of sphenoid in vomer).
2. Syndesmosis: Bones connected by an interosseous ligament/membrane — inferior tibiofibular joint, middle radioulnar & tibiofibular interosseous membranes.
3. Gomphosis (Peg-and-Socket): Root of tooth anchored in alveolar socket by periodontal ligament.
slides.remember: Fibrous Joints = Su-Syn-Go (Sutures, Syndesmosis, Gomphosis)! Inferior tibiofibular = Fibrous syndesmosis!
slides.q: Which joint is a fibrous syndesmosis?
slides.why: The inferior tibiofibular joint is united by the interosseous tibiofibular ligament (syndesmosis), whereas the superior tibiofibular joint is a plane synovial joint.

lessons.exam: General Anatomy IMP order: Definition → 3 types (Sutures with 5 subtypes, Syndesmosis, Gomphosis) → Examples & clinical note (craniosynostosis, diastasis of inferior tibiofibular joint).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Cartilaginous Joint & Secondary Cartilaginous Joint

slides.p: Cartilaginous joints unite bones via hyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage and lack a joint cavity:
bullets: Primary Cartilaginous (Synchondrosis / Hyaline): Temporary joints united by hyaline cartilage; immovable; ossify with age (synostosis). Examples: epiphyseal growth plate, 1st sternocostal joint, spheno-occipital synchondrosis.

Secondary Cartilaginous (Symphysis / Fibrocartilage): Permanent midline joints; articular ends covered by thin hyaline cartilage united by a thick pad of fibrocartilage; permit slight movement. Examples: pubic symphysis, intervertebral discs, manubriosternal joint, symphysis menti.
slides.remember: Primary = Hyaline + Temporary (Growth plate)! Secondary = Fibrocartilage + Midline + Permanent (Symphysis)!
slides.q: Which of the following is a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis)?
slides.why: The manubriosternal joint (angle of Louis), pubic symphysis, and intervertebral discs are midline secondary cartilaginous joints united by fibrocartilage.

lessons.exam: General Anatomy IMP order: Definition → Primary cartilaginous (synchondrosis) vs Secondary cartilaginous (symphysis) comparison table → Examples → Diagram of intervertebral disc / symphysis.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Pivot Joint (Trochoid Joint)

slides.h: 1. Structure, Axis & Examples of Pivot Joints
slides.p: A pivot (trochoid) joint is a uniaxial synovial joint allowing rotation around a single longitudinal axis:
bullets: Structure: A central bony pivot rotates within an osteoligamentous ring (or a ring rotates around a central peg).

Examples: 1. Median atlantoaxial joint (dens of axis rotates in ring formed by anterior arch of atlas and transverse ligament — 'No' movement), 2. Superior radioulnar joint (head of radius rotates in annular ligament), 3. Inferior radioulnar joint (ulnar notch of radius rotates around head of ulna).
slides.remember: 3 Pivot Joints in the body: Median atlantoaxial + Superior radioulnar + Inferior radioulnar!
slides.q: Which movement occurs primarily at the median atlantoaxial pivot joint?
slides.why: Rotation of the atlas (with skull) around the odontoid process (dens) of the axis produces the 'No' movement at the median atlantoaxial pivot joint.

lessons.exam: General Anatomy IMP order: Definition & axis → Osteoligamentous ring structure → All 3 examples (median atlantoaxial, superior & inferior radioulnar) → Labelled diagram + clinical note (pulled elbow).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Sesamoid Bone

slides.h: 1. Peculiarities, Functions & Examples of Sesamoid Bones
slides.p: Sesamoid bones are seed-like bony nodules embedded within certain tendons or joint capsules where they rub over bony surfaces:
bullets: Peculiarities (Exam Favorites): No periosteum, no Haversian systems, ossify after birth (cartilaginous nodules in fetal life), and have one articular surface covered by hyaline cartilage.
Functions: Reduce friction, alter angle of pull of tendon (increasing mechanical advantage), protect tendon from wear, and maintain local circulation.

Examples: Patella (largest, in quadriceps femoris tendon), pisiform (in flexor carpi ulnaris tendon), fabella (in lateral head of gastrocnemius), 2 sesamoids under 1st metatarsal head (flexor hallucis brevis).
slides.remember: Sesamoid = NO periosteum + NO Haversian canals + Ossifies AFTER birth! Patella = Largest!
slides.q: Which histological/structural feature is characteristically ABSENT in a sesamoid bone?
slides.why: Sesamoid bones lack both a periosteum and Haversian systems and ossify postnatally within tendons.

lessons.exam: General Anatomy IMP order: Definition → 4 peculiarities (no periosteum, no Haversian systems, postnatal ossification) → 4 functions → Examples (patella, pisiform, fabella, 1st MTP sesamoids).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Epiphysis – Types & Clinical Significance

slides.p: An epiphysis is the end or secondary ossification center of a long bone separated from the diaphysis (shaft) during growth by the epiphyseal cartilage plate:
bullets: 1. Pressure Epiphysis: Articular, weight-bearing/force-transmitting ends — e.g., head of femur, condyles of femur & tibia, head of humerus.
2. Traction Epiphysis: Non-articular sites of major muscle/tendon pull (ossify later than pressure epiphyses) — e.g., greater & lesser trochanters of femur, tubercles of humerus, mastoid process.
3. Atavistic Epiphysis: Phylogenetically independent bone fused to host bone — e.g., coracoid process of scapula, os trigonum.
4. Aberrant Epiphysis: Not always present — e.g., epiphysis at base of 2nd metacarpal or head of 1st metacarpal.
slides.remember: 4 Epiphyses: Pressure (articular) + Traction (muscle pull) + Atavistic (coracoid) + Aberrant (metacarpal)!
slides.q: The coracoid process of the scapula is a classic example of which type of epiphysis?
