slides.why: The coracoid process was an independent bone in lower vertebrates that fused onto the human scapula, making it an atavistic epiphysis.

lessons.exam: General Anatomy IMP order: Definition & parts of young long bone → 4 types of epiphyses with examples → Growing end law & clinical note (slipped capital femoral epiphysis, bone age estimation).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Blood Supply of Long Bone

slides.h: 1. Four Arterial Sources & Growing End Direction
slides.p: A typical long bone receives blood from four distinct arterial sets that anastomose richly:
bullets: 1. Nutrient Artery: Enters obliquely through the nutrient foramen, divides in medullary cavity into ascending and descending branches → supplies bone marrow and inner 2/3 of cortex. Directed away from the growing end ('To the elbow I go, from the knee I flee').
2. Periosteal Arteries: Ramify beneath periosteum, enter Volkmann's canals → supply outer 1/3 of compact cortex.
3. Metaphyseal Arteries: Arise from neighbouring systemic vessels; form end-arterial hairpin loops in children (common site of acute hematogenous osteomyelitis!).
4. Epiphyseal Arteries: Enter via vascular foramina around capsule attachment (scanty blood supply to femoral head predisposes to avascular necrosis).
slides.remember: Nutrient = Inner 2/3 cortex + Marrow! Periosteal = Outer 1/3 cortex! Metaphyseal hairpin loops = Osteomyelitis site!
slides.q: Which part of a long bone's compact cortex is supplied primarily by the nutrient artery?
slides.why: The nutrient artery supplies the medullary marrow and inner two-thirds of the compact cortex, while periosteal arteries supply the outer one-third.

lessons.exam: General Anatomy IMP order: 4 arterial sources (Nutrient, Periosteal, Metaphyseal, Epiphyseal) → Direction of nutrient canal → Labelled diagram → Applied anatomy (osteomyelitis in metaphysis, avascular necrosis of femoral head/scaphoid).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Stratified Squamous Epithelium (Histology)

slides.p: Stratified squamous epithelium is a multilayered protective epithelium subjected to mechanical friction and wear-and-tear:
bullets: Layering: Basal cuboidal/columnar germinative layer (stratum basale) resting on basement membrane → intermediate polygonal prickle cells (desmosomes) → superficial flattened squamous cells.
1. Non-Keratinized Type: Superficial cells remain nucleated and moist. Sites: esophagus, oral cavity, tongue, vagina, cornea, vocal cords.
2. Keratinized Type: Superficial cells lose nuclei and fill with tough waterproof keratin (stratum corneum). Site: epidermis of skin (thick skin has stratum lucidum; thin skin lacks it).
slides.remember: Wet friction = Non-keratinized (Esophagus, Vagina, Cornea)! Dry friction = Keratinized (Skin)!
slides.q: Which of the following organs is lined by stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium?
slides.why: The esophagus is subjected to food bolus friction and is lined by moist, nucleated stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium.

lessons.exam: Histology IMP order: Identifying H&E features (basal columnar, middle polyhedral, superficial flat cells) → Keratinized vs Non-keratinized comparison → Sites & functions → Neat H&E labelled diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Muscular Artery (Medium-Sized Artery – Histology)

slides.h: 1. Three Tunics & Prominent Internal Elastic Lamina
slides.p: Muscular (distributing) arteries (e.g., radial, femoral, coronary arteries) regulate regional blood flow via smooth muscle contraction:
bullets: Tunica Intima: Endothelium + thin subendothelial connective tissue + prominent, scalloped (wavy) internal elastic lamina (IEL) (hallmark identification feature on H&E slide!).
Tunica Media: Thickest coat, composed predominantly of circularly arranged smooth muscle fibers (10–40 layers) with few elastic fibers.
Tunica Adventitia: Collagen and elastic fibers with external elastic lamina (EEL) at media-adventitia junction and vasa vasorum.
slides.remember: Muscular Artery = Wavy bright pink Internal Elastic Lamina + Thick smooth muscle Tunica Media!
slides.q: What is the most characteristic light-microscopic feature distinguishing a muscular artery from a vein?
opts: Prominent scalloped internal elastic lamina and thick smooth muscle tunica media
slides.why: A wavy, refractile internal elastic lamina and a thick circular smooth muscle tunica media distinguish muscular arteries from veins and elastic arteries.

lessons.exam: Histology IMP order: 3 coats (Intima with wavy IEL, thick smooth muscle Media, Adventitia with EEL) → Comparison with Elastic Artery & Medium Vein → Labelled H&E diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Compact Bone (Ground Section – Histology)

slides.p: In a transverse ground section, compact bone is organized into cylindrical structural units called osteons (Haversian systems):
bullets: Haversian Canal: Central longitudinal neurovascular canal surrounded by 4–20 concentric rings of calcified matrix (concentric lamellae).
Lacunae & Canaliculi: Spider-shaped lacunae housing osteocytes lie between lamellae, interconnected by radiating canaliculi (gap junctions for nutrition).

Other Lamellae & Canals: Interstitial lamellae (remnants between osteons), outer & inner circumferential lamellae, and transverse/oblique Volkmann's canals connecting Haversian canals with periosteal/endosteal vessels.
slides.remember: Haversian = Longitudinal canal! Volkmann = Transverse/oblique perforating canal! Osteocytes live in Lacunae!
slides.q: Which transverse canals connect adjacent Haversian canals with periosteal and endosteal blood vessels?
slides.why: Volkmann's (perforating) canals run transversely or obliquely without concentric lamellae to link Haversian canals to the periosteum and marrow cavity.

lessons.exam: Histology IMP order: Osteon (Haversian canal, concentric lamellae, lacunae with osteocytes, canaliculi) → Interstitial & circumferential lamellae → Volkmann's canals → Labelled transverse ground section diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Adrenal (Suprarenal) Gland – Histology

slides.p: Covered by a fibrous capsule, the adrenal gland has a mesoderm-derived outer cortex (90%) and a neural-crest-derived inner medulla (10%):
bullets: 1. Zona Glomerulosa (Outer 15%): Arched cords/clusters of columnar cells → secretes mineralocorticoids (Aldosterone) (regulated by RAAS).
2. Zona Fasciculata (Middle 75%): Long straight parallel cords (2 cells thick) separated by sinusoids; pale foamy lipid-rich cells (spongiocytes) → secretes glucocorticoids (Cortisol).
3. Zona Reticularis (Inner 10%): Anastomosing cords of smaller acidophilic cells with lipofuscin → secretes adrenal androgens (DHEA).
4. Adrenal Medulla: Basophilic polyhedral chromaffin cells (modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons) + large medullary veins → secretes adrenaline & noradrenaline.
slides.remember: GFR = Glomerulosa (Salt/Aldosterone), Fasciculata (Sugar/Cortisol - Spongiocytes), Reticularis (Sex/Androgens)!
slides.q: Which cortical zone of the adrenal gland consists of parallel cords of pale, lipid-laden 'spongiocytes'?
slides.why: The wide middle zona fasciculata features straight cords of foamy, lipid-droplet-filled spongiocytes that synthesize cortisol.

lessons.exam: Histology IMP order: Capsule → Cortex (Zona glomerulosa, fasciculata with spongiocytes, reticularis + hormones) → Medulla (chromaffin cells + catecholamines) → Labelled H&E diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Spleen – Histology

slides.h: 1. Capsule, Trabeculae, White Pulp & Red Pulp
slides.p: The spleen is the largest secondary lymphoid organ and lacks a cortex-medulla division or afferent lymphatics:
bullets: Fibromuscular Capsule & Trabeculae: Thick capsule sends trabeculae into parenchyma carrying trabecular vessels.

White Pulp (20%): Basophilic lymphoid nodules (Malpighian corpuscles) pierced by an eccentric central arteriole surrounded by a periarteriolar lymphatic sheath (PALS — T-cells) and B-cell germinal center.
Red Pulp (80%): Vascular splenic cords of Billroth (macrophages, RBCs, plasma cells) alternating with wide splenic sinusoids lined by stave cells.
slides.remember: Spleen = NO cortex/medulla + Eccentric central arteriole in White Pulp + Cords of Billroth & Sinusoids in Red Pulp!
slides.q: What is the hallmark identifying feature of a splenic lymphoid nodule (Malpighian corpuscle) on H&E microscopy?
slides.why: Each splenic white pulp follicle contains an eccentrically located central arteriole surrounded by the T-cell-rich PALS.

lessons.exam: Histology IMP order: Fibromuscular capsule & trabeculae → White pulp (Malpighian corpuscle, PALS, eccentric central arteriole) → Red pulp (cords of Billroth + sinusoids) → Comparison with Lymph Node + Labelled diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Lymph Node – Histology

slides.p: A lymph node is a bean-shaped encapsulated lymphoid organ with both afferent and efferent lymphatics:
bullets: Capsule & Subcapsular Sinus: Connective tissue capsule pierced by afferent lymphatics draining into the subcapsular (marginal) sinus.
Outer Cortex (B-cell zone): Packed with primary and secondary lymphoid follicles with pale germinal centers and dark mantles.
Paracortex (Inner Cortex — T-cell zone): Diffuse lymphoid tissue with high endothelial venules (HEVs) for lymphocyte homing.
Medulla: Medullary cords (B-cells, plasma cells, macrophages) alternating with medullary sinuses draining to efferent lymphatics at the hilum.
slides.remember: Lymph Node = Subcapsular sinus + Cortical B-cell follicles + Paracortical T-cells + Medullary cords & sinuses!
slides.q: Which zone of a lymph node is the thymus-dependent T-lymphocyte zone containing high endothelial venules?
slides.why: The paracortex is the T-cell-dependent region of a lymph node and contains specialized cuboidal-lined high endothelial venules (HEVs).

lessons.exam: Histology IMP order: Capsule & subcapsular sinus → Outer cortex (follicles/germinal centers) → Paracortex (T-zone, HEVs) → Medulla (cords & sinuses) → Labelled diagram.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Testes**, Ovary & Kidney – Histology High-Yield Slides

slides.p: Exam slides for gonads focus on gametogenic and endocrine cells:
bullets: Testes** (H&E): Thick tunica albuginea → coiled seminiferous tubules lined by stratified germinal epithelium (spermatogonia → primary & secondary spermatocytes → spermatids → spermatozoa) + tall supporting Sertoli cells (blood-testis barrier, ABP, inhibin). Interstitial stroma contains Leydig cells (secrete testosterone).

Ovary (H&E): Simple cuboidal germinal epithelium → dense tunica albuginea → outer cortex housing ovarian follicles at all stages (primordial, primary, secondary, Graafian follicle with cumulus oophorus & antrum, corpus luteum) + inner vascular medulla.
slides.remember: Testes: Sertoli = Support/Inhibin, Leydig = Testosterone! Ovary: Cortex = Follicles, Medulla = Vessels!
slides.q: Which cells located in the interstitial connective tissue between seminiferous tubules secrete testosterone?
slides.why: Eosinophilic polyhedral interstitial cells of Leydig secrete testosterone under LH stimulation.

slides.p: The kidney slide is instantly recognized by renal corpuscles in the cortex and parallel tubules in the medulla:
bullets: Renal Cortex: Renal (Malpighian) corpuscles = Glomerulus + Bowman's capsule (visceral podocytes, urinary space, parietal squamous layer); PCT (numerous, brush border, narrow star-shaped lumen, strongly eosinophilic) vs DCT (fewer, no brush border, wide clear lumen, pale cuboidal cells) + macula densa.
Renal Medulla: No glomeruli; contains Loops of Henle (thin squamous segments) and Collecting ducts (distinct cell borders, pale cuboidal/columnar cells).
slides.remember: PCT = Pink, fuzzy brush border, narrow lumen! DCT = Pale, clean lumen, wider! Medulla = NO glomeruli!
slides.q: How do proximal convoluted tubules (PCT) differ from distal convoluted tubules (DCT) on an H&E kidney section?
opts: PCT has no brush border and a wide lumen
PCT has a prominent microvillous brush border, strongly eosinophilic cytoplasm, and narrow lumen
PCT is found only in the renal medulla
slides.why: PCT cells possess an apical brush border, abundant mitochondria (intense eosinophilia), and a small stellate lumen compared to DCT.

lessons.exam: Histology IMP order: Draw neat H&E diagrams for Testes (seminiferous tubule, Sertoli, Leydig), Ovary (cortex with primordial to Graafian follicles, medulla), and Kidney (renal corpuscle, PCT vs DCT, medullary collecting ducts).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Phases of Fertilisation

slides.h: 1. Site, Capacitation, Acrosome Reaction & Three Phases
slides.p: Fertilisation normally occurs in the ampulla of the uterine (fallopian) tube within 12–24 hours of ovulation after sperm undergo capacitation (removal of glycoprotein coat in female tract) and the acrosome reaction (release of hyaluronidase & acrosin):
bullets: Phase 1 — Penetration of Corona Radiata: Capacitated sperm disperse follicular cells via hyaluronidase and flagellar motility.

Phase 2 — Penetration of Zona Pellucida: Sperm binds ZP3 glycoprotein, releases acrosin to penetrate zona; contact triggers cortical & zona reactions (lysosomal enzymes make zona impermeable → prevents polyspermy).

Phase 3 — Fusion of Oocyte & Sperm Cell Membranes: Secondary oocyte completes Meiosis II (extruding 2nd polar body), male & female pronuclei replicate DNA and fuse (syngamy) to restore diploid zygote (46 chromosomes).
slides.remember: Site = Ampulla! 3 Phases: Corona radiata → Zona pellucida (Zona reaction blocks polyspermy) → Membrane fusion & Meiosis II completion!
slides.q: Which mechanism prevents polyspermy immediately after a single spermatozoon penetrates the zona pellucida?
slides.why: Release of cortical granules alters zona pellucida glycoproteins (zona reaction), rendering it impermeable to additional spermatozoa.

lessons.exam: Embryology IMP order: Definition & site (ampulla) → Capacitation & acrosome reaction → 3 phases of fertilisation → Cortical/zona reaction → 4 results of fertilisation (diploid restoration, sex determination, cleavage initiation).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Primitive Streak & Notochord

slides.p: At the start of the 3rd week, epiblast cells proliferate along the caudal midline of the bilaminar disc to form the primitive streak, ending cranially at the primitive node (Hensen's node) with its primitive pit:
bullets: Gastrulation: Epiblast cells invaginate through the primitive groove to form all three germ layers — intraembryonic endoderm (displaces hypoblast), mesoderm, and remaining ectoderm.
Clinical Correlation: Remnants of the primitive streak give rise to sacrococcygeal teratoma (most common germ-cell tumor in newborns, containing derivatives of all 3 germ layers).
slides.remember: Primitive Streak = Week 3 Gastrulation (forms all 3 germ layers)! Remnant = Sacrococcygeal teratoma!
slides.q: Persistence of remnants of the primitive streak most commonly leads to which congenital tumor?
slides.why: Pluripotent remnants of the primitive streak in the sacrococcygeal region develop into a sacrococcygeal teratoma.

slides.p: Cells migrating cranially from the primitive pit form the hollow notochordal process, which fuses transiently with endoderm (notochordal plate + transient neurenteric canal) and folds into the solid midline notochord (from primitive node to prochordal plate):
bullets: Functions: Defines primitive cranial-caudal axis, acts as primary inductor for overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate (neurulation), and guides vertebral body development.

Adult Remnants & Tumor: Degenerates in vertebral bodies but persists as the nucleus pulposus of intervertebral discs and apical ligament of the dens. Remnants can form a malignant midline tumor called chordoma (at clivus/base of skull or sacrum).
slides.remember: Notochord adult remnants = Nucleus pulposus + Apical ligament of dens! Tumor = Chordoma!
slides.q: Which adult anatomical structure is a direct remnant of the embryonic notochord?
slides.why: The notochord persists in adults as the gelatinous nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs and the apical ligament of the dens.

lessons.exam: Embryology IMP order: Primitive streak formation & gastrulation → Notochord formation (notochordal process, neurenteric canal, solid notochord) → Functions → Adult remnants (nucleus pulposus) & clinical notes (sacrococcygeal teratoma, chordoma).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Neural Tube Defects (Neurulation & Spina Bifida)

slides.h: 1. Neuropore Closure & Spectrum of Neural Tube Defects
slides.p: During neurulation (3rd–4th week), neural folds fuse in the midline; the anterior (cranial) neuropore closes on Day 25 and the posterior (caudal) neuropore closes on Day 27/28:
bullets: Anencephaly: Failure of anterior neuropore closure → absence of cranial vault (acrania) and cerebral hemispheres; causes polyhydramnios and markedly elevated maternal serum/amniotic alpha-fetoprotein (AFP).

Spina Bifida Spectrum (Caudal closure failure): Spina bifida occulta (vertebral arch defect only, tuft of hair, normal AFP); Meningocele (meninges + CSF herniate); Meningomyelocele (meninges + spinal cord/nerve roots herniate → neurological deficits); Rachischisis (completely open neural plate).
Prevention: Periconceptional folic acid (400 µg/day) supplementation starting before conception reduces NTD risk by >70%.
slides.remember: Anterior neuropore = Day 25 (Anencephaly)! Posterior neuropore = Day 27–28 (Spina bifida)! High AFP + Folic acid prevents!
slides.q: Failure of closure of the anterior (cranial) neuropore around Day 25 results in which condition?
slides.why: Failure of anterior neuropore closure prevents forebrain and cranial vault development, resulting in anencephaly.

lessons.exam: Embryology IMP order: Neuropore closure dates (Day 25 & Day 27/28) → Cranial NTD (Anencephaly) → Caudal NTDs (Spina bifida occulta, meningocele, meningomyelocele, rachischisis) → Screening (elevated AFP) & prevention (folic acid).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Fate and Derivatives of Yolk Sac & Vitello-Intestinal Duct

slides.p: The yolk sac evolves through primary (Day 9) and secondary/definitive (Day 13) stages; during embryonic folding, its dorsal roof is incorporated into the embryo while its ventral part remains connected via the vitello-intestinal (omphalomesenteric) duct:
bullets: 1. Primitive Gut Tube: Roof of yolk sac forms endodermal lining of foregut, midgut, and hindgut (plus allantois).
2. Primordial Germ Cells (PGCs): Appear in caudal wall of yolk sac (Week 3) and migrate along dorsal mesentery to developing gonads.
3. Earliest Hematopoiesis & Angiogenesis: Blood islands in yolk sac mesoderm produce primitive blood cells and vitelline vessels (Weeks 3–6) before liver takes over.
slides.remember: Yolk Sac 3 Big Jobs: Primitive gut endoderm + Primordial germ cells + First blood islands!
slides.q: Where do primordial germ cells first arise during human embryonic development?
slides.why: Primordial germ cells originate in the endodermal wall of the yolk sac near the allantois and migrate to the genital ridges.

slides.p: The vitello-intestinal (omphalomesenteric) duct connects the midgut loop to the yolk sac and normally obliterates completely by the end of the 6th–7th week. Partial or complete persistence causes classic anomalies:
bullets: Meckel's Diverticulum (2% population): Persistence of proximal (ileal) end; 'Rule of 2s' — 2 inches long, 2 feet proximal to ileocecal valve, 2% prevalence, 2 types of ectopic mucosa (gastric & pancreatic).
Vitelline Fistula (Umbilical Fecal Fistula): Complete patency of entire duct → fecal/meconium discharge at umbilicus.
Vitelline Cyst (Enterocystoma) & Fibrous Cord: Middle segment remains patent (cyst) or fibroses (band causing intestinal obstruction).
slides.remember: Proximal patent = Meckel's diverticulum! Whole duct patent = Fecal fistula at umbilicus! Middle patent = Vitelline cyst!
slides.q: Complete failure of obliteration of the entire vitello-intestinal duct results in:
slides.why: A completely patent vitello-intestinal duct creates a direct communication between the ileum and the umbilicus, causing fecal discharge.

lessons.exam: Embryology IMP order: Primary & secondary yolk sac → 3 derivatives (gut tube, PGCs, hematopoiesis) → Vitello-intestinal duct obliteration → 4 anomalies (Meckel's diverticulum, vitelline fistula, cyst, fibrous band) + neat diagrams.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Rotation of Gut & Development of Pancreas*

slides.h: 1. Physiological Herniation & 270° Counter-Clockwise Rotation of Midgut
slides.p: Rapid elongation of the midgut loop around the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) axis causes temporary herniation into the umbilical cord (Week 6) and return (Week 10) with a total 270° counter-clockwise rotation (viewed from front):
bullets: Stage 1 (Week 6 — 90° CCW): Cranial (prearterial) limb moves to right; caudal (postarterial) limb moves to left inside umbilical cord.
Stage 2 (Week 10 — Additional 180° CCW): Prearterial limb (jejunum/ileum) returns first behind SMA to left; postarterial limb (cecum/colon) returns later anterior to SMA to upper right.

Stage 3 (Fixation): Cecum descends to right iliac fossa; ascending & descending colon become retroperitoneal. Anomalies: Omphalocele (failure of return), Non-rotation / Malrotation (volvulus, Ladd's bands), Subhepatic cecum.
slides.remember: Midgut rotates 270° Counter-Clockwise around SMA (90° out + 180° back)! Failure of return = Omphalocele!
slides.q: In which direction and through what total angle does the midgut loop rotate around the superior mesenteric artery?
slides.why: The midgut undergoes a 270° counter-clockwise rotation (90° during herniation + 180° during return) around the SMA axis.

slides.p: The pancreas develops from two endodermal buds arising from the junction of foregut and midgut (2nd part of duodenum):
bullets: Dorsal Pancreatic Bud: Larger; forms upper head, neck, body, and tail.

Ventral Pancreatic Bud: Arises with hepatic diverticulum; rotates posteriorly around duodenum (with duodenal rotation) to fuse below/behind dorsal bud, forming uncinate process and lower part of head.

Ducts & Anomalies: Main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung) = distal dorsal duct + entire ventral duct; Accessory duct (of Santorini) = proximal dorsal duct. Bifid ventral bud encircling 2nd part of duodenum causes annular pancreas (duodenal obstruction).
slides.remember: Ventral bud = Uncinate process + Lower head! Bifid ventral bud = Annular pancreas!
slides.q: Which parts of the adult pancreas develop from the ventral pancreatic bud?
opts: Uncinate process and lower part of the head
slides.why: After rotating behind the duodenum, the ventral pancreatic bud forms the uncinate process and inferior part of the head of the pancreas.

lessons.exam: Embryology IMP order: Midgut 270° CCW rotation (3 stages) + anomalies (omphalocele, malrotation, subhepatic cecum) → Pancreas dorsal & ventral buds + duct formation + annular pancreas.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Mesonephric Duct, Urinary Bladder & Developmental Anomalies of Kidney

slides.h: 1. Derivatives of Mesonephric (Wolffian) Duct & Urinary Bladder
slides.p: The mesonephric (Wolffian) duct drains the mesonephros into the urogenital sinus and plays vital roles in both sexes:
bullets: Common Derivatives (Both Sexes): Gives off the ureteric bud (forms ureter, renal pelvis, calyces, collecting tubules) and is absorbed into posterior bladder wall to form the trigone of urinary bladder.
Male Derivatives (Stimulated by Testosterone): Appendix of epididymis, duct of epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle, and ejaculatory duct (regresses in females except Gartner's duct cyst).

Urinary Bladder Development: Develops mainly from cranial vesical part of endodermal urogenital sinus (urorectal septum divides cloaca), except trigone (mesodermal, from absorbed mesonephric ducts); apex connects to umbilicus via urachus (median umbilical ligament).
slides.remember: Mesonephric duct = SEED (Seminal vesicle, Epididymis, Ejaculatory duct, Ductus deferens) + Ureteric bud + Bladder trigone!
slides.q: Which part of the urinary bladder is mesodermal in origin and derived from the absorbed caudal ends of the mesonephric ducts?
slides.why: While most bladder epithelium comes from the endodermal urogenital sinus, the trigone forms from incorporation of the mesodermal mesonephric ducts.

slides.p: The definitive kidney (metanephros) develops via reciprocal induction between the ureteric bud (collecting system) and metanephric blastema (nephrons) and ascends from pelvis to lumbar region:
bullets: Horseshoe Kidney: Lower poles fuse across midline; ascent is arrested at root of inferior mesenteric artery (IMA) (at L3).
Pelvic Kidney & Crossed Renal Ectopia: Failure of ascent from sacral/pelvic position.
Renal Agenesis (Bilateral → Potter sequence): Failure of ureteric bud to induce metanephric blastema → oligohydramnios.
Polycystic Kidney & Bifid Ureter: Abnormal branching/canalization of ureteric bud and collecting tubules.
slides.remember: Horseshoe kidney gets hooked under the Inferior Mesenteric Artery (IMA) during ascent!
slides.q: Which blood vessel arrests the upward ascent of a horseshoe kidney?
slides.why: As the fused lower poles of a horseshoe kidney ascend from the pelvis, the isthmus catches beneath the origin of the inferior mesenteric artery.

lessons.exam: Embryology IMP order: Mesonephric duct derivatives (male genital tract + ureteric bud + bladder trigone) → Urinary bladder (urogenital sinus + trigone + urachus) → Kidney anomalies (horseshoe kidney arrested by IMA, pelvic kidney, renal agenesis, polycystic kidney).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Descent of Testes*

slides.h: 1. Timeline, Factors & Anomalies of Testicular Descent
slides.p: The testes develop retroperitoneally on the posterior abdominal wall (T10–T12) and descend through the inguinal canal into the scrotum (for 2–3°C cooler temperature needed for spermatogenesis):
bullets: Timeline: Reach deep inguinal ring by 7th month → traverse inguinal canal during 7th–8th month → reach bottom of scrotum by birth (9th month).

Factors Guiding Descent: Shortening/contraction of gubernaculum testis, differential growth of body wall, intra-abdominal pressure, and hormones (INSL3 for transabdominal phase; testosterone/androgens for inguinoscrotal phase).

Anomalies: Cryptorchidism (Undescended testis) (risk of infertility and testicular malignancy), Ectopic testis (superficial inguinal pouch, perineal, femoral), Congenital inguinal hernia & hydrocele (persistent processus vaginalis).
slides.remember: Deep ring = 7th month! Scrotum = Birth (9th month)! Gubernaculum + Testosterone guide descent!
slides.q: By which month of intrauterine life do the testes normally reach the deep inguinal ring?
slides.why: Testes descend across the posterior abdominal wall to reach the deep inguinal ring by the 7th month and enter the scrotum by birth.

lessons.exam: Embryology IMP order: Origin (posterior abdominal wall) → Timeline (3rd, 7th, 8th, 9th months) → Factors (gubernaculum, INSL3, testosterone) → Anomalies (cryptorchidism, ectopic testis, patent processus vaginalis).
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Barr Body* & Lyon's Hypothesis

slides.h: 1. Barr Body (Sex Chromatin) & Lyon's Hypothesis of X-Inactivation
slides.p: A Barr body is a small, darkly staining plano-convex mass of condensed facultative heterochromatin attached to the inner nuclear membrane of interphase somatic cells (e.g., buccal smear, neutrophil 'drumstick'):
bullets: Number Rule: Number of Barr bodies = (Number of X chromosomes − 1). Normal female (46,XX) = 1; Normal male (46,XY) = 0; Turner's (45,X) = 0; Klinefelter's (47,XXY) = 1.

Lyon's Hypothesis (Mary Lyon, 1961): (1) Only one X chromosome is genetically active in somatic cells of females; (2) Inactivation of the second X is random (maternal or paternal X) early in embryonic life (~Day 16, blastocyst stage); (3) Inactivation is permanent and clonal in all descendants of that cell (resulting in genetic mosaicism and dosage compensation).
slides.remember: Barr Bodies = (X − 1)! Lyon's 3 Rules: Dosage compensation + Random (Day 16) + Permanent/Clonal!
slides.q: How many Barr bodies are present in the somatic cells of a patient with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)?
slides.why: Using the formula (Number of X chromosomes − 1), 47,XXY has 2 − 1 = 1 Barr body, whereas Turner's (45,X) has 0.

lessons.exam: Genetics IMP order: Definition & appearance of Barr body → Formula (N − 1) with examples → 3 postulates of Lyon's hypothesis (dosage compensation, random inactivation, clonal permanence) → Clinical significance.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Karyotyping*

slides.p: Karyotyping is the standardized photographic/digital arrangement of a person's complete chromosome complement arranged in pairs by size and centromere position:
bullets: Steps: Venous blood sample → culture T-lymphocytes with phytohemagglutinin (PHA) (mitogen) for 72 hrs at 37°C → add colchicine to arrest mitosis at metaphase (spindle inhibitor) → hypotonic KCl solution to swell cells → fix & stain (G-banding with Giemsa after trypsin).
Classification (Denver): Groups A–G based on size and centromere position (metacentric, submetacentric, acrocentric; humans have no telocentric chromosomes).
Clinical Applications: Diagnosis of Down's, Turner's, Klinefelter's syndromes, recurrent abortions, ambiguous genitalia, and Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) in CML.
slides.remember: PHA stimulates division → Colchicine arrests at Metaphase → Hypotonic KCl swells → Giemsa G-banding!
slides.q: At which stage of the cell cycle does colchicine arrest dividing lymphocytes during karyotyping?
slides.why: Colchicine inhibits mitotic spindle microtubule polymerization, arresting chromosomes at metaphase when they are maximally condensed.

lessons.exam: Genetics IMP order: Definition → Step-by-step protocol (PHA, colchicine at metaphase, hypotonic solution, G-banding) → Chromosome morphology (metacentric, submetacentric, acrocentric) → Clinical uses.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Turner's Syndrome* & Monosomy of Sex Chromosome

slides.h: 1. 45,X Karyotype, Clinical Features & Barr Body Status
slides.p: Turner's syndrome is the most common sex-chromosome monosomy (45,X / 45,XO) compatible with live birth, caused by meiotic non-disjunction (usually loss of paternal sex chromosome):
bullets: Karyotype & Barr Body: 45,X (monosomy X); Barr body negative (0).

Clinical Features: Short stature, webbed neck (pterygium colli), low posterior hairline, shield-like broad chest with widely spaced nipples, cubitus valgus, congenital lymphedema of hands/feet at birth, streak ovaries (primary amenorrhea, infertility), and coarctation of aorta / bicuspid aortic valve; normal intelligence.
slides.remember: Turner's = 45,X + 0 Barr bodies + Short stature + Webbed neck + Streak ovaries + Coarctation of aorta!
slides.q: Which cardiovascular anomaly is classically associated with Turner's syndrome (45,X)?
slides.why: Coarctation of the aorta (and bicuspid aortic valve) is a hallmark cardiac association in Turner's syndrome.

lessons.exam: Genetics IMP order: Genetic basis (45,X sex chromosome monosomy via non-disjunction) → Barr body status (0) → Cardinal clinical features (short stature, webbed neck, streak ovaries, coarctation of aorta) → Diagnosis.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Down's Syndrome* (Trisomy 21)

slides.p: Down's syndrome is the most common autosomal trisomy in live births, caused by extra chromosome 21 material:
bullets: Genetic Causes: 1. Meiotic non-disjunction (95%) — karyotype 47,XX,+21 or 47,XY,+21 (strongly linked to advanced maternal age >35 yrs); 2. Robertsonian translocation (4%) — usually t(14;21) (familial, independent of maternal age); 3. Mosaicism (1%) — 46/47,+21.

Clinical Features: Intellectual disability, hypotonia, flat facial profile, upward-slanting palpebral fissures with epicanthic folds, Brushfield spots in iris, protruding furrowed tongue, single transverse palmar crease (simian crease), sandal gap between 1st & 2nd toes, and endocardial cushion defects (AV septal defect).
slides.remember: Down's = Trisomy 21 (95% non-disjunction, 4% Robertsonian translocation) + Simian crease + Upward palpebral slant + AV septal defect!
slides.q: What percentage of Down's syndrome cases result from maternal meiotic non-disjunction (47,+21)?
slides.why: Approximately 95% of Down's syndrome cases arise from meiotic non-disjunction (47,+21), 4% from Robertsonian translocation, and 1% from mosaicism.

lessons.exam: Genetics IMP order: 3 genetic causes (95% non-disjunction, 4% Robertsonian translocation, 1% mosaicism) → Craniofacial, palmar, cardiac (AV canal defect), and GI features → Prenatal screening.
lessons.subject: Anatomy

lessons.title: Structural and Numerical Chromosome Abnormalities with Examples

slides.p: Chromosomal aberrations are divided into numerical (abnormal chromosome count) and structural (breakage and rearrangement):
bullets: Numerical Abnormalities: Euploidy/Polyploidy (exact multiples of haploid n=23: triploidy 69,XXY — lethal) vs Aneuploidy (gain/loss of individual chromosomes via non-disjunction): Trisomy (2n+1) — Down's (+21), Edwards (+18), Patau (+13), Klinefelter (47,XXY); Monosomy (2n−1) — Turner's (45,X).

Structural Abnormalities: 1. Deletion — Cri-du-chat syndrome (5p−); 2. Translocation — Reciprocal t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome in CML, Robertsonian t(14;21) in Down's; 3. Inversion (pericentric vs paracentric); 4. Ring chromosome; 5. Isochromosome — i(Xq) in Turner's; 6. Duplication.
slides.remember: Numerical = Aneuploidy (Down's +21, Turner's 45,X)! Structural = Deletion (5p− Cri-du-chat), Translocation (t9;22, t14;21), Ring, Isochromosome!
slides.q: Cri-du-chat syndrome is caused by which type of structural chromosomal abnormality?
opts: Terminal deletion of short arm of chromosome 5 (5p−)
slides.why: Cri-du-chat ('cat-cry') syndrome results from a terminal deletion on the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p−).

lessons.exam: Genetics IMP order: Classification chart → Numerical (Polyploidy vs Aneuploidy: monosomy & trisomy with examples) → Structural (Deletion, Translocation [reciprocal & Robertsonian], Inversion, Ring, Isochromosome, Duplication with examples).

lessons.title: Autosomal Dominant Inheritance

slides.p: In autosomal dominant (AD) inheritance, a single mutant allele on an autosome is sufficient to express the trait:
bullets: Pedigree Rules: Appears in every generation (vertical transmission, no skipping); affected parent transmits trait to 50% of offspring; affects males and females equally; male-to-male transmission occurs (excludes X-linked inheritance); unaffected individuals do not transmit the trait (unless reduced penetrance).
Modifying Concepts: Variable expressivity (varying severity), incomplete penetrance, and new spontaneous mutations (e.g., advanced paternal age in achondroplasia).
Examples: Marfan syndrome, Achondroplasia, Huntington's disease, Familial hypercholesterolemia, Adult polycystic kidney disease, Neurofibromatosis-1.
slides.remember: Autosomal Dominant = Vertical pedigree (no skipping) + 50% risk + Male-to-male transmission! Examples: Marfan, Achondroplasia, Huntington's!
slides.q: Which pedigree finding definitively rules out X-linked inheritance and supports autosomal dominant inheritance?
slides.why: Fathers pass only their Y chromosome (never their X) to sons, so male-to-male transmission excludes X-linked inheritance.

lessons.exam: Genetics IMP order: Definition → 5 pedigree criteria (vertical pattern, 50% recurrence risk, equal sex ratio, male-to-male transmission) → Penetrance & expressivity → 5 examples + neat pedigree chart.
